Ensure Modifications to the Respiratory Care Plan

Initiate and Conduct Patient and Family Education

questions.stem: What is the normal adult reference range for platelet count?
opts: 12–14 seconds
questions.why: Platelets 150,000–400,000/mm³. A low count means slow clotting and should be checked before an arterial puncture. 4,500–11,500/mm³ is the WBC range, 12–14 s is PT, and 0.8–1.2 is INR.

questions.stem: A troponin I level is reported as 2.1 μg/L. Relative to the reference range, this value is:
opts: Elevated; the normal value is < 0.4 μg/L
Normal; the reference range is 0.4–4.0 μg/L
Low; the normal value is > 5 μg/L
Normal for a patient older than 65
questions.why: Troponin I is normally < 0.4 μg/L. It rises 3–6 hours after the insult, peaks at 12 hours, and can persist for 7 days, making it useful for AMI/acute coronary syndrome.

questions.stem: Which B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP) result best helps RULE IN a diagnosis of congestive heart failure?
opts: > 500 pg/mL
< 20 pg/mL
4–6% of total CK
questions.why: A BNP > 500 pg/mL helps rule in CHF, whereas < 100 pg/L helps rule it out. The normal value is < 20 pg/mL. The 4–6% figure refers to CK-MB as a percentage of total CK.

questions.stem: Which set represents the normal adult arterial blood gas reference ranges?
opts: pH 7.35–7.45, PaCO₂ 35–45 torr, PaO₂ 80–100 torr, HCO₃ 22–26 mEq/L, BE 0 ± 2
pH 7.30–7.50, PaCO₂ 30–50 torr, PaO₂ 60–100 torr, HCO₃ 18–28 mEq/L, BE 0 ± 5
pH 7.35–7.45, PaCO₂ 20–30 torr, PaO₂ 100–120 torr, HCO₃ 30–35 mEq/L, BE 0 ± 2
pH 7.40–7.50, PaCO₂ 35–45 torr, PaO₂ 80–100 torr, HCO₃ 22–26 mEq/L, BE +2 to +7
questions.why: Table 1-4 gives pH 7.35–7.45, PaCO₂ 35–45 torr, PaO₂ 80–100 torr (room air), HCO₃ 22–26 mEq/L, BE 0 ± 2, and SaO₂ 95–98% on room air.

questions.stem: What is the normal carboxyhemoglobin (COHb) level in a healthy nonsmoker?
questions.why: Normal CO levels are < 1.5%. Levels of 3–6% can be normal for smokers, inner-city dwellers, and people living near industrial areas.

questions.stem: During inhaled nitric oxide (INO) therapy, what is the normal methemoglobin (metHb) level in a healthy subject?
opts: < 1.5% of total Hb
< 5% of total Hb
5–10% of total Hb
> 10% of total Hb
questions.why: Normal metHb is usually < 1.5% of total Hb. INO combines with hemoglobin to form nitrosylhemoglobin, which is rapidly oxidized to methemoglobin; excess metHb causes tissue hypoxia because it increases Hb affinity for oxygen.

questions.stem: In a patient with healthy lungs, the normal reference range for the diffusing capacity for carbon monoxide (DLCO) is:
opts: 25–30 mL/min/mm Hg
5–10 mL/min/mm Hg
40–60 mL/min/mm Hg
80–120 mL/min/mm Hg
questions.why: Normal DLCO is 25–30 mL/min/mm Hg. It is low in pulmonary fibrosis and emphysema from thickening and destruction of the alveolar surface, and may be higher than normal in polycythemia.

questions.stem: Using the basic classification of hypoxemia severity, a PaO₂ of 45 torr is categorized as:
opts: Moderate hypoxemia
Mild hypoxemia
Severe hypoxemia
Normal
questions.why: Mild hypoxemia is a PaO₂ of 60–79 torr, moderate is 40–59 torr, and severe is < 40 torr. A PaO₂ of 45 torr falls in the moderate range.

questions.stem: On a 6-minute walk test, what screening result indicates abnormal functional capacity?
opts: 6MWD < 500–600 meters
6MWD < 200 meters
6MWD > 600 meters
A pre-/post-treatment gain of ≥ 10–20%
questions.why: A 6-minute walking distance below 500–600 meters indicates abnormal functional capacity and may require further evaluation. A pre-/post-treatment gain of ≥ 10–20% describes a treatment effect, not a screening threshold.

questions.stem: A PFT result reported at 58% of predicted represents what degree of impairment?
opts: Moderate
Mild
Severe
Normal
questions.why: The percent-predicted classification is: normal 80–120%, mild 70–79%, moderate 50–69%, and severe < 49%. 58% falls in the moderate range.

questions.stem: Post-bronchodilator testing shows an increase in flows of 14%. This result indicates:
opts: Significant reversibility of airway obstruction
No significant response
A restrictive process
An invalid test requiring repetition
questions.why: An increase in flows of 12–15% or more after bronchodilator therapy suggests significant reversibility.

questions.stem: An elevated serum lactate level (normal 0.4–2.3 mEq/L) is most consistent with:
opts: Tissue hypoxia and shock
Renal failure
Liver disease or malnutrition
Metabolic alkalosis
questions.why: Lactic acid is normally 0.4–2.3 mEq/L, and a high value signals tissue hypoxia and shock. Renal failure elevates BUN, and low total protein/albumin suggests liver disease or malnutrition.

questions.stem: A patient breathing room air has pH 7.36, PaCO₂ 58 torr, PaO₂ 62 torr, HCO₃ 34 mEq/L, BE +7. This pattern is most consistent with:
opts: Fully compensated respiratory acidosis with mild hypoxemia, as seen in COPD with CO₂ retention
Uncompensated respiratory alkalosis with moderate hypoxemia
Partially compensated metabolic acidosis with normal oxygenation
Combined respiratory and metabolic acidosis with severe hypoxemia
questions.why: The pH is within 7.35–7.45 while the PaCO₂ and HCO₃ are both markedly elevated — full compensation. A PaO₂ of 62 torr on room air is mild hypoxemia. Table 1-5 lists this exact pattern for moderate to severe COPD with CO₂ retention.

questions.stem: A patient with uncontrolled diabetes has pH 7.32, PaCO₂ 28 torr, PaO₂ 108 torr on room air, HCO₃ 14 mEq/L, BE −10. The correct interpretation is:
opts: Partially compensated metabolic acidosis with normal oxygenation
Fully compensated respiratory acidosis
Uncompensated metabolic acidosis with mild hypoxemia
Partially compensated respiratory alkalosis
questions.why: The pH is low (acidemia) with a PaCO₂ of 28 torr, which is ≤ 45 torr, so the primary disturbance is metabolic acidosis. The low PaCO₂ and BE of −10 show respiratory compensation that has not returned the pH to normal, hence partial. The PaO₂ of 108 torr is not hypoxemic.

questions.stem: A patient on 2 L/min by cannula has pH 7.53, PaCO₂ 27 torr, PaO₂ 53 torr, HCO₃ 22 mEq/L. What is the most likely explanation?
opts: Uncompensated respiratory alkalosis caused by hyperventilation secondary to hypoxemia
Primary metabolic alkalosis from diuretic use
Fully compensated respiratory alkalosis
Laboratory error, because the pH and PaCO₂ are inconsistent
questions.why: A high pH with a PaCO₂ below 35 torr is a respiratory alkalosis, and the normal HCO₃ of 22 mEq/L shows it is uncompensated. Table 1-5 attributes this pattern to hyperventilation driven by the moderate hypoxemia, as occurs in pneumonia, asthma, or pulmonary embolism.

questions.stem: Using only pH and PaCO₂, a patient with pH 7.28 and PaCO₂ 33 torr has which primary acid-base disturbance?
opts: Metabolic acidosis
Respiratory acidosis
Respiratory alkalosis
Metabolic alkalosis
questions.why: With acidemia (pH < 7.35), a PaCO₂ of 45 torr or less points to metabolic acidosis; a PaCO₂ above 45 torr would indicate respiratory acidosis. Metabolic involvement is confirmed by a base excess below −2.

questions.stem: A registered nurse tells you the physician has ordered a bronchodilator treatment for a patient. You should:
opts: Verify that the order has been entered in the patient's record before proceeding
Administer the treatment because the RN is a licensed professional
Ask the RN to sign the order on the physician's behalf
Refuse all care until the physician arrives on the unit
questions.why: Orders may not be accepted from unauthorized third parties such as registered nurses. If an order reaches you through a third party, you must verify it has been entered into the record before proceeding.

questions.stem: Which order should you question as unacceptable?
opts: "Resume preoperative respiratory orders"
"Albuterol 2.5 mg in 3 mL normal saline via SVN q4h"
"O₂ at 2 L/min by nasal cannula, continuous"
"Volume control ventilation, VT 450 mL, rate 12, PEEP 5, FiO₂ 0.40"
questions.why: Blanket orders such as "continue previous medications" or "resume preoperative orders" must not be accepted. The other three orders each specify the therapy and the requisite details.

questions.stem: An order reads: "Bronchodilator therapy q6h." What is missing that makes this order incomplete?
opts: The drug name, administration route, and dose/concentration
The frequency of therapy
The date and time of the order
Nothing; the order is complete as written
questions.why: An order for a drug — including oxygen — must contain the drug name, administration route, and dose or concentration. Frequency is present here. When an element is missing, contact the originator for clarification.

questions.stem: You are authorized to accept a verbal order during an urgent situation. To complete the order correctly, you must document that:
opts: You read the order back to the originator and the originator confirmed its accuracy
A second therapist witnessed you receiving the order
The order was entered into CPOE within 24 hours
The charge nurse approved the order
questions.why: For verbal or telephone orders, you must document that you read the order back to the originator and that the originator confirmed the accuracy of the order as read back. When the provider is in the house and the situation is not an emergency, obtain a written order or CPOE instead.

questions.stem: The daughter of a patient with a written DNR order tells you her mother now wants the order revoked. You should:
opts: Immediately notify the attending physician, who must document the new request in the record
Honor the request at once and begin full resuscitation status
Explain that a DNR order cannot be revoked once written
Require the request to be submitted in writing before any action
questions.why: A patient or surrogate can change or revoke a DNR order at any time, in writing or orally. When asked to do so, you must immediately notify the attending physician, who is obliged to document the new request in the patient record.

questions.stem: Before performing an arterial puncture, which set of laboratory values would most concern you?
opts: INR 3.4, platelets 88,000/mm³
INR 1.0, platelets 250,000/mm³
WBC 13,000/mm³, hematocrit 46%
Sodium 138 mEq/L, potassium 4.2 mEq/L
questions.why: A low platelet count or abnormally prolonged PT, INR, or PTT indicates potential for excessive bleeding during invasive procedures such as ABG sampling, thoracentesis, suctioning, or bronchoscopy. Normal INR is 0.8–1.2 and normal platelets are 150,000–400,000/mm³.

questions.stem: A patient receiving frequent albuterol treatments develops premature ventricular contractions. Which laboratory value should you check first?
opts: Serum potassium
Serum sodium
Blood urea nitrogen
Total protein
questions.why: Low serum potassium may lead to dysrhythmias such as PVCs and may be associated with respiratory muscle weakness. Certain respiratory medications, albuterol among them, may lower serum potassium. Normal potassium is 3.5–5 mEq/L.

questions.stem: A patient with long-standing COPD has an elevated red blood cell count. This finding most likely reflects:
opts: Polycythemia secondary to chronic hypoxemia
Acute bacterial infection
Recent hemorrhage
Hemodilution from fluid overload
questions.why: Increased RBCs (polycythemia) may be associated with chronic hypoxemia; decreased levels are related to bleeding or anemia. An elevated WBC count with a left shift, not an elevated RBC count, suggests acute bacterial infection.

questions.stem: An anteroposterior neck radiograph on a child shows a "steeple sign." This finding is associated with:
opts: Croup
Epiglottitis
Foreign-body aspiration
Right mainstem intubation
questions.why: Tracheal edema and inflammation produce the steeple sign of croup on an AP film. Epiglottitis produces the thumb sign on a lateral neck x-ray.

questions.stem: A chest radiograph shows increased vascular markings, a cardiothoracic ratio greater than 50%, pleural effusions, and Kerley B lines. These findings are most consistent with:
opts: Congestive heart failure
Emphysema
Pneumothorax
Acute respiratory distress syndrome
questions.why: CHF produces increased vascular markings, cardiomegaly with a cardiothoracic ratio > 50%, and pleural effusions with Kerley B lines. ARDS shows nonhomogeneous bilateral opacities with a NORMAL heart size.

questions.stem: A supine chest film shows loss of peripheral lung markings, a radiolucent space between the lung margin and chest wall, and deepening of the costophrenic angle. This is:
opts: Pneumothorax, with the deep sulcus sign
Pleural effusion
Atelectasis
Consolidation
questions.why: Pneumothorax shows loss of peripheral lung markings, air between the lung margin and chest wall, possible mediastinal shift to the opposite side, and the deep sulcus sign on supine films. Atelectasis instead shifts the trachea and mediastinum TOWARD the affected side.

questions.stem: During bedside thoracic ultrasound, absence of the gliding sign indicates:
opts: Pneumothorax
Pleural effusion
Pulmonary edema
Normal pleural motion
questions.why: The gliding sign is a normal shimmering of the parietal/visceral pleural line during breathing; its absence indicates pneumothorax. Proliferation of B lines ("lung rockets") indicates interstitial/alveolar syndrome such as pulmonary edema or pneumonia, and an echo-free dark zone in a dependent region indicates pleural effusion.

questions.stem: A ventilation-perfusion scan shows multiple segmental perfusion defects without corresponding ventilation defects. This indicates:
opts: High probability of pulmonary embolism
Lobar pneumonia
Diffuse emphysema
A normal study
questions.why: A high probability of pulmonary embolism is indicated when multiple segmental perfusion defects appear without matching ventilation defects. V/Q scans are being replaced by high-resolution CT angiography, now the gold standard for diagnosing PE.

questions.stem: A mechanically ventilated patient must be transported for an MRI. The ventilator is labeled "MR Conditional." You should:
opts: Follow the manufacturer's operational protocol, which usually requires locking the device a safe distance from the magnet
Use the ventilator anywhere in the scanner room, because MR Conditional means fully compatible
Refuse transport, because only MR Safe devices may enter the facility
Disconnect the patient and manually ventilate throughout the scan
questions.why: Ventilator support during MRI requires an FDA-approved ventilator labeled either "MR Safe" or "MR Conditional." If MR Conditional, you must follow the manufacturer's operational protocol, which usually includes at least locking the device a safe distance from the MRI magnet.

questions.stem: A Glasgow Coma Scale total score of 8 or less indicates:
opts: Severe impairment (coma)
Mild impairment
Moderate impairment
A normal level of consciousness
questions.why: GCS ranges from a low of 3 (deep coma) upward. Mild impairment is 13–15, moderate is 9–12, and severe impairment (coma) is a score of 8 or less.

questions.stem: In the AVPU scale, the letter P signifies that the patient:
opts: Responds to Pain
Is Pale on inspection
Has a Patent airway
Is in Position of comfort
questions.why: AVPU stands for Alert; response to Verbal stimulus; response to Pain; Unresponsive. If the patient does not respond to verbal stimuli, firmly pinch the skin and note any response such as moaning or withdrawal.

questions.stem: Sputum production above what daily volume indicates the need for airway clearance?
opts: 30 mL/day
5 mL/day
15 mL/day
100 mL/day
questions.why: As a rule of thumb, sputum production greater than 30 mL/day indicates the need for airway clearance. Familiar measures are helpful when interviewing: a teaspoon is 5 mL, a tablespoon 15 mL, and a shot glass 1 oz or 30 mL.

questions.stem: An Apgar score is assigned at which intervals after birth?
opts: 1 and 5 minutes
Immediately and at 10 minutes
5 and 10 minutes
30 seconds and 3 minutes
questions.why: The Apgar score is used to assess neonates at 1 and 5 minutes after birth. Its five dimensions — Appearance, Pulse, Grimace, Activity, Respirations — are each rated 0 to 2 for a maximum of 10.

questions.stem: Normal gestation lasts how many weeks?
opts: 38–42 weeks
34–38 weeks
40–44 weeks
36–40 weeks
questions.why: Normal gestation lasts 38–42 weeks. An infant born at full term typically scores in the 35–45 range on the Ballard assessment, while a composite score of 10 or less indicates significant prematurity at 28 weeks or less.

questions.stem: A neck circumference above which value in men is associated with obstructive sleep apnea and difficult intubation?
questions.why: A neck circumference greater than 43 cm (17 in.) in men, or greater than 37 cm (15 in.) in women, is associated with obstructive sleep apnea, difficult endotracheal intubation, and difficult tracheostomy tube fit.

questions.stem: The normal range of diaphragm motion measured by percussion in adults is:
opts: 5–7 cm
1–2 cm
questions.why: The difference between maximum inspiratory and expiratory levels represents the full range of diaphragm motion, which in adults ranges from 5 to 7 cm. Motion is decreased in neuromuscular disorders and severe hyperinflation.

questions.stem: On a chest radiograph, the tip of an endotracheal tube should ideally be positioned:
opts: 4–6 cm above the carina, between T2 and T4
At the level of the carina
1–2 cm above the carina, at T6
Below the carina in the right mainstem bronchus
questions.why: An AP chest x-ray is the most common method used to confirm ET or tracheostomy tube placement. The tip should sit 4–6 cm above the carina, corresponding to a location between thoracic vertebrae T2 and T4, about the level of the superior border of the aortic arch.

questions.stem: Which breath sound is normally heard only over the trachea?
opts: Bronchial
Vesicular
Bronchovesicular
Stridor
questions.why: Bronchial sounds are high-pitched, loud, and tubular with an expiratory phase equal to or longer than the inspiratory phase, and are normal only over the trachea. Vesicular sounds are normal at the lung periphery; bronchovesicular sounds are normal around the upper sternum and between the scapulae.

questions.stem: A patient's Glasgow Coma Scale is recorded as "E3, V2, M2." This patient's total score and degree of impairment are:
opts: 7 — severe impairment
5 — severe impairment
7 — moderate impairment
9 — moderate impairment
questions.why: The three component scores are summed: 3 + 2 + 2 = 7. Because a total of 8 or less indicates coma, this represents severe impairment.

questions.stem: A patient rates the degree to which pain interferes with daily activities as 6 out of 10. You should:
opts: Report this finding to the patient's physician
Document it and reassess in 24 hours
Take no action, because a rating below 8 is acceptable
Repeat the assessment using the Borg Scale
questions.why: After determining severity, assess how much the pain interferes with daily activities on a 10-point scale. Whenever the interference rating is greater than 4, report the finding to the patient's physician.

questions.stem: Which scale should you use to quantify a patient's shortness of breath at the end of a 6-minute walk?
opts: The Borg Scale
The Glasgow Coma Scale
The AVPU scale
The Apgar score
questions.why: The Borg Scale is the most common method used to quantify shortness of breath or dyspnea. It runs 0 to 10 and is always applied in association with a predefined level of activity, such as an exercise test level or the end of a 6-minute walk.

questions.stem: Which combination of findings always indicates an increased work of breathing?
opts: Tachypnea, thoracic–abdominal dyssynchrony, and accessory muscle use
Bradycardia, clubbing, and pursed-lip breathing
Diaphoresis, fever, and a productive cough
Pedal edema, jugular venous distention, and an S3 heart sound
questions.why: In combination with shortness of breath, tachypnea, thoracic–abdominal dyssynchrony or paradox ("seesaw" motion), and use of accessory muscles of respiration indicate an abnormally high work of breathing.

questions.stem: A patient with diabetic ketoacidosis would most likely demonstrate which breathing pattern?
opts: Kussmaul breathing — deep and fast
Biot breathing — irregular with periods of apnea
Cheyne-Stokes breathing — waxing and waning
Prolonged inspiration
questions.why: Kussmaul breathing, which is deep and fast, is associated with diabetic ketoacidosis. Biot breathing points to increased intracranial pressure, and Cheyne-Stokes breathing to CNS disease or severe CHF.

questions.stem: A patient's chest radiograph and exam show a barrel chest with prolonged exhalation. These findings suggest:
opts: COPD with expiratory airway obstruction
Upper airway obstruction such as croup
Loss of lung volume from atelectasis
Restrictive disease from kyphoscoliosis
questions.why: Prolonged exhalation indicates expiratory obstruction as in asthma or COPD, and a barrel chest configuration is associated with COPD. Prolonged INSPIRATION instead suggests upper airway obstruction such as croup or epiglottitis.

questions.stem: Central cyanosis with a normal hemoglobin content generally first appears when the SaO₂ drops below:
opts: 80% (PaO₂ 45–50 torr)
90% (PaO₂ 60 torr)
70% (PaO₂ 35 torr)
95% (PaO₂ 80 torr)
questions.why: With normal Hb content, central cyanosis generally first appears when SaO₂ drops below 80%, corresponding to a PaO₂ of 45–50 torr. It appears as a bluish tint of the mucous membranes of the lips and mouth.

questions.stem: Why can a patient with anemia be severely hypoxic before any cyanosis appears?
opts: The intensity of cyanosis increases with the amount of hemoglobin in the blood
Anemia raises the SaO₂ above the threshold for cyanosis
Anemic patients have increased peripheral perfusion
Cyanosis depends only on cardiac output, not hemoglobin
questions.why: Regardless of type, the intensity of cyanosis increases with the amount of Hb in the blood. Patients with polycythemia can therefore look cyanotic yet still have adequate O₂ content, while anemic patients can be severely hypoxic before cyanosis ever appears.

questions.stem: A Mallampati Class IV airway means that on examination:
opts: Only the hard palate is visible
The tonsils, uvula, and soft palate are fully visible
The hard and soft palate and upper tonsils are visible
The soft and hard palate and base of the uvula are visible
questions.why: Mallampati Class IV means only the hard palate is visible, and it is associated with difficult intubation as well as a high incidence of sleep apnea. Class I is full visibility of tonsils, uvula, and soft palate.

questions.stem: A patient expectorates pink, watery, frothy secretions. This finding suggests:
opts: Pulmonary edema
Aspiration pneumonia
Tuberculosis
Asthma
questions.why: Bloody sputum that is pink, watery, and frothy suggests pulmonary edema. Red bloody sputum points to tuberculosis, lung cancer, or pulmonary infarction; yellow-to-green purulent sputum suggests aspiration pneumonia, bronchiectasis, or lung abscess.

questions.stem: A newborn has an Apgar score of 3 at 1 minute. The appropriate action is to:
opts: Begin resuscitation
Provide routine newborn care
Observe and repeat the score at 5 minutes
Administer supplemental O₂ only
questions.why: An Apgar of 7–10 is normal, 4–6 typically needs more intensive support, and 0–3 usually undergoes resuscitation. Needed interventions should never be delayed in order to obtain the Apgar score.

questions.stem: Amniotic fluid analysis shows a lecithin/sphingomyelin (L/S) ratio of 2.4 and the presence of phosphatidylglycerol. This indicates:
opts: Fetal lung maturity
Fetal lung immaturity with high risk of IRDS
An unreliable result requiring repeat testing
Post-term gestation
questions.why: Fetal maturity is indicated by an L/S ratio greater than 2, the presence of phosphatidylglycerol (PG), or an L/A ratio greater than 40.0 mg/g. These measurements are used primarily to indicate fetal lung maturity and predict infant respiratory distress syndrome.

questions.stem: During transillumination of an infant's chest, the underlying chest broadly "lights up" in an irregular fashion. This indicates:
opts: A likely pneumothorax
A normal finding
Pulmonary edema
Consolidated lung tissue
questions.why: Normally a halo of only about 1 cm forms under the light. If the underlying chest broadly lights up in an irregular fashion, a pneumothorax is likely. If the test is negative but signs persist, recommend an immediate chest x-ray.

questions.stem: A second clinician measures the apical rate as 96/min while you palpate a radial rate of 78/min. This pulse deficit most likely indicates:
opts: A cardiac arrhythmia such as atrial fibrillation, PVCs, or heart block
Severe hypovolemia
An error requiring remeasurement in the other arm
Normal sinus arrhythmia in an adult
questions.why: If the apical rate exceeds the peripheral rate, a pulse deficit exists. A pulse deficit usually indicates a cardiac arrhythmia such as atrial fibrillation or flutter, premature ventricular contractions, or heart block.

questions.stem: A pulse that weakens during inspiration (pulsus paradoxus) is associated with:
opts: Severe airway obstruction such as status asthmaticus, or cardiac tamponade
Left-sided heart failure
Aortic insufficiency or patent ductus arteriosus
Septic shock with loss of vascular tone
questions.why: Pulsus paradoxus is a variation in pulsations with the breathing cycle, with weaker pulses during inspiration, caused by severe airway obstruction such as status asthmaticus or by cardiac tamponade. Pulsus alternans, where the pulse alternates in strength beat to beat, points to left-sided heart failure.

questions.stem: You detect crepitus over the neck and chest of a mechanically ventilated patient. You should:
opts: Assess for pneumothorax, notify the physician, and recommend a chest x-ray
Document the finding as a harmless expected change
Increase PEEP to re-expand the tissue
Apply firm pressure to disperse the subcutaneous gas
questions.why: Gas leaking into tissues forms subcutaneous emphysema, which produces crepitus on palpation. Although subcutaneous emphysema itself is harmless, it often occurs with a pneumothorax, so assess for pneumothorax, communicate the finding immediately, and recommend a chest x-ray in ventilated patients.

questions.stem: Percussion over a patient's right chest produces a hollow, loud, low-pitched note. This increased resonance indicates:
opts: Hyperinflation such as acute asthma or COPD, or a pneumothorax
Pneumonia or atelectasis
Fluid in the pleural space
Normal air-filled lung tissue
questions.why: A hollow, loud, low-pitched note is increased resonance (tympanic or hyperresonant), typically indicating hyperinflation from acute asthma or COPD, or a pneumothorax. A dull or flat note occurs over increased tissue density as in pneumonia, atelectasis, or tumor.

questions.stem: Using the R-I-P-E mnemonic, adequate inspiration on a PA chest film is confirmed when the diaphragm is at the level of:
opts: The 10th posterior rib, or the 6th anterior rib on the right
The 6th posterior rib
The 3rd rib, where the clavicle lies
The 8th anterior rib
questions.why: Inspiration is adequate if the diaphragm is at the level of the 10th posterior rib — 8th to 9th posterior ribs on AP films — or the 6th anterior rib on the right. In the AP view, the clavicle should be at about the level of the third rib, which checks angulation, not inspiration.

questions.stem: A patient has a tracheal shift to the LEFT, absent breath sounds on the right, and hyperresonance to percussion on the right. The most likely problem is:
opts: Right-sided pneumothorax
Right lower lobe atelectasis
Right-sided pleural effusion with fluid
Right lower lobe pneumonia
questions.why: The trachea shifts TOWARD areas of collapse such as atelectasis and AWAY from space-occupying lesions such as pneumothoraces and large pleural effusions. A shift away from the right, with absent breath sounds and increased resonance on the right, identifies a right pneumothorax. A pleural effusion would produce decreased, not increased, resonance.

questions.stem: A bedridden older patient has an S3 gallop, pedal edema pitting to mid-calf, jugular venous distention, and bilateral basilar crackles. These findings together point to:
opts: Congestive heart failure
Acute asthma exacerbation
Tension pneumothorax
Pulmonary fibrosis
questions.why: An S3 heard in an older patient usually indicates CHF. Distended jugular veins reflect right heart failure, and gravity-dependent pitting edema is typical of chronic heart failure — the farther up the legs the edema extends, the more severe the failure.

questions.stem: A child presents with a barking cough and stridor. The AP chest film shows a steeple sign, and the lateral neck film appears normal. This is most consistent with:
opts: Croup
Epiglottitis
Foreign-body aspiration
Bronchiolitis
questions.why: In croup, the AP chest film shows the steeple sign from subglottic edema while the lateral neck film may appear normal because there is little supraglottic involvement. In epiglottitis the pattern reverses: the chest film usually appears normal and the lateral neck film shows the thumb sign from a swollen epiglottis. A barking cough is associated with croup and epiglottitis.

questions.stem: How many electrodes are actually placed on the patient to obtain a 12-lead ECG?
questions.why: There are only 10 actual leads to place, not 12. The right leg does not count as a recording lead because it is a ground. The difference is made up by the three augmented limb leads (aVR, aVL, aVF), which derive their data from the RA, LA, and LL electrodes.

questions.stem: Chest lead V4 is placed at which location?
opts: Fifth intercostal space, midclavicular line
Fourth intercostal space, right sternal border
Fifth intercostal space, midaxillary line
Fourth intercostal space, left sternal border
questions.why: V4 goes at the fifth intercostal space, midclavicular line. V1 is the fourth intercostal space at the right sternal border, V2 the fourth intercostal space at the left sternal border, V5 the fifth intercostal space at the anterior axillary line, and V6 the fifth intercostal space at the midaxillary line.

questions.stem: Low SpO₂ alarm limits are typically set at what range for adults?
questions.why: For continuous monitoring, set the low alarm according to institutional protocol, typically 90–94% for adults and 85–88% for infants.

questions.stem: PetCO₂ typically runs how much lower than the PaCO₂ in a patient without significant deadspace?
opts: 1–5 torr
10–15 torr
20 torr
They are normally identical
questions.why: Compare the monitored PetCO₂ with the patient's current arterial PCO₂. PetCO₂ typically runs 1–5 torr less than the PaCO₂, and the gap widens with high deadspace ventilation.

questions.stem: The transcutaneous sensor temperature is usually set to what value when monitoring both PtcO₂ and PtcCO₂?
questions.why: Ensure proper temperature setting — usually 44°C when monitoring PtcO₂ and PtcCO₂, with temperatures as low as 37°C adequate if monitoring only PtcCO₂.

questions.stem: The preferred site for arterial puncture is the radial artery in part because:
opts: The ulnar artery provides collateral circulation
It is the largest accessible artery
It requires no assessment of collateral flow
It lies directly adjacent to a large vein
questions.why: The radial artery is preferred because it is located near the skin surface and not close to any large veins, and because the ulnar artery provides collateral circulation. Brachial, femoral, and dorsalis pedis sites carry greater risk.

questions.stem: To reduce the likelihood of ventilator-induced lung injury, plateau pressure should generally be kept below:
opts: 30 cm H₂O
40 cm H₂O
20 cm H₂O
50 cm H₂O
questions.why: In general, plateau pressures should be kept below 30 cm H₂O during mechanical ventilation to reduce the likelihood of ventilator-induced lung injury. Pplat is measured with an inspiratory pause using a square flow pattern during volume-targeted ventilation.

questions.stem: Tracheal cuff pressures above what range can obstruct tissue blood flow and cause ulceration and necrosis?
opts: 25–30 cm H₂O
15–20 cm H₂O
35–40 cm H₂O
10–15 cm H₂O
questions.why: Cuff pressures over 25–30 cm H₂O can obstruct tissue blood flow (ischemia), causing ulceration and necrosis. If pressures are too low, leakage-type aspiration can occur, which may lead to ventilator-associated pneumonia.

questions.stem: On a neonatal apnea monitor, the apnea time alarm limit is typically set at:
opts: 15–20 seconds
5–10 seconds
30–45 seconds
60 seconds
questions.why: Set the apnea time alarm limit at typically 15–20 seconds. Low/high heart rate alarm limits are typically 80–210 for neonates, with lower limits for older babies.

questions.stem: The apnea test for brain death assesses whether breathing is stimulated by a PaCO₂ of at least:
opts: 60 torr
45 torr
50 torr
70 torr
questions.why: The apnea test is one of three major components of the neurologic evaluation for brain death. It assesses whether high levels of blood/brain CO₂ — a PaCO₂ of 60 torr or more — stimulate breathing.

questions.stem: One metabolic equivalent of task (MET) equals:
opts: 3.5 mL O₂ consumption/kg of body weight
1.0 mL O₂ consumption/kg of body weight
10 mL O₂ consumption/kg of body weight
3.5 L O₂ consumption/min
questions.why: The standard work unit for exercise testing is the MET: 1 MET equals 3.5 mL O₂ consumption per kg of body weight, about equal to normal resting O₂ consumption per minute. Most protocols increase intensity by 1–2 METs at each step-up.

questions.stem: The ATS standardized 6-minute walk test requires a walking course of what length?
opts: 30 meters, marked in 3-meter increments
100 meters, marked in 10-meter increments
50 meters, marked in 5-meter increments
6 meters, marked in 1-meter increments
questions.why: The ATS protocol specifies a walking course 30 meters in length with a clear starting line and turnaround point, and the distance marked in 3-meter increments. Equipment needed is a stopwatch, a movable chair, and a recording worksheet.

questions.stem: You cannot obtain an ECG signal. The most likely cause is:
opts: A loose, missing, or defective lead, or hair preventing skin contact
An improperly set paper speed
A patient who is hypotensive
An expired calibration certificate
questions.why: Failure to obtain a signal usually is due to a loose, missing, or defective lead or the patient's hair preventing the lead from making proper skin contact. A noisy signal instead comes from a poor electrical connection, motion artifact, or improper filtering.

questions.stem: An SpO₂ probe placed on a finger reads erratically. Which action addresses a common source of error?
opts: Remove nail polish and clean the site with an alcohol prep pad
Tighten the probe firmly to improve contact
Warm the site to 44°C before reading
Switch to the largest available probe regardless of patient size
questions.why: When selecting a site, check for adequate perfusion, remove any nail polish if applied on a finger, and clean the site with an alcohol prep pad. Note that overly tight probes may cause venous pooling with inaccurate readings or skin damage, so tightening is wrong.

questions.stem: Transcutaneous blood gas monitoring is a poor choice in which situation?
opts: An emergency, because setup and stabilization take 5–20 minutes
Noninvasive ventilation, where capnography is difficult
Continuous assessment of ventilation in a child
A neonate requiring trend monitoring of PtcCO₂
questions.why: Lengthy setup and stabilization time of 5–20 minutes makes transcutaneous monitoring a poor choice in emergencies. It should also be avoided with poor skin integrity, adhesive allergy, shock, or poor peripheral circulation. It is useful during noninvasive or high-frequency ventilation when capnography is not available.

questions.stem: To avoid burns and skin damage during transcutaneous monitoring, the sensor site should be changed:
opts: Every 2–6 hours
Every 12 hours
Every 24 hours
Only if erythema appears
questions.why: Change the sensor site frequently — every 2–6 hours — depending on the sensor temperature, infant size, and manufacturer's recommendation.

questions.stem: During peak flow measurement, how many acceptable efforts are required and which value is recorded?
opts: Repeat until three values vary by less than 10%; record the highest
Obtain three values and record the average
Obtain two values and record the lower
Obtain one maximal effort only
questions.why: The measurement should be repeated until three values are obtained that vary by less than 10%, and the highest of the three is recorded. The patient inhales fully to TLC and exhales in a sharp burst with maximum force; complete exhalation is not needed.

questions.stem: A peak flow is reported as 6 L/sec. Expressed in L/min this is:
opts: 360 L/min
60 L/min
600 L/min
100 L/min
questions.why: To convert L/sec to L/min, multiply by 60; to convert L/min to L/sec, divide by 60. Thus 6 L/sec × 60 = 360 L/min.

questions.stem: A patient breathes at 38/min with a minute ventilation of 11.4 L/min. What is the rapid shallow breathing index?
questions.why: First compute tidal volume: VT = minute ventilation ÷ frequency = 11.4 L ÷ 38 = 0.3 L. RSBI = f ÷ VT in liters = 38 ÷ 0.3 = approximately 127.

questions.stem: Unless otherwise indicated, deadspace should be assumed to be approximately:
opts: 1 mL per pound of predicted body weight
1 mL per kilogram of predicted body weight
2 mL per pound of actual body weight
150 mL regardless of size
questions.why: Unless otherwise indicated, assume a deadspace of approximately 1 mL per pound of predicted body weight. Roughly 30% deadspace ventilation is considered normal.

questions.stem: Maximum inspiratory pressure (MIP/NIF) is measured with a manometer and a one-way valve that allows:
opts: Exhalation but not inspiration, so the patient "bucks down" toward residual volume
Inspiration but not exhalation, so the patient inflates toward total lung capacity
Both inspiration and exhalation for a full minute
Neither, because the airway is fully occluded
questions.why: MIP is measured using a manometer attached to a one-way valve configured to allow exhalation but not inspiration. The patient bucks down toward residual volume on each successive breath, at which point a maximum effort is ensured — so the patient need not be conscious.

questions.stem: A modified Allen's test on the right wrist shows no flushing after 15 seconds. You should:
opts: Assess the other wrist; if both lack collateral circulation, use the brachial artery
Proceed with the right radial puncture using a smaller needle
Proceed immediately to a femoral puncture
Cancel the ABG and request a venous sample
questions.why: If collateral circulation is not present on the initial side, assess the other wrist. If both sides lack collateral circulation, use the brachial artery. On a normal test the palmar surface flushes within 5–10 seconds.

questions.stem: When drawing an ABG from an arterial line using a three-way stopcock, how much waste blood should be aspirated?
opts: 5–6 mL, at least 6 times the "dead" volume
1 mL
None; discard is unnecessary with a closed system
questions.why: With three-way stopcock sampling, attach a waste syringe, turn the stopcock off to the flush solution, and aspirate 5–6 mL of blood — at least 6 times the "dead" volume — before collecting the sample in a heparinized syringe.

questions.stem: A mixed venous sample drawn from a pulmonary artery catheter must be aspirated slowly from the distal port with the balloon deflated because:
opts: Rapid aspiration contaminates the sample with arterialized blood and falsely raises O₂ levels
Rapid aspiration causes hemolysis of red cells
Slow aspiration prevents catheter migration
The balloon must stay inflated to obtain a wedge sample
questions.why: To avoid contamination with arterialized blood and falsely high O₂ levels, the sample must be drawn slowly from the catheter's distal port with the balloon deflated. Attention must also be paid to the IV infusion rate to prevent sample dilution.

questions.stem: Capillary blood gas sampling is contraindicated in which situation?
opts: When accurate analysis of oxygenation is needed, and in neonates less than 24 hours old
Whenever arterial access is unavailable
In any infant under 1 year of age
When only acid-base status is required
questions.why: CBG sampling is used in infants and toddlers when arterial access is not available but ventilation and acid-base status must be assessed. It is contraindicated when accurate analysis of oxygenation is needed and in neonates less than 24 hours old.

questions.stem: When performing a heel stick for a capillary blood gas, you should:
opts: Warm the site for 3–5 minutes to no higher than 42–45°C and puncture the lateral side only
Warm the site to 50°C and puncture the posterior curvature
Squeeze the heel firmly to encourage blood flow
Collect the first drop of blood for analysis
questions.why: Warm the site for 3–5 minutes to no higher than 42–45°C. For heel sticks, avoid the posterior curvature and puncture the lateral side only. Wipe away the FIRST drop, collect from the middle of the blood drop, and do not squeeze the site.

questions.stem: An ABG sample cannot be analyzed for more than 30 minutes. It should be:
opts: Placed in a glass syringe chilled to 0–4°C
Left at room temperature in the plastic syringe
Frozen until analysis
Discarded and redrawn only after 2 hours
questions.why: A sample in a plastic syringe at room temperature must be analyzed in under 30 minutes. If it will be kept longer than 30 minutes, it should be in a glass syringe chilled to 0–4°C. Shunt-study samples must be run in under 5 minutes, and samples from patients with elevated leukocyte or platelet counts immediately.

questions.stem: For accurate CVP and pulmonary artery pressure measurement, the transducer must be leveled at the phlebostatic axis, which is the intersection of:
opts: The fourth intercostal space and the midaxillary line
The fifth intercostal space and the midclavicular line
The second intercostal space and the sternal border
The sixth intercostal space and the anterior axillary line
questions.why: The transducer must be at the same level as the pressure it measures. For CVP and PA pressures this is the phlebostatic axis, the intersection of the fourth intercostal space and midaxillary line.

questions.stem: A patient is receiving PEEP of 8 cm H₂O. To measure the PAWP you should:
opts: Leave the patient on PEEP and obtain the end-expiratory reading
Remove the patient from PEEP briefly to obtain a true reading
Apply a correction factor because PEEP exceeds 5 cm H₂O
Measure at end-inspiration to avoid PEEP effects
questions.why: Do not remove patients from PEEP or CPAP to measure CVP or PAWP. If PEEP is 10 cm H₂O or less, simply obtain the end-expiratory reading; a correction is applied only when PEEP exceeds 10 cm H₂O. Measurements are made at end-expiration to minimize the effect of intrathoracic pressure changes.

questions.stem: A damped arterial pressure waveform with reduced amplitude is most likely caused by:
opts: Air bubbles or a small clot partially obstructing the measurement system
The stopcock being turned off to the patient
An incorrect scale selection on the monitor
Electrical interference from nearby equipment
questions.why: Any partial obstruction in the measurement system, such as air bubbles or small clots, can dampen the pressure signal by reducing its amplitude. A stopcock off to the patient or a disconnected transducer produces an ABSENT waveform, not a damped one.

questions.stem: Which set of findings indicates a patient is ready for a spontaneous breathing trial?
opts: P/F ≥ 150–200, PEEP ≤ 5–8 cm H₂O, FiO₂ ≤ 0.4–0.5, pH ≥ 7.25, hemodynamically stable
P/F ≥ 100, PEEP ≤ 12 cm H₂O, FiO₂ ≤ 0.7, pH ≥ 7.20
Any patient able to initiate an inspiratory effort, regardless of gas exchange
questions.why: Readiness criteria include evidence of some reversal of the underlying cause of respiratory failure, adequate oxygenation (P/F ≥ 150–200, PEEP ≤ 5–8 cm H₂O, FiO₂ ≤ 0.4–0.5), pH ≥ 7.25, hemodynamic stability, and the capability to initiate an inspiratory effort.

questions.stem: After a patient tolerates the brief screening phase, the SBT should continue for:
opts: At least 30 minutes but no more than 120 minutes
5 to 10 minutes
At least 4 hours
Until the next scheduled ABG
questions.why: The screening phase is a brief supervised period of 2–5 minutes of monitored spontaneous breathing. If the patient tolerates it, continue the SBT for at least 30 minutes but no more than 120 minutes; if ABGs are acceptable and the patient remains stable, ventilation can be discontinued.

questions.stem: Why must you always adjust — never merely measure — cuff pressure when using a manometer and syringe?
opts: Attaching the manometer and syringe to the pilot line causes volume loss that lowers cuff pressure
The manometer adds volume to the cuff, raising the pressure
Measurement alone violates infection control policy
The manometer cannot display pressures below 20 cm H₂O
questions.why: Attaching a manometer and syringe to a pilot tube line causes volume loss and lowers cuff pressure; for this reason you must always adjust the pressure, never just measure it. Most hospitals, including the NBRC hospital, set 25 cm H₂O as the high-pressure limit.

questions.stem: A patient on volume control has VT 500 mL, PIP 40, Pplat 25, PEEP 5 cm H₂O, flow 60 L/min. What are the static compliance and airway resistance?
opts: Crs 25 mL/cm H₂O; Raw 15 cm H₂O/L/sec
Crs 14 mL/cm H₂O; Raw 15 cm H₂O/L/sec
Crs 25 mL/cm H₂O; Raw 0.25 cm H₂O/L/sec
Crs 20 mL/cm H₂O; Raw 10 cm H₂O/L/sec
questions.why: Crs = VT ÷ (Pplat − PEEP) = 500 ÷ (25 − 5) = 25 mL/cm H₂O. Raw = (PIP − Pplat) ÷ inspiratory flow in L/sec. Convert flow: 60 L/min ÷ 60 = 1 L/sec, so Raw = (40 − 25) ÷ 1 = 15 cm H₂O/L/sec. Note the flow must be converted from L/min to L/sec.

questions.stem: You suspect auto-PEEP in a ventilated COPD patient. Which statement correctly describes its detection?
opts: It is not visible on the normal pressure-versus-time graphic and requires an end-expiratory pause to measure
It appears as an elevated plateau pressure during an end-inspiratory hold
It is read directly from the peak inspiratory pressure
It is visible only on the pressure-volume loop
questions.why: Auto-PEEP is residual pressure above set PEEP in the alveoli due to air-trapping, and it is not visible on a normal pressure-versus-time graphic — hence the name occult PEEP. Detection requires inspecting the flow-versus-time waveform or the flow–volume loop, and measurement requires an end-expiratory pause. Patients at greatest risk have high airway resistance and high compliance on modes that limit expiratory time.

questions.stem: During sputum induction in an asthmatic patient, the FEV₁ falls 22% below the post-bronchodilator baseline. You should:
opts: Terminate the procedure
Continue and increase the saline concentration
Continue but reduce the nebulizer output
Administer a second bronchodilator and continue to 20 minutes
questions.why: Because hypertonic saline can cause bronchospasm, patients with reactive airway disease are pretreated with a fast-acting beta agonist and the FEV₁ is measured at the end of each induction attempt. Terminate the procedure if the FEV₁ falls by 20% or more from the initial post-bronchodilator value, or if signs of respiratory distress occur.

questions.stem: At a standard recording speed of 25 mm/sec, each small 1-mm box on ECG paper represents:
opts: 0.04 sec
0.20 sec
0.10 sec
0.02 sec
questions.why: At 25 mm/sec each small 1-mm box represents 0.04 sec, and each large box represents 5 × 0.04 or 0.20 sec.

questions.stem: A PR interval is considered prolonged when it exceeds:
opts: 0.20 sec
0.12 sec
0.45 sec
0.60 sec
questions.why: A PR interval greater than 0.20 sec indicates first-degree or Mobitz type I AV block. A QRS complex is widened when greater than 0.12 sec, and a QT interval is prolonged when greater than 0.45 sec.

questions.stem: The normal range for arterial oxygen content (CaO₂) is:
opts: 16–22 mL/dL
14–16 mL/dL
8–12 mL/dL
22–28 mL/dL
questions.why: Normal CaO₂ is 16–22 mL/dL, computed as (total Hb × 1.36 × SaO₂) + (0.003 × PaO₂). Normal mixed venous O₂ content is lower at 14–16 mL/dL.

questions.stem: A normal P/F ratio is:
opts: Greater than 350–380
Greater than 200
Greater than 100
Greater than 500
questions.why: A normal P/F ratio is greater than 350–380. A P/F of 200–300 indicates V/Q mismatch or mild ARDS, 100–200 indicates some shunting or moderate ARDS, and below 100 indicates refractory hypoxemia with severe shunting.

questions.stem: Normal mixed venous oxygen saturation obtained from a PA catheter is:
questions.why: Normal mixed venous values from a PA catheter are a PvO₂ of 38–42 torr, saturation of 68–77%, and content of 14–16 mL/dL. Values from a CVP catheter are typically slightly lower.

questions.stem: Compensation for a primary acid-base disturbance is described as "full" when:
opts: The pH has returned into the normal range of 7.35–7.45
The PaCO₂ has normalized
The base excess has returned to 0
The HCO₃ has returned to 24 mEq/L
questions.why: Compensation is full if the pH is in the normal range of 7.35–7.45; otherwise it is termed partial. Renal compensation for primary respiratory disorders is slow, taking hours to days, whereas respiratory compensation for metabolic disorders is fast, within minutes.

questions.stem: Using the rule of 300, an R-R interval spanning four large boxes corresponds to a heart rate of about:
opts: 75/min
100/min
60/min
150/min
questions.why: As long as the rhythm is regular, divide 300 by the number of large boxes spanned by the R-R interval. 300 ÷ 4 = 75/min.

questions.stem: Which 12-lead ECG pattern is most common in patients with chronic lung disease?
opts: Right axis deviation with right ventricular hypertrophy
Left axis deviation with left ventricular hypertrophy
Extreme right axis deviation with pathologic Q waves
Normal axis with prolonged QT interval
questions.why: The most common pattern in patients with chronic lung disease is right axis deviation with right ventricular hypertrophy. Right axis deviation shows a QRS that is negative in lead I but positive in aVF.

questions.stem: Why can a 12-lead ECG alone not diagnose a myocardial infarction?
opts: Other clinical data including patient presentation and cardiac biomarkers are required
The ECG cannot detect ST-segment changes
Axis deviation masks infarct patterns
A 12-lead ECG only records atrial activity
questions.why: The 12-lead ECG alone cannot diagnose an MI; other clinical data including patient presentation and cardiac biomarkers are needed. Distinguishing STEMI from NSTEMI matters because STEMI typically gets thrombolytic therapy and angioplasty while NSTEMI usually receives antiplatelet drugs and anticoagulants.

questions.stem: A firefighter rescued from a structure fire has an SpO₂ of 99% but appears confused. The SpO₂ is unreliable because:
opts: Carboxyhemoglobin causes standard two-wavelength oximeters to falsely overestimate saturation
Carboxyhemoglobin causes a falsely low saturation reading
Soot on the skin blocks the light signal
Oximeters cannot read above 95%
questions.why: As measured by standard two-wavelength pulse oximeters, SpO₂ overestimates oxyhemoglobin saturation when abnormal hemoglobins such as carboxyhemoglobin are present, as in smoke inhalation. Multiple-wavelength oximeters can detect HbCO.

questions.stem: Using the "40–50–60/70–80–90" rule, an SpO₂ of 80% corresponds to an approximate PaO₂ of:
opts: 50 torr
40 torr
60 torr
70 torr
questions.why: The rule of thumb pairs PaO₂ values of 40, 50, and 60 torr with SpO₂ values of 70%, 80%, and 90% respectively. An SpO₂ of 80% therefore corresponds to a PaO₂ of about 50 torr.

questions.stem: Dual pre-/postductal pulse oximetry screening for critical congenital heart defects is positive when:
opts: Both right hand and foot SpO₂ are < 95%, or the difference between them is ≥ 3%
Both readings are < 90%, or the difference is ≥ 10%
The foot reading exceeds the right hand reading by ≥ 5%
Either reading falls below 88% at any point
questions.why: Dual pulse oximetry is used to screen for critical congenital heart defects in neonates. A CCHD may be present if both right hand (preductal) and foot (postductal) SpO₂ are less than 95%, or the difference between them is 3% or more.

questions.stem: A ventilated patient's PetCO₂ suddenly drops to 0 torr. Which causes are consistent with this finding?
opts: Circuit leak or disconnection, esophageal intubation, or tube obstruction/dislodgement
Gradual hypoventilation
Malignant hyperthermia
Injection of sodium bicarbonate
questions.why: A sudden fall in PetCO₂ can result from a sudden drop in cardiac output or cardiac arrest, circuit leak or disconnection, esophageal intubation, or ET/tracheostomy tube obstruction or dislodgement — and these starred causes can drive the PetCO₂ to 0 torr. Hypoventilation and bicarbonate injection raise PetCO₂.

questions.stem: A neonate's PtcO₂ reads much lower than a simultaneously drawn PaO₂. The most likely explanation is:
opts: Poor peripheral circulation
An overheated sensor
A recent increase in FiO₂
Sensor placement on the abdomen
questions.why: If more precision is needed the PtcO₂ must be calibrated against a simultaneous PaO₂. If the PaO₂ value is substantially higher than the PtcO₂, poor peripheral circulation is the likely cause. PtcO₂ also underestimates PaO₂ when the sensor is underheated, placed on a bony surface, or when too much pressure or gel is applied.

questions.stem: Using the simplified bedside rule, a patient with normal lungs receiving 50% O₂ should have a PaO₂ of at least about:
opts: 250 torr
100 torr
150 torr
500 torr
questions.why: For rapid bedside assessment, the expected minimum PaO₂ is about five times the FiO₂ percentage. At 50% O₂ this is 5 × 50 = about 250 torr. A PaO₂ significantly lower than this estimate indicates abnormal oxygenation.

questions.stem: Working in Denver at an altitude of 5000 ft, the expected normal room-air PaO₂ is about:
opts: 75 torr
100 torr
50 torr
90 torr
questions.why: Barometric pressure drops about 5 torr per 1000 ft up to 10,000 ft. At 5000 ft the estimate is 100 − (5 × 5) = 100 − 25 = 75 torr. At 10,000 ft the PaO₂ would be about 50 torr lower than at sea level.

questions.stem: You repeat a 6-minute walk test after pulmonary rehabilitation. What improvement in 6MWD indicates the treatment was effective?
opts: At least 10–20%
At least 5%
At least 50%
Any measurable increase
questions.why: If you are using the 6MWT to assess treatment, expect at least a 10–20% improvement in the 6MWD to consider it effective. A 6MWD less than 500–600 meters screens for abnormal functional capacity but is not diagnostic of any specific condition.

questions.stem: During exercise testing to detect exercise-induced bronchospasm, a positive result is:
opts: At least a 20% drop in FEV₁ post-exercise
Any drop in FEV₁ post-exercise
A 10% drop in FVC post-exercise
A rise in breathing reserve above 30%
questions.why: If the test is being done to detect exercise-induced bronchospasm, look for at least a 20% drop in FEV₁ post-exercise. To justify pulmonary rehabilitation, VO₂max should be less than 75% of predicted with a breathing reserve of less than 30%.

questions.stem: pH 7.22, PCO₂ 65 torr, HCO₃ 26 mEq/L, BE −1 mEq/L. The interpretation is:
opts: Acute (uncompensated) respiratory acidosis
Fully compensated respiratory acidosis
Partially compensated metabolic acidosis
Combined respiratory and metabolic acidosis
questions.why: The pH is below 7.35 (acidemia) and the PCO₂ is above 45 torr, so the primary problem is respiratory acidosis. HCO₃ and BE are within normal limits, so no compensation has occurred — the disturbance is acute.

questions.stem: pH 7.35, PCO₂ 62 torr, HCO₃ 33 mEq/L, BE +7 mEq/L. The interpretation is:
opts: Fully compensated respiratory acidosis
Acute respiratory acidosis
Partially compensated respiratory acidosis
Combined respiratory acidosis and metabolic alkalosis
questions.why: PCO₂ is above 45 torr and BE is above +2, and because both have risen together compensation is occurring. The pH of 7.35 sits on the acid side but within normal limits, so the primary problem is respiratory acidosis and the compensation is complete.

questions.stem: pH 7.32, PCO₂ 24 torr, HCO₃ 12 mEq/L, BE −13 mEq/L. The interpretation is:
opts: Partially compensated metabolic acidosis
Acute metabolic acidosis
Fully compensated metabolic acidosis
Combined metabolic and respiratory acidosis
questions.why: The pH is below 7.35 with a PCO₂ under 45 torr, so the primary problem is metabolic acidosis. Because PCO₂ and BE have both fallen together, compensation is occurring — but the pH remains below the normal limit, so compensation is only partial.

questions.stem: pH 6.90, PCO₂ 100 torr, HCO₃ 19 mEq/L, BE −12 mEq/L. The interpretation is:
opts: Combined respiratory and metabolic acidosis
Fully compensated respiratory acidosis
Partially compensated respiratory acidosis
Acute metabolic acidosis with respiratory compensation
questions.why: The PCO₂ and BE are diverging in opposite directions. The PCO₂ is abnormally high, which alone would cause respiratory acidosis, and the BE is abnormally low, which alone would cause metabolic acidosis. Together they drive the pH to a lethally low level. When PaCO₂ and BE diverge, a combined disturbance exists.

questions.stem: A blood gas shows PaCO₂ and BE both abnormally LOW, with a pH of 7.48. The primary disturbance is:
opts: Respiratory alkalosis with metabolic compensation
Metabolic acidosis with respiratory compensation
Combined respiratory and metabolic alkalosis
Combined respiratory and metabolic acidosis
questions.why: Compensation is occurring when both the PaCO₂ and BE are abnormally high or low in the same direction. Once that is established, look at the pH: above 7.40 the primary problem is the one causing alkalosis — here the low PaCO₂, a respiratory alkalosis. Because the pH is outside 7.35–7.45, compensation is partial.

questions.stem: A patient breathing 100% O₂ has a P(A-a)O₂ of 300 torr. The approximate percent shunt is:
questions.why: Rule of thumb: when breathing 100% oxygen, every 100 torr of P(A-a)O₂ difference equals about a 5% shunt. Here 300 ÷ 100 = 3, and 3 × 5 = approximately 15%.

questions.stem: A ventilated patient has a PaO₂ of 76 torr on an FiO₂ of 0.60. The P/F ratio and its meaning are:
opts: 127 — some shunting, consistent with moderate ARDS
127 — normal oxygenation
46 — refractory hypoxemia with severe shunting
211 — V/Q mismatch or mild ARDS
questions.why: P/F = PaO₂ ÷ FiO₂ = 76 ÷ 0.60 = about 127. A P/F of 100–200 indicates some shunting and moderate ARDS. Normal is greater than 350–380; below 100 is refractory hypoxemia with severe shunting.

questions.stem: An a/A ratio is calculated as 0.28. This indicates:
opts: Hypoxemia due to shunting
Normal oxygenation
Hypoxemia likely due to V/Q mismatch
An invalid calculation
questions.why: A normal a/A ratio is greater than 0.75. A ratio of 0.35–0.75 indicates hypoxemia likely due to V/Q mismatch, and a ratio below 0.35 indicates hypoxemia due to shunting.

questions.stem: A neonate on mechanical ventilation has an oxygenation index of 45. This indicates:
opts: High mortality; an indication for ECMO
Normal oxygenation
Moderate RDS with a P/F below 200
Severe hypoxemia that may justify HFOV
questions.why: A normal OI is less than 5–8. An OI of about 20 indicates severe hypoxemia and may justify HFOV in neonates, while an OI greater than 40 carries high mortality and is an indication for ECMO.

questions.stem: A patient's mixed venous saturation falls from 70% to 45% with a stable hemoglobin. This indicates:
opts: Impaired tissue oxygenation from decreased O₂ delivery or increased O₂ consumption
Improved cardiac output
Decreased oxygen demand from hypothermia
A normal physiologic variation
questions.why: With a normal Hb level, a mixed venous saturation below 50% or a PvO₂ below 27 torr indicates impaired tissue oxygenation. Mixed venous O₂ falls if O₂ delivery decreases or O₂ consumption increases — for example from anemia, hypoxemia, low cardiac output, hyperthermia, trauma, shivering, or seizures.

questions.stem: A septic patient has a HIGH mixed venous oxygen saturation despite clinical signs of tissue hypoxia. The best explanation is:
opts: In sepsis and cyanide poisoning, mixed venous O₂ can exceed normal even with tissue hypoxia, so lactate is a better indicator
Sepsis always increases cardiac output enough to correct tissue hypoxia
The sample was contaminated with arterialized blood
High mixed venous saturation rules out tissue hypoxia
questions.why: In both cyanide poisoning and sepsis, mixed venous oxygen can be higher than normal even if tissue hypoxia is present. For this reason, in patients with pathologic conditions that decrease O₂ demand, mixed venous lactate may be a better indicator of tissue oxygenation.

questions.stem: A comprehensive exercise capacity test shows a breathing reserve of 22% with desaturation during exercise, a normal anaerobic threshold, and a normal O₂ pulse. This points to:
opts: A pulmonary disorder limiting exercise capacity
A cardiovascular disorder limiting exercise capacity
Poor physical conditioning
A normal study
questions.why: A pulmonary limitation is characterized by a breathing reserve below 30% with desaturation common. A cardiovascular disorder instead shows a decreased anaerobic threshold, decreased O₂ pulse, and decreased HRmax, while poor conditioning shows a normal anaerobic threshold.

questions.stem: Which test should be recommended to detect an ACTIVE tuberculosis infection?
opts: Serial sputum specimen collection for acid-fast bacilli stain
Mantoux tuberculin skin test
Chest x-ray alone
Allergy skin testing
questions.why: A tuberculin skin test is recommended for diagnosis of a LATENT TB infection, whereas serial sputum specimen collection for AFB stain is recommended to detect an ACTIVE infection. Chest x-ray and interferon-gamma release assays can be recommended concurrently to help confirm the diagnosis.

questions.stem: What is the only major contraindication to bronchoalveolar lavage?
opts: A predisposition for bleeding
Nonresolving pneumonia
Interstitial lung disease
Suspected ventilator-associated pneumonia
questions.why: The only major contraindication to BAL is a predisposition for bleeding. BAL is indicated in nonresolving pneumonia, unexplained lung infiltrates, suspected alveolar hemorrhage, and interstitial lung disease, and is a key tool for diagnosing bacterial VAP.

questions.stem: Exhaled CO readings below what level signify nonsmoking status?
opts: 6–8 ppm
20 ppm
1 ppm
15 ppm
questions.why: Readings below 6–8 ppm signify nonsmoking status, with values below 3–4 ppm typically confirming true smoking abstinence. Readings above 6–8 ppm indicate smoking has likely occurred within the past 12–24 hours.

questions.stem: During CPR, PetCO₂ remains low at what level when blood flow to the lungs is poor or absent?
opts: Less than 10 torr
Less than 25 torr
Less than 35 torr
Less than 45 torr
questions.why: The utility of capnography during CPR rests on PetCO₂ correlating well with cardiac output. With poor or absent blood flow to the lungs, PetCO₂ levels remain low — under 10 torr. With effective compressions or restored cardiac function, PetCO₂ rises.

questions.stem: A post-bronchodilator improvement in peak expiratory flow rate of what magnitude is considered significant?
opts: 12% or more
5% or more
25% or more
50% or more
questions.why: A post-bronchodilator improvement of 12% or more is considered significant. PEFR is used to monitor airway tone over time via diary and to assess changes in response to bronchodilator therapy, though FEV spirometry is preferred.

questions.stem: Limited polysomnography for in-home assessment monitors up to how many key parameters?
opts: Seven
Three
Twelve
Twenty
questions.why: Limited PSG has mostly replaced overnight oximetry for in-home assessment of sleep disorders. It monitors up to seven key parameters including SpO₂, airflow, and respiratory effort, though it does not assess sleep stages.

questions.stem: A patient shows evidence of tissue hypoxia despite a normal PaO₂ and SpO₂. Which tests should you recommend?
opts: Hemoglobin/hematocrit, hemoximetry, and lactic acid
White blood cell count and blood cultures
d-Dimer and ischemia-modified albumin
Liver enzymes and a drug-screening panel
questions.why: For tissue hypoxia with a normal PaO₂ and SpO₂, recommend Hb and Hct to determine O₂-carrying capacity, hemoximetry to assess actual SaO₂ and abnormal saturations such as HbCO and metHb, and lactic acid to assess for tissue hypoxia and anaerobic metabolism.

questions.stem: A postoperative patient develops sudden dyspnea, hemoptysis, chest pain, and tachycardia. Which tests should you recommend?
opts: d-Dimer, ischemia-modified albumin, and arterial blood gases
Liver enzymes and bilirubin
Thyroid-stimulating hormone and glucose
Urinalysis and glomerular filtration rate
questions.why: These are signs of pulmonary embolism. Recommend a d-Dimer test, ischemia-modified albumin, and arterial blood gases to assess the degree of hypoxemia.

questions.stem: A patient's urine output falls below 25 mL/h. Which tests should you recommend?
opts: Urinalysis, electrolytes, BUN and creatinine, and glomerular filtration rate
Cardiac biomarkers and electrolytes
Platelet count and coagulation measures
Blood culture and sensitivities
questions.why: Decreased (under 25 mL/h) or absent urine output over time is oliguria. Recommend urinalysis for specific gravity and pH, electrolytes, BUN and creatinine to assess for possible renal disease or failure, and glomerular filtration rate.

questions.stem: Which chest x-ray position should be recommended for an ambulatory outpatient?
opts: Posteroanterior (PA), standing upright with a deep breath
Anteroposterior (AP) portable
Lateral decubitus
Supine AP
questions.why: PA films are recommended for ambulatory patients, who stand upright and take a deep breath. The AP projection is most commonly used for ICU portable films, and lateral views combined with AP or PA films help assess for pleural effusions.

questions.stem: Thoracic MRI is contraindicated in patients with:
opts: Pacemakers, metallic surgical clips or heart valves, or infusion pumps
Suspected aortic aneurysm
Posterior mediastinal masses
An allergy to radiographic contrast media
questions.why: MRI is contraindicated in patients with pacemakers, metallic surgical clips or heart valves, or infusion or chemotherapy pumps. Ventilatory support must be provided by a manual all-plastic resuscitator or a ventilator certified for MRI use. MRI is actually recommended for staging lung cancer in patients allergic to contrast media.

questions.stem: Why is transthoracic ultrasound ineffective for imaging through aerated lung tissue?
opts: Ultrasound is generally ineffective at imaging tissues or organs through aerated lung or a pneumothorax
The probe frequency is too low for lung tissue
Rib shadows block the entire thorax
Lung tissue reflects no sound at all
questions.why: Transthoracic ultrasound is generally ineffective in imaging tissues or organs through aerated lung tissue or pneumothorax. It is useful for detecting free fluid, pneumothorax, atelectasis, consolidation, and for guiding thoracentesis and needle biopsies.

questions.stem: According to the AARC, bronchoscopy should be avoided in patients who:
opts: Cannot be adequately oxygenated, have an uncorrectable bleeding disorder, severe obstructive airway disease, severe refractory hypoxemia, or are hemodynamically unstable
Have recurrent atelectasis
Have unexplained hemoptysis
Require selective mainstem intubation
questions.why: The AARC advises against bronchoscopy in patients who cannot be adequately oxygenated during the procedure, have a bleeding disorder that cannot be corrected, have severe obstructive airway disease, have severe refractory hypoxemia, or are hemodynamically unstable. Recurrent atelectasis, hemoptysis, and selective intubation are indications, not contraindications.

questions.stem: Which pulmonary function test should be recommended to differentiate among chronic bronchitis, emphysema, and asthma in a patient with an obstructive pattern?
opts: Carbon monoxide diffusing capacity (DLCO)
Maximum voluntary ventilation (MVV)
Peak expiratory flow rate (PEFR)
Bronchial provocation testing
questions.why: DLCO is recommended to differentiate among chronic bronchitis, emphysema, and asthma in patients with obstructive patterns. It is also used to follow interstitial lung diseases, evaluate drugs known to cause pulmonary damage such as amiodarone and bleomycin, and help predict arterial desaturation during exercise.

questions.stem: A methacholine challenge test should be recommended to:
opts: Assess the presence and severity of airway hyperreactivity
Measure the degree of hyperinflation
Quantify total lung capacity
Assess respiratory muscle strength
questions.why: Bronchial provocation such as the methacholine challenge test is recommended to assess the presence and severity of airway hyperreactivity, evaluate occupational asthma, determine the relative risk of developing asthma, and assess response to therapeutic interventions.

questions.stem: A patient requires accurate measurement of carboxyhemoglobin after smoke inhalation. You should recommend:
opts: Hemoximetry (CO-oximetry)
Standard ABG analysis alone
Pulse oximetry
Transcutaneous PO₂ monitoring
questions.why: Standard ABG analysis does not measure actual Hb content, Hb saturation, or abnormal hemoglobins such as HbCO or metHb. The most common scenario for recommending hemoximetry is smoke inhalation or CO poisoning; it is also used during inhaled nitric oxide therapy to monitor metHb.

questions.stem: Which monitoring method is the best way to assess for hyperoxemia in an infant and help prevent retinopathy of prematurity?
opts: Transcutaneous PtcO₂ monitoring
Pulse oximetry
Capnography
Standard ABG sampling every 4 hours
questions.why: PtcO₂ monitoring is most accurate in infants, less so in children and adults. Infant PtcO₂ monitoring is the best way to assess for hyperoxemia and help prevent retinopathy of prematurity. Pulse oximetry should be recommended AGAINST when there is a need to monitor for hyperoxemia.

questions.stem: To assess V/Q relationships, deadspace, and CO₂ production, you should recommend:
opts: Volumetric capnography
Standard capnometry
Transcutaneous PCO₂ monitoring
Overnight oximetry
questions.why: Volumetric capnography simultaneously measures expired CO₂ levels and tidal volumes, allowing computation of deadspace and CO₂ production. There is some evidence these measurements can also be used to titrate PEEP levels in ventilated patients.

questions.stem: An exhaled CO reading of 48 ppm corresponds to an approximate HbCO saturation of:
questions.why: To estimate HbCO% from exhaled CO, divide the CO concentration in ppm by 6. Here 48 ÷ 6 = about 8%.

questions.stem: Why should a higher exhaled CO cutoff of 10–11 ppm be applied to patients with asthma or COPD?
opts: Airway inflammation boosts endogenous CO production
These patients exhale less total volume
Bronchodilators artificially raise CO readings
Their CO analyzers require different calibration
questions.why: A higher cutoff of 10–11 ppm should be applied to patients with inflammatory lung diseases such as asthma or COPD because inflammation boosts endogenous CO production.

questions.stem: Allergy skin testing should NOT be performed routinely on which patient?
opts: A patient with poorly controlled asthma, who is at high risk for anaphylaxis
A patient with suspected penicillin allergy
A patient with suspected latex allergy
A patient with allergic rhinitis and conjunctivitis
questions.why: Skin testing should not be performed routinely on patients at high risk for an anaphylactic reaction, such as those with poorly controlled asthma, or on those taking medications that interfere with the IgE immune response such as antihistamines, steroids, and anti-IgE antibodies like omalizumab. Penicillin and latex allergy are supported indications.

questions.stem: A patient has had a thoracentesis in which fluid was aspirated without difficulty. Regarding a post-procedure chest x-ray, the American College of Radiology recommends:
opts: A chest x-ray only if a pneumothorax is suspected, such as when air rather than fluid is aspirated
A routine chest x-ray after every thoracentesis
A chest x-ray only after 24 hours
No chest x-ray under any circumstances
questions.why: Although performing a chest x-ray after thoracentesis is common practice, the American College of Radiology recommends it only if a pneumothorax is suspected — for example if air rather than fluid is aspirated. Similarly, routine daily chest x-ray is no longer recommended to monitor mechanically ventilated patients.

questions.stem: In a patient with confirmed asthma, fractional exhaled nitric oxide (FeNO) analysis can be recommended to:
opts: Predict corticosteroid response, titrate anti-inflammatory medication, monitor control, predict exacerbation, and monitor adherence
Measure total lung capacity
Quantify airway resistance
Screen for critical congenital heart defects
questions.why: NO concentration increases in the presence of airway inflammation, particularly in asthma. In patients with confirmed asthma, exhaled NO analysis can predict the response to corticosteroids, titrate anti-inflammatory medication, monitor the level of asthma control, predict impending exacerbation, and monitor medication adherence.

questions.stem: A ventilated patient is being transported. Regarding capnography during transport:
opts: It is required for monitoring the adequacy of ventilation during transport of mechanically ventilated patients
It is optional if pulse oximetry is in use
It should be replaced by transcutaneous monitoring
It is contraindicated during movement due to artifact
questions.why: Monitoring the adequacy of ventilation in patients receiving mechanical ventilation is an indication for capnography, and it is required during transport of mechanically ventilated patients. Transcutaneous monitoring is a poor substitute here because of lengthy setup times.

questions.stem: Documented hypoxemia warranting O₂ therapy is defined as:
opts: PaO₂ < 60 torr or SaO₂ < 90% on room air
PaO₂ < 80 torr or SaO₂ < 95% on room air
PaO₂ < 50 torr or SaO₂ < 85% on room air
PaO₂ < 70 torr on any FiO₂
questions.why: Select or recommend O₂ therapy for patients with documented hypoxemia — a PaO₂ below 60 torr or SaO₂ below 90% on room air — or signs of hypoxemia such as dyspnea, tachypnea, tachycardia, cyanosis, or confusion.

questions.stem: What total flow should generally be provided to ensure a stable FiO₂ from an air-entrainment device?
opts: At least 40 L/min
At least 15 L/min
At least 60 L/min
At least 10 L/min
questions.why: In general, the best way to ensure a stable FiO₂ is to provide a total flow of at least 40 L/min. For an input flow of 10 L/min this occurs only at or below the 40% setting.

questions.stem: All air/oxygen blenders require what gas source pressure?
opts: 50 psi air and oxygen
35 psi air and oxygen
2200 psi air and oxygen
15 psi air and oxygen
questions.why: All blenders require a 50-psi air and oxygen source. Most blenders output 50 psi at the set O₂%, which can power respiratory equipment directly or control flow to the patient via a flowmeter.

questions.stem: Most oxygen concentrators produce what concentration of oxygen and at what maximum flow?
opts: About 90–95% O₂ at flows up to 10 L/min
About 100% O₂ at flows up to 15 L/min
About 80% O₂ at flows up to 6 L/min
About 70% O₂ at flows up to 4 L/min
questions.why: An O₂ concentrator physically separates the O₂ in room air from nitrogen. Most use sodium-aluminum silicate pellets to absorb nitrogen, CO₂, and water vapor, producing about 90–95% O₂ at flows up to 10 L/min.

questions.stem: One liter of liquid oxygen vaporizes into approximately how much gaseous oxygen?
questions.why: Since 1 L of liquid O₂ vaporizes into 860 L of gaseous O₂, LOX systems are an efficient way to store supplemental O₂. Separately, 1 pound of LOX equals approximately 344 L of gaseous O₂ at normal operating pressures.

questions.stem: Oxygen-conserving devices reduce O₂ usage by approximately:
questions.why: All O₂-conserving devices minimize the O₂ waste that occurs during exhalation with standard nasal cannulas. They can reduce O₂ usage by 50–75%, doubling or tripling the duration of flow from bulk sources.

questions.stem: What input gas flow produces optimal particle size from a small-volume nebulizer?
opts: 6–8 L/min
2–4 L/min
10–12 L/min
15 L/min
questions.why: An SVN delivers small volumes (2.5–4 mL) of respirable aerosol in the 1–5 micron range, and the input gas flow should be 6–8 L/min for optimal particle size.

questions.stem: Using the open-mouth pMDI technique, the inhaler is positioned how far from the mouth?
opts: 4 cm, about two finger widths
1 cm
10 cm
Directly against the lips
questions.why: With the open-mouth technique the MDI is positioned 4 cm — about two finger widths — away from the open mouth, with the tongue kept down. With the closed-mouth technique the MDI is placed between the lips with the tongue down.

questions.stem: After actuating a pMDI, the patient should hold their breath for:
opts: 10 seconds
3 seconds
30 seconds
1 minute
questions.why: Have the patient hold the breath for 10 seconds to allow maximum drug deposition, and wait about 1 minute between puffs.

questions.stem: Dry-powder inhalers require what inspiratory flow compared to an MDI?
opts: Higher flows, greater than 60 L/min
Lower flows, less than 30 L/min
The same flow as an MDI
Flow is irrelevant for a DPI
questions.why: Higher inspiratory flows greater than 60 L/min are needed for a DPI compared to an MDI. Timing and coordination are not needed because the drug only moves with inspiratory flow — there is no propellant — and a breath-hold is encouraged but not required.

questions.stem: Typical HFNC flow settings for an infant are:
opts: 1–8 L/min
1–20 L/min
1–40 L/min
10–30 L/min
questions.why: HFNC flow settings depend on patient age and size: adults 1–40 L/min or higher, children 1–20 L/min, and infants 1–8 L/min.

questions.stem: A full oxygen cylinder is assumed to be at what pressure when computing duration of flow?
opts: 2200 psi
50 psi
1000 psi
3000 psi
questions.why: Duration-of-flow calculations assume a full cylinder is at 2200 psi. Cylinder filling pressures may vary, so always check before computing.

questions.stem: Which change will INCREASE the FiO₂ delivered by a low-flow oxygen system?
opts: A lower patient inspiratory flow
A higher patient tidal volume
A faster rate of breathing
A leak in the mask
questions.why: Less air dilution and a higher FiO₂ result from higher O₂ flow input, a reservoir present, no leak, and valves present on the device side; and from a lower inspiratory flow, lower tidal volume, slower breathing rate, and lower minute ventilation on the patient side.

questions.stem: Obstructing the entrainment port of an air-entrainment device results in:
opts: A higher delivered O₂ concentration but a lower total flow
A lower O₂ concentration and higher total flow
