No change in either concentration or flow
A higher O₂ concentration and higher total flow
questions.why: Obstructing an entrainment device's entrainment port decreases air entrainment, producing a higher delivered O₂ concentration but a lower overall flow, with an unpredictable effect on the actual inspired O₂ concentration reaching the patient.

questions.stem: A high-flow oxygen device must be titrated by changing:
opts: The FiO₂, not the flow
The flow, not the FiO₂
Either the flow or the FiO₂ interchangeably
The patient's minute ventilation
questions.why: High-flow devices must be titrated by changing FiO₂, not flow. Reducing the flow leaves the FiO₂ unchanged but may make it insufficient to meet inspiratory demand, so delivered O₂ becomes variable. With a reservoir system, flow reductions can also cause CO₂ rebreathing and suffocation.

questions.stem: At an FiO₂ of 0.24, each 1 L/min set on the flowmeter produces approximately how much total output?
opts: 26 L/min
1.3 L/min
10 L/min
4 L/min
questions.why: The lower the FiO₂, the higher the total output of an air-entrainment device. At 0.24 FiO₂, for every 1 L/min set on the flowmeter there is 26 L/min of output; at 0.8 FiO₂ the output is only 1.3 L/min per L/min set.

questions.stem: An air-entrainment nebulizer set at 60% cannot meet an ICU patient's high inspiratory demand. The best correction is:
opts: Connect two air-entrainment nebulizers in parallel to double the flow
Reduce the O₂ input flow to increase entrainment
Obstruct the entrainment port to raise the FiO₂
Switch to a simple mask at 10 L/min
questions.why: Total output flow can be increased somewhat by raising O₂ input flow, but backpressure at the jet limits this to typically 12–15 L/min. An alternative is to combine two air-entrainment nebulizers, which doubles the flow so the mist does not disappear on inspiration.

questions.stem: A blender sounds a loud, high-pitched alarm after both gas hoses are connected. Your first steps should be:
opts: Verify both gas sources are at the required inlet pressures, usually ≥ 35 psig, and check for leaks
Immediately replace the blender
Disconnect the air hose to silence the alarm
Increase the flowmeter setting
questions.why: If a blender pressure alarm sounds after both gas sources are attached, verify that both gas sources are at the required inlet pressures — usually at least 35 psig — then check for leaks between the gas source and the blender. If these check out, replace the blender.

questions.stem: How does a high-flow nasal cannula benefit a patient with hypercapnia?
opts: It washes out CO₂ from upper airway deadspace, decreasing ventilatory demand
It chemically absorbs CO₂ in the humidifier
It increases anatomic deadspace
It raises the PaCO₂ set point
questions.why: For patients with hypercapnia, a high-flow nasal cannula can decrease ventilatory demand by washing out CO₂ from upper airway deadspace. High flows can also produce CPAP, which may benefit neonates and infants with hypoxemic respiratory failure.

questions.stem: An unstable COPD patient requires a precise low FiO₂. The best device is:
opts: An air-entrainment mask at 24 or 28%
A nasal cannula at 2 L/min
A nonrebreathing mask at 10 L/min
A simple mask at 6 L/min
questions.why: For an unstable COPD patient requiring a precise low FiO₂, the recommended system is an air-entrainment mask at 24 or 28%. A nasal cannula and simple mask are variable-performance low-flow devices.

questions.stem: A patient arrives in the emergency department with chest pain and suspected MI. The recommended O₂ system is:
opts: A nonrebreathing mask at > 10 L/min or a high-flow nasal cannula at ≥ 20 L/min at 100%
A nasal cannula at 2 L/min
An air-entrainment mask at 28%
A tracheostomy collar at 35%
questions.why: For a patient admitted to the ED with chest pain and suspected MI, recommend a nonrebreathing mask at greater than 10 L/min, or a high-flow nasal cannula at 20 L/min or more at 100%.

questions.stem: An infant requires a high FiO₂ with temperature control. The recommended system is:
opts: An oxyhood at 6–8 L/min with servo-controlled heated humidification, or a high-flow nasal cannula at 1–8 L/min
A simple O₂ mask
A nasal cannula at ¼–2 L/min
A partial rebreathing mask
questions.why: For an infant requiring high FiO₂ and temperature control, recommend an oxyhood at 6–8 L/min with a servo-controlled heated humidification system, or a high-flow nasal cannula at 1–8 L/min. A simple O₂ mask suits an infant needing short-term moderate O₂.

questions.stem: An infant oxyhood meets the definition of a high-flow device when used at:
opts: The recommended flow of 6–8 L/min
Any flow above 2 L/min
Flows above 15 L/min
Only when combined with a blender
questions.why: Although technically a reservoir system, the infant oxyhood meets the definition of a high-flow device when used at the recommended flow of 6–8 L/min.

questions.stem: When opening a cylinder valve you should:
opts: Open it all the way, then turn back half a turn to prevent valve freezing
Open it only a quarter turn
Open it rapidly to seat the seal
Leave it half open during use
questions.why: Slowly open the cylinder valve all the way and then turn back half a turn to prevent valve freezing when fully open. Then record the pressure and compute flow duration.

questions.stem: You hear a hissing sound from a cylinder regulator. The most likely cause is:
opts: A loose connection or missing/damaged washers on the PISS regulator
Normal pressure equalization
An overfilled cylinder
Condensation in the valve stem
questions.why: If you hear the tank leaking with a hissing sound, check for a loose connection or missing or damaged washers on PISS regulators.

questions.stem: Which flowmeter should be used on a cylinder during patient transport?
opts: A Bourdon gauge or integrated regulator/variable-orifice flow controller, because they are unaffected by gravity
A back-pressure-compensated Thorpe tube
Any uncompensated Thorpe tube
No flowmeter is needed during transport
questions.why: When using cylinders for transport, use a flowmeter unaffected by gravity — either a Bourdon gauge or an integrated regulator/variable orifice flow controller such as the Praxair Grab 'n Go or Western Medica Oxytote.

questions.stem: A ventilated patient must be transported for an MRI. Regarding the gas equipment, you must:
opts: Use iron-free equipment such as aluminum cylinders and carts and brass or aluminum regulators
Use standard steel cylinders secured to the wall
Remove all regulators and bag the patient by mouth
Use any cylinder provided it is chained to a cart
questions.why: If the patient is being transported for an MRI study, you must use iron-free equipment — for example aluminum cylinders and carts, and brass and aluminum regulators. A ventilator certified for MRI use is also required.

questions.stem: Why can most pulse-dose-only portable oxygen concentrators be inadequate in an airliner cabin?
opts: Only continuous-flow units can provide more than 30% O₂, which is needed at high altitude
Pulse-dose units cannot run on battery power
Cabin pressure disables the sensing circuit
Pulse-dose units deliver more than the prescribed dose at altitude
questions.why: Most POCs deliver O₂ only in pulse-dose mode, which suffices for those with low O₂ needs of 30% or less. In general, only continuous-flow units can provide more than 30% O₂, which is needed to provide adequate FiO₂ at high altitudes such as in airliner cabins.

questions.stem: When connecting a portable oxygen concentrator, the preferred order of power sources is:
opts: AC first, auto-DC next, battery last
Battery first, AC next, DC last
DC first, battery next, AC last
Any order; all provide equal output
questions.why: Connect the unit to the best available power source — AC first, auto-DC next, battery last. After start-up the unit should reach maximum O₂ output in approximately 1–2 minutes.

questions.stem: If an oxygen-conserving (demand-flow) device fails, the patient must switch to:
opts: A continuous O₂ source at 2–3 times the conserving device flow
The same flow on a continuous source
Half the conserving device flow
Room air until a replacement arrives
questions.why: Pulse-dose and demand-flow systems use sensors to trigger a valve delivering O₂ only during inspiration, and flow must be individually adjusted to achieve the desired SpO₂. If the device fails, the patient must switch to a continuous O₂ source at 2–3 times the conserving device flow.

questions.stem: A demand-flow device is delivering oxygen continuously rather than in pulses. The likely cause is:
opts: The unit is in bypass mode from failure to sense inspiration, or the selector is set to continuous flow
The oxygen source is empty
The delivery tubing is kinked
The cannula is too large for the patient
questions.why: Oxygen delivered continuously means the unit is in bypass mode due to failure to sense inspiration, and/or the selector knob is set to continuous flow mode. Reset by turning the unit off then on, check the cannula and tubing connections, adjust the cannula fit, and confirm the selector is set to pulse.

questions.stem: Infant CPAP prongs that are too LARGE can cause:
opts: Tissue erosion
Difficulty maintaining the prescribed pressure
Excessive deadspace
Auto-triggering
questions.why: A proper fit is essential for pressure maintenance and patient tolerance. Prongs that are too small can cause difficulty maintaining the prescribed pressure, whereas prongs that are too large can cause tissue erosion.

questions.stem: Which nebulizer is preferred for delivering medication to a mechanically ventilated patient?
opts: A vibrating-mesh nebulizer, because it adds no additional flow or volume to the circuit
A large-volume air-entrainment nebulizer
A standard jet SVN at 8 L/min
A continuous nebulizer with an external flowmeter
questions.why: A vibrating-mesh nebulizer creates aerosol droplets by vibration and needs inspiratory or circuit flow to deliver. It is preferred with mechanically ventilated patients because no additional flow or volume is introduced into the circuit.

questions.stem: Aerosol mist from a large-volume nebulizer disappears during the patient's inspiration. Appropriate corrections include:
opts: Maximize input flow, add an open reservoir to the expiratory side of the T-tube, or connect multiple nebulizers in parallel
Reduce the input flow to conserve gas
Obstruct the entrainment port
Switch to a dry-powder inhaler
questions.why: Mist disappearing during inspiration reflects inadequate flow relative to the patient's inspiratory demand. Corrections are to maximize input flow, add an open reservoir to the expiratory side of the T-tube, connect multiple nebulizers in parallel, or use a gas injection nebulizer.

questions.stem: Why should plastic spacers and valved holding chambers be air dried rather than towel dried?
opts: Manual drying can generate an electrostatic charge that draws medication to the chamber walls
Towels leave lint that blocks the valve
Manual drying warps the plastic
Air drying sterilizes the device
questions.why: Manually drying plastic spacers and chambers may generate an electrostatic charge on their surface that draws medication to the insides of the chamber or spacer. Most manufacturers recommend periodic cleaning with soap and water and letting them air dry.

questions.stem: During a ventilator pre-use check, why must you never use a "cheater hose" in place of the actual circuit?
opts: The actual circuit must be checked for leaks, have its compressible volume measured and compensated, and withstand the applied flow and pressure
Cheater hoses are not approved for sterilization
The ventilator cannot detect a cheater hose
Cheater hoses add excessive deadspace
questions.why: Never use a cheater hose for the pre-use check. Use the actual circuit so it can be checked for leaks, measured and compensated for compressible volume, and so you can ensure the circuit withstands the flow and pressure applied during the check.

questions.stem: A ventilated patient triggers multiple alarms and you cannot immediately identify the cause. Your FIRST action is to:
opts: Remove the patient from the ventilator and support them with a manual resuscitator with a PEEP valve connected to O₂
Run a circuit leak test
Silence the alarms and reassess in 2 minutes
Increase the high-pressure limit and continue
questions.why: Because you must always attend to patient needs first, when any major problem is suspected immediately remove the patient from the ventilator and provide support using a manual resuscitator with a PEEP valve connected to an O₂ source. If that resolves the problem, the ventilator or circuit was the cause and others can troubleshoot while you support the patient.

questions.stem: A ventilator alarms LOW volume together with LOW pressure. This combination indicates:
opts: A leak
An inspiratory obstruction
An expiratory obstruction
A jammed expiratory valve
questions.why: Leaks produce low-volume plus low-pressure alarms. Both inspiratory and expiratory obstructions instead produce low-volume plus HIGH-pressure alarms.

questions.stem: Why is expiratory obstruction more dangerous than inspiratory obstruction, and what is its most dangerous form?
opts: It can cause rebreathing, asphyxia, or barotrauma; the most dangerous form is obstruction of the exhalation port on a single-limb circuit
It causes only a nuisance low-pressure alarm; the most dangerous form is a kinked inspiratory limb
It reduces FiO₂; the most dangerous form is a clogged HEPA filter
It triggers auto-PEEP only; the most dangerous form is condensate in the wye
questions.why: Circuit obstructions are always associated with low-volume and high-pressure alarms. Expiratory obstruction is the more serious of the two because it can result in rebreathing, asphyxia, or barotrauma. The most dangerous type occurs when the exhalation port on a single-limb circuit becomes obstructed, so prevent patients from grasping the circuit and keep bedding clear of the port.

questions.stem: A patient is on NPPV. Which circuit type is appropriate and why does it minimize deadspace?
opts: A single-limb circuit with a leakage-type exhaust port; continuous flow plus interface leakage forces expired gas out, preventing rebreathing
A dual-limb wye circuit; the separate expiratory limb removes all expired gas
A single-limb circuit with a mushroom expiratory valve; the valve vents all expired gas
Any circuit, because NPPV has no mechanical deadspace
questions.why: NPPV ventilators use a single-limb circuit with a leakage-type exhaust port. The continuous flow these ventilators provide forces expired gas out the exhaust port during exhalation and, combined with the leakage common to all NPPV interfaces, prevents rebreathing of most expired gas — minimizing mechanical deadspace.

questions.stem: A patient with hypercapnic respiratory failure needs an NPPV interface. Which is preferred and why?
opts: Nasal appliances, because of their lesser deadspace
A full face mask, because of its lower leakage
Nasal pillows, because they never cause pressure sores
An oral device, because it prevents all leakage
questions.why: For patients with hypercapnic respiratory failure, nasal appliances are preferred due to their lesser deadspace. Full face masks have lower leakage and may be best for short-term treatment of hypoxemic and hypercapnic failure in acute care, but should be avoided when there is a high risk of vomiting or aspiration.

questions.stem: Which action will INCREASE mechanical deadspace in a dual-limb ventilator circuit?
opts: Adding an HME, MDI adapter, or end-tidal CO₂ adaptor between the wye and the patient's airway
Adding a water trap to the expiratory limb
Lengthening the inspiratory limb
Adding a HEPA filter at the ventilator gas outlet
questions.why: The mechanical deadspace or rebreathed volume in dual-limb circuits lies between the circuit wye and the patient's airway. Any tubing or device added between these connections — such as an HME, MDI, or end-tidal CO₂ adaptor — will increase mechanical deadspace. An HME always adds some deadspace.

questions.stem: A ventilated patient on an HME develops copious, thick secretions and now requires aerosolized medication. You should:
opts: Switch to heated (active) humidification
Add a second HME in series
Increase the ventilator flow rate
Instill saline before each suction pass
questions.why: Copious, thick secretions indicate inadequate humidification; assure good systemic hydration and switch to heated active humidification. The need to administer aerosolized medications is a separate indication to switch, because the HME filters the medication and can itself become obstructed by it.

questions.stem: An AED indicates "no shock advised" in a pulseless patient. You should:
opts: Resume CPR, because the rhythm is likely asystole or pulseless electrical activity
Repeat the analysis immediately
Increase the energy setting and shock anyway
Check for a pulse every 30 seconds without compressions
questions.why: If the unit says no shock is needed, resume CPR — remember the patient is pulseless. Pulseless nonshockable situations include asystole and pulseless electrical activity. Repeat analysis and the steps that follow every 2 minutes, about five CPR cycles, switching rescuer positions at that time.

questions.stem: You are about to apply AED pads to a patient with an implanted defibrillator and a transdermal medication patch on the chest. You should:
opts: Avoid placing pads directly over the device, remove the medication patch, and wipe the area
Place a pad directly over the implanted device for best conduction
Leave the patch in place and apply pads over it
Withhold defibrillation entirely
questions.why: Do not place pads directly over implanted defibrillators or pacemakers, or on top of transdermal medication patches; remove the medication patch and wipe the area. Similarly, a wet chest must be dried and a hairy chest shaved or stripped with a spare set of pads.

questions.stem: Droplet transmission involves particles of what size, and requires what proximity?
opts: Larger than 5 μm; close contact, generally 3 feet or less
5 μm or smaller; any distance including between rooms
Larger than 10 μm; contact with the patient's skin
Any size; only direct contact matters
questions.why: Droplet transmission is the spread of microorganisms in the air via large droplets larger than 5 μm. Because large droplets fall out of suspension quickly they travel only short distances, so droplet transmission requires close contact, generally 3 feet or less. Airborne transmission involves droplet nuclei 5 μm or smaller that can travel long distances, even between rooms.

questions.stem: Which set of conditions requires airborne precautions?
opts: Tuberculosis, measles, chickenpox, Aspergillus, SARS, smallpox
Bacterial meningitis, pertussis, influenza, mumps, rubella
C. difficile, norovirus, MRSA, wound and skin infections
Epiglottitis and group A streptococcal infections
questions.why: Airborne precautions apply to tuberculosis, measles (rubeola), chickenpox (varicella-zoster), Aspergillus infections, SARS, and smallpox (variola). Bacterial meningitis, whooping cough, influenza, mumps, rubella, diphtheria, group A Streptococcus, and epiglottitis require DROPLET precautions, while C. difficile, norovirus, MRSA, and wound/skin infections require CONTACT precautions.

questions.stem: A patient on airborne precautions must be placed in:
opts: A private negative-pressure airborne infection isolation room with the door closed
A private room with the door open and no special air handling
Any semiprivate room with a curtain divider
A positive-pressure room
questions.why: Airborne precautions require placing the patient in a private negative-pressure airborne infection isolation room (AIIR) with the door closed, and wearing a fit-tested N95 respirator certified by NIOSH when entering. Droplet precautions require only a private room; special air handling and ventilation are not needed and the door can stay open.

questions.stem: What is the correct sequence for APPLYING personal protective equipment?
opts: Hair and foot coverings, gown, mask, goggles or face shield, gloves
Gloves, gown, mask, goggles, hair and foot coverings
Gown, gloves, mask, goggles, hair and foot coverings
Mask, goggles, gown, gloves, hair and foot coverings
questions.why: PPE is applied in the order: hair and foot coverings, gown, mask, goggles or face shield, then gloves. It is REMOVED in the order: hair and foot coverings, goggles or face shield, mask, gloves (pulled down from the wrist and turned inside out), then gown (removed from the inside out).

questions.stem: Which term describes the destruction of ALL forms of microbial life, including bacteria, viruses, spores, and fungi?
opts: Sterilization
High-level disinfection
Decontamination
Sanitation
questions.why: Sterilization is the destruction of all forms of microbial life, including bacteria, viruses, spores, and fungi. High-level disinfection destroys vegetative bacteria, mycobacteria, fungi, and viruses but not necessarily bacterial spores, although some high-level disinfectants can sterilize given adequate contact time.

questions.stem: What is the best way to help prevent transmission of hospital-acquired infections?
opts: Good hand hygiene
Wearing gloves at all times
Routine environmental sanitation
Annual respirator fit testing
questions.why: Because most hospital-acquired infections occur due to direct contact between patients and healthcare workers, good hand hygiene is the best way to help prevent transmission of infections. It is also part of the CDC respiratory hygiene/cough etiquette guideline applying to patients, visitors, and healthcare workers.

questions.stem: Which term describes the reproducibility or repeatability of an analyzer's results for the same analyte over multiple measurements?
opts: Precision
Accuracy
Bias
Linearity
questions.why: Precision is the reproducibility or repeatability of an analyzer's results for the same analyte over multiple measurements. Accuracy is the degree to which a reading coincides with its true value, and bias is systematic inaccuracy — consistently high or low variation from the true value.

questions.stem: Errors caused by mistakes in the collection, handling, or storage of samples BEFORE analysis are called:
opts: Preanalytical errors
Analytical errors
Postanalytical errors
Bias errors
questions.why: Preanalytical errors are result errors due to mistakes in the collection, handling, or storage of samples before analysis. Analytical errors occur during measurement and analysis, and postanalytical errors occur in data handling, results reporting, or interpretation.

questions.stem: The most common preanalytical errors affecting blood gas and hemoximetry measurements are:
opts: Air contamination, venous admixture, and continued blood metabolism
Incorrect gas concentrations and contaminated buffers
Transcription mistakes and mislabeled reports
Drift and poor linearity
questions.why: The most common preanalytical errors affecting blood gas and hemoximetry measurements are air contamination, venous admixture, and continued blood metabolism. These errors can yield invalid measurements leading to incorrect decisions and potential patient harm.

questions.stem: Calibration verification typically involves analysis of how many levels of control media, and how often?
opts: At least three levels spanning the expected range, at least daily
One level, once per week
Two levels, once per month
Five levels, once per shift
questions.why: Calibration verification involves analysis of prepared control media — analytes independently certified to provide a known measurement value. It typically involves at least three different levels of control media spanning the full range of expected results and is conducted at least daily, plus after any instrument maintenance and whenever instrument performance is questioned.

questions.stem: What is the gold standard procedure for calibration verification of PO₂ and PCO₂ measurements?
opts: Tonometry
Levy-Jennings charting
Proficiency testing
Inter-instrumental comparison
questions.why: The gold standard for calibration verification of PO₂ and PCO₂ measurements is tonometry, which involves exposing and equilibrating liquid media — blood or control solution — to a reference gas with known partial pressures.

questions.stem: On a Levy-Jennings chart, bounding limits are typically set at:
opts: ±2 standard deviations from the mean
±1 standard deviation from the mean
±3 standard deviations from the mean
±10% of the mean
questions.why: A Levy-Jennings chart plots individual control values over multiple measurements against the mean and standard deviation. Bounding limits are typically set to within ±2 SD. Control measurements consistently within these limits indicate the analyzer is in control and ready for sample measurement.

questions.stem: A single control value on day 16 falls outside the ±2 SD limit, but all subsequent measurements are within limits. You should:
opts: Take no remedial action, because this is a random error of measurement
Immediately remove the analyzer from service
Recalibrate and re-report all prior patient results
Switch permanently to point-of-care testing
questions.why: Single irregular values are relatively common and are due to random errors of measurement that occur with any instrument. If subsequent measures are within the control limits, no remedial action is needed. Frequent random errors would instead indicate a lack of precision, and an instrument with poor repeatability over time is out of control.

questions.stem: A Levy-Jennings chart shows a sustained upward trend in the 40-torr PCO₂ control beginning at observation 20. This represents:
opts: Systematic error (bias), which is more serious than random error and requires correction before any patient samples are analyzed
A random error requiring no action
Normal analyzer drift within specification
Evidence that the control media is expired but the analyzer is fine
questions.why: An upward trend over time shifts the mean above the control value, producing a positive measurement bias. Bias errors are generally more serious than random errors, indicating either an incorrect procedure or instrument failure. Whenever instrument bias is identified, no patient samples should be analyzed until the problem is corrected.

questions.stem: A point-of-care analyzer fails to calibrate. The correct sequence of actions is:
opts: Rerun the test with a new cartridge; if a second attempt fails, remove the device from service and obtain a replacement or send the sample to the central lab
Immediately report the result with a quality disclaimer
Recalibrate manually using room air
Continue testing and compare against the bench-top analyzer later
questions.why: Most POCT cartridges include solutions for automated calibration. If a POCT device fails to calibrate, rerun the test with a new cartridge. If a second attempt fails, remove the device from service and either obtain a replacement analyzer or send the sample to the central lab.

questions.stem: A Mallampati Class IV airway means the examiner can visualize:
opts: Only the hard palate
The soft palate, uvula, and pillars/tonsils
The soft palate and a portion of the uvula
The soft palate and only the base of the uvula
questions.why: Mallampati Class IV means only the hard palate is visible, predicting very difficult intubation. Class I is the soft palate, uvula, and pillars/tonsils (easiest); Class II the soft palate and part of the uvula; Class III the soft palate and only the base of the uvula (difficult).

questions.stem: The M-O-A-N-S mnemonic for predicting difficult bag-valve-mask ventilation stands for:
opts: Mask seal, Obesity/Obstruction, Aged, No teeth, Stiff lungs
Mouth opening, Oxygenation, Airway, Neck, Suction
Mandible, Occlusion, Age, Nares, Sedation
Mask, Oral airway, Anesthesia, Nasal, Stridor
questions.why: M-O-A-N-S stands for Mask seal, Obesity/Obstruction, Aged, No teeth (edentulous), and Stiff lungs. It helps the clinician predict difficult BVM ventilation.

questions.stem: The L-E-M-O-N mnemonic for predicting difficult intubation stands for:
opts: Look externally, Evaluate external anatomy, Mallampati classification, Obesity/Obstruction, Neck mobility
Laryngoscope, Endotracheal tube, Mask, Oxygen, Nasal airway
Level of consciousness, Edema, Mandible, Oropharynx, Nares
Lubricate, Elevate, Measure, Observe, Note
questions.why: L-E-M-O-N stands for Look externally, Evaluate external anatomy, Mallampati classification, Obesity/Obstruction, and Neck mobility.

questions.stem: The recommended endotracheal tube for an adult male is:
opts: 8.0–9.0 mm ID, inserted 21–23 cm
7.0–8.0 mm ID, inserted 19–21 cm
6.5 mm ID, inserted 17–19 cm
8.5+ mm ID, inserted 23+ cm
questions.why: For an adult male, select an 8.0–9.0 mm ID tube with an insertion length of 21–23 cm measured from the incisors to the tube tip. Adult females use 7.0–8.0 mm ID at 19–21 cm. For the nasotracheal route in adults, add 2 cm to the insertion length.

questions.stem: After intubation, the ETT cuff should be inflated to:
opts: 20–30 cm H₂O
40–50 cm H₂O
60 cm H₂O
10–15 cm H₂O
questions.why: Inflate the cuff to 20–30 cm H₂O. This limit applies to infants and children as well when cuffed tubes are used, per manufacturer's specifications.

questions.stem: The LMA cuff should be inflated to a maximum pressure of:
opts: 60 cm H₂O
30 cm H₂O
20 cm H₂O
100 cm H₂O
questions.why: Inflate the LMA cuff to 60 cm H₂O. Avoid pressures greater than 60 cm H₂O, which can cause malpositioning or tissue damage. Table 9-7 maximum volumes should never be exceeded, though lesser volumes are often sufficient to achieve a seal at 60 cm H₂O.

questions.stem: For an adult weighing 50–70 kg, the recommended LMA size and maximum cuff volume are:
opts: Size 4, 30 mL
Size 5, 40 mL
Size 3, 20 mL
Size 6, 50 mL
questions.why: Adults 50–70 kg use LMA size 4 with a maximum cuff volume of 30 mL. Adults 70–100 kg use size 5 at 40 mL, and adults over 100 kg use size 6 at 50 mL.

questions.stem: A subglottic (Hi-Lo) endotracheal tube connects its extra lumen to continuous suction at approximately:
opts: −25 cm H₂O
−80 cm H₂O
−120 cm H₂O
−5 cm H₂O
questions.why: Subglottic ETTs have an extra-small lumen opening just above the ETT cuff, with the proximal end connected to continuous low-level suction at approximately −25 cm H₂O. They continuously remove secretions that would otherwise pool above the cuff, reducing aspiration risk and ventilator-associated infection.

questions.stem: A tracheostomy tube's outside diameter should generally be no more than what fraction of the tracheal internal diameter?
opts: Two-thirds to three-fourths
One-half
Nine-tenths
One-fourth
questions.why: When a doctor selects a trach tube, primary consideration is given to the outside diameter, especially for cuffed tubes. The OD should generally be no more than two-thirds to three-fourths of the ID of the trachea. Bigger tubes impede airflow around a deflated cuff; smaller tubes may need unacceptably high cuff pressures to seal.

questions.stem: A patient with a suspected cervical spine injury requires airway opening. You should use:
opts: The jaw-thrust maneuver without head extension
The head-tilt/chin-lift maneuver
The sniffing position
Full Trendelenburg positioning
questions.why: The jaw-thrust maneuver without head extension minimizes neck movement in patients with a suspected cervical spine injury. The sniffing position is used for intubation but is not to be used with a suspected cervical spine injury.

questions.stem: To help prevent ventilator-associated pneumonia, the head of the bed should be elevated:
opts: 30 degrees or more, unless contraindicated
10 degrees
45 degrees exactly
Flat, to promote drainage
questions.why: Elevating the head of the bed by 30 degrees or more, unless contraindicated, helps prevent gastric reflux aspiration and improves the distribution of ventilation and efficiency of diaphragmatic action.

questions.stem: Prone positioning is indicated for ARDS when:
opts: The P/F ratio is < 150 with FiO₂ > 0.60 and PEEP ≥ 5 cm H₂O
The P/F ratio is < 300 on any FiO₂
The patient has unilateral lung disease
The patient requires postural drainage
questions.why: Prone position is used if severe ARDS is present — a P/F ratio below 150 with FiO₂ above 0.60 and PEEP of at least 5 cm H₂O. Proning recruits collapsed lung units and shifts blood flow away from shunt regions, improving V/Q balance and oxygenation.

questions.stem: A patient has unilateral left lower lobe pneumonia. To improve oxygenation you should position them:
opts: Right lateral decubitus, with the good lung down
Left lateral decubitus, with the affected lung down
Supine with the head of the bed flat
Prone
questions.why: The lateral decubitus position with the good lung down improves oxygenation by diverting blood flow and ventilation to the dependent (good) lung. With left-sided disease, the good right lung goes down. Exceptions to the keep-the-good-lung-down rule include lung abscess or bleeding, where the good lung is kept up to prevent blood or pus from entering it, and infants with unilateral PIE.

questions.stem: How do you tailor the size of an oropharyngeal airway to an individual patient?
opts: Measure from the corner of the mouth to the angle of the jaw, or to the earlobe
Measure from the nares to the earlobe
Measure the neck circumference
Use the largest size that will fit past the teeth
questions.why: Size is based primarily on patient age, but tailor it by measuring from the corner of the mouth to the angle of the jaw or from the corner of the mouth to the earlobe. Too large or too small an airway can worsen obstruction. The nares-to-earlobe measurement is used for NASOPHARYNGEAL airways.

questions.stem: An awake, conscious patient gags on an oropharyngeal airway. You should:
opts: Remove it immediately and consider a nasopharyngeal airway or a repositioning maneuver
Tape it in place until the gag reflex subsides
Insert a larger airway to seat it past the tongue
Sedate the patient and leave the airway in place
questions.why: To avoid vomiting and aspiration, if the patient gags or otherwise does not tolerate the airway, remove it immediately. Oropharyngeal airways are not recommended for awake, conscious patients — consider a nasopharyngeal airway or reposition the patient using the head-tilt/chin-lift or jaw-thrust maneuver.

questions.stem: A lubricated nasopharyngeal airway will not pass through the selected naris. You should:
opts: Insert it through the opposite naris; if unsuccessful, select a smaller airway
Apply firm steady force until it passes
Remove the lubricant and retry
Switch immediately to an oropharyngeal airway
questions.why: If a lubricated nasopharyngeal airway does not pass, the patient may have a deviated septum or nasal polyps. Insert the airway through the opposite naris; if that is unsuccessful, select and insert a smaller airway. The airway should always be advanced without force along the floor of the nasal passage.

questions.stem: How far past the vocal cords should an endotracheal tube be advanced?
opts: Until the cuff disappears, about 2–3 cm beyond the cords
About 6 cm beyond the cords
Until resistance is met at the carina
Just until the tip passes the cords
questions.why: Insert the ETT between the vocal cords until the cuff disappears, about 2–3 cm beyond the cords. Placement is then verified by breath sounds, chest wall movement, and CO₂ detection or capnography, and confirmed by x-ray.

questions.stem: How long should a single intubation attempt last, and what is done between attempts?
opts: No more than 20 seconds per attempt, with 1–2 minutes of oxygenation between attempts
No more than 60 seconds, with 30 seconds of oxygenation between
As long as needed if SpO₂ stays above 85%
No more than 10 seconds, with no interruption for oxygenation
questions.why: Always provide 1–2 minutes of oxygenation and, if necessary, ventilation between intubation attempts. Intubation attempts should last no more than 20 seconds per attempt.

questions.stem: Using a colorimetric CO₂ detector, correct ETT placement in the lungs is confirmed by:
opts: A purple to yellow color change over six or more breaths
A yellow to purple color change on the first breath
No color change over three breaths
A blue to green color change over two breaths
questions.why: If using a colorimetric CO₂ detector, ETT placement in the lungs is confirmed by observing a purple to yellow color change over six or more breaths, indicating 2.0–5.0% exhaled CO₂ or about 15–38 torr. During resuscitation the AHA recommends continuous quantitative waveform capnography, with a CO₂ detector acceptable if capnography is unavailable.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of the blunt obturator used during tracheostomy tube insertion?
opts: It prevents tissue trauma ("snowplowing") during insertion and is removed immediately afterward
It holds the cuff deflated during insertion
It serves as an inner cannula during the first 24 hours
It anchors the tube to the flange
questions.why: The blunt obturator prevents tissue trauma — snowplowing — during insertion. Remove it immediately after insertion but keep it at the bedside for tube reinsertion.

questions.stem: Before inserting an LMA, the cuff should be:
opts: Fully deflated into a smooth wedge shape without wrinkles
Partially inflated to ease passage
Fully inflated to the maximum volume
Inflated to 60 cm H₂O before insertion
questions.why: Fully deflate the cuff by pulling back firmly on the deflating syringe until it forms a smooth wedge shape without wrinkles; insertion with a partially deflated cuff can obstruct the airway. Lubricate the posterior side of the mask with water-soluble lubricant and preoxygenate the patient.

questions.stem: After intubation you hear gurgling over the epigastrium and no breath sounds. You should:
opts: Immediately deflate the cuff, remove the tube, and reintubate the patient
Advance the tube 2 cm and reassess
Inflate the cuff further to seal the leak
Obtain a stat chest x-ray before acting
questions.why: Stomach (epigastric) gurgling sounds indicate esophageal intubation. Correct it by immediately deflating the cuff, removing the tube, and reintubating the patient. Be prepared to suction the oropharynx if vomitus occurs.

questions.stem: Breath sounds and chest movement are decreased on the LEFT after intubation. This most likely indicates:
opts: Right mainstem intubation; slowly withdraw the tube until bilateral breath sounds are confirmed
Left mainstem intubation; advance the tube further
Esophageal intubation; remove and reintubate
A left pneumothorax; insert a chest tube
questions.why: Decreased breath sounds or chest movement on the left suggests intubation of the right mainstem bronchus — left-sided intubation can occur but is much less common. Correct it by slowly withdrawing the tube until you confirm bilateral breath sounds, then confirm proper position by chest x-ray.

questions.stem: A suction catheter will not pass through a recently placed ETT. This suggests:
opts: The tube may be kinked or displaced out of the trachea; reposition it or reintubate
The catheter is too small and should be upsized
Normal resistance requiring more force
The cuff is overinflated and should be deflated
questions.why: If a suction catheter does not pass after placement, the tube may be kinked or displaced out of the trachea. Reposition it or reintubate the patient.

questions.stem: During direct laryngoscopy you obtain a Cormack-Lehane Grade IV view. This means:
opts: The epiglottis cannot be visualized, and difficult intubation is over 90% likely
Only the epiglottis is visible, with moderate difficulty expected
The cords are fully visible and intubation should be easy
The view is obscured by secretions and should be suctioned
questions.why: On the Cormack-Lehane scale a Grade III view allows visualization of the epiglottis only, with Grade IV indicating that the epiglottis cannot be visualized. The likelihood of difficult intubation increases to over 90% with a Grade IV view.

questions.stem: After inserting an oropharyngeal airway, the obstruction is not relieved. Which explanation fits an airway that is TOO SMALL?
opts: It forces the tongue against the posterior pharynx
It blocks the patient's airway directly
It causes the patient to gag
It cannot be taped in place
questions.why: Remove and reinsert the airway and confirm it extends past the base of the tongue. If the airway is too large or long it will block the patient's airway; if it is too small or short it can force the tongue against the posterior pharynx.

questions.stem: An LMA develops a leak with decreased tidal volumes. Which action is specifically warned against?
opts: Simply adding more air to the cuff, because this may worsen leakage by pushing the cuff off the larynx
Confirming the airway is securely taped
Readjusting the airway position by pressing the tube downward
Resecuring the airway in its new position
questions.why: For a leak, confirm the airway is securely taped, readjust the position by pressing the tube downward, and resecure it. Do NOT simply add more air to the cuff — this may worsen leakage by pushing the cuff off the larynx.

questions.stem: Regurgitation occurs in a patient with an LMA in place. Your immediate actions are:
opts: Place the patient head-down or side-lying and disconnect ventilation equipment so gastric contents are not forced into the lungs
Increase PEEP to keep the airway pressurized
Add air to the LMA cuff and continue ventilating
Suction the airway tube with the LMA in place before repositioning
questions.why: For regurgitation, place the patient in a head-down or side-lying rescue position and disconnect all ventilation equipment so gastric contents are not forced into the lungs. Then reposition the LMA so its distal end presses against the esophageal sphincter, suction through the airway tube, and prepare for immediate tracheal intubation.

questions.stem: Using the pediatric formula, what uncuffed ETT internal diameter is estimated for a 4-year-old?
opts: 5.0 mm
4.0 mm
6.0 mm
3.0 mm
questions.why: For infants and children, uncuffed tube size ID = (age/4) + 4, so (4/4) + 4 = 5.0 mm. Cuffed tube size ID = (age/4) + 3, because cuffed tubes must be slightly smaller.

questions.stem: Why is the nasotracheal route discouraged for intubation?
opts: Higher incidence of VAP, sinusitis, and otitis media; smaller or longer tubes raise airway resistance; and nasal septal or naris necrosis can occur
It cannot be performed without fiberoptic guidance
Capnography cannot confirm nasal tube placement
Nasal tubes cannot be cuffed
questions.why: The nasotracheal route is discouraged because the incidence of VAP, sinusitis, and otitis media is higher; smaller or longer ETTs are required, which increases airway resistance; and necrosis of the nasal septum and naris can occur.

questions.stem: The recommended starting vacuum pressure range for tracheal suctioning in ADULTS is:
opts: −100 to −120 mm Hg
−80 to −100 mm Hg
−60 to −80 mm Hg
−150 to −200 mm Hg
questions.why: For centrally piped vacuum systems the recommended starting range is −100 to −120 mm Hg for adults, −80 to −100 mm Hg for children, and −60 to −80 mm Hg for infants. Always select the lowest level needed to remove secretions effectively.

questions.stem: Each suctioning pass should be limited to:
opts: Less than 15 seconds
Less than 30 seconds
Less than 60 seconds
Less than 5 seconds
questions.why: Limit the duration of suctioning to less than 15 seconds. Preoxygenate and postoxygenate with 100% O₂ — 10% above baseline for neonates — for at least 30–60 seconds.

questions.stem: A suction catheter should occlude no more than what percentage of the ETT internal diameter?
opts: Less than 50% in adults, less than 70% in infants
Less than 70% in adults, less than 90% in infants
Less than 25% in all patients
Less than 90% in all patients
questions.why: To ensure adequate space for gas to flow around the catheter and prevent atelectasis, always select a suction catheter that occludes less than 50% of the ETT internal diameter, or less than 70% in infants.

questions.stem: Each postural drainage position should be maintained for:
opts: 10–15 minutes as tolerated
2–3 minutes
30 minutes
1 hour
questions.why: Position the patient for drainage beginning with the most dependent zones first, and maintain the position for 10–15 minutes as tolerated while performing percussion and vibration over the identified areas.

questions.stem: During incentive spirometry, the patient should perform a full inspiratory capacity breath with a breath-hold of:
opts: 5 to 10 seconds, 6–10 times per hour
1 to 2 seconds, once per hour
20 seconds, 3 times per hour
30 seconds, continuously
questions.why: Instruct the patient in a full inspiratory capacity breath with a 5- to 10-second breath-hold, allowing adequate recovery time between breaths to avoid hyperventilation, performed 6–10 times per hour.

questions.stem: What is the ONLY absolute contraindication to intermittent positive-pressure breathing?
opts: Untreated tension pneumothorax
Intracranial pressure above 15 mm Hg
Active hemoptysis
Recent esophageal surgery
questions.why: Untreated tension pneumothorax is the only absolute contraindication to IPPB. ICP above 15 mm Hg, hemodynamic instability, recent facial/oral/skull surgery, tracheoesophageal fistula, recent esophageal surgery, active hemoptysis, and radiographic evidence of bleb are relative contraindications.

questions.stem: Which airway clearance technique is recommended for a patient with neuromuscular disease such as muscular dystrophy?
opts: Insufflation–exsufflation, forced expiratory technique/directed cough, and suction
Postural drainage, percussion, and vibration only
High-frequency chest wall oscillation only
No airway clearance therapy is indicated
questions.why: For neuromuscular disease — muscular dystrophy, myasthenia, poliomyelitis — the recommended techniques are insufflation–exsufflation (I-E), forced expiratory technique/directed cough, and suction. Uncomplicated pneumonia requires NO airway clearance therapy, and uncomplicated postoperative patients need early mobility and ambulation.

questions.stem: Patients with cystic fibrosis should generally NOT be placed in a head-down position during PDPV because:
opts: They are at higher risk for gastroesophageal reflux
Head-down positioning raises intracranial pressure
Their secretions are too viscous to drain by gravity
Head-down positioning causes bronchospasm in CF
questions.why: Because patients with cystic fibrosis are at higher risk for gastroesophageal reflux, it is generally recommended that they no longer be placed in a head-down position during PDPV.

questions.stem: PDPV should be discontinued when:
opts: Sputum production drops below 30 mL/day and the patient can generate an effective spontaneous cough
The patient reports the treatments are uncomfortable
Two treatments have been completed
The chest x-ray shows any improvement at all
questions.why: In general, when sputum production drops below 30 mL/day and the patient can generate an effective spontaneous cough, PDPV is no longer indicated and should be discontinued. Effectiveness is monitored by chest x-ray changes, vital signs including SpO₂, sputum production, and auscultation.

questions.stem: Using the quick estimate, what French suction catheter suits a 6.0-mm ID tracheal tube?
opts: 10 Fr
12 Fr
8 Fr
14 Fr
questions.why: Estimate the catheter size in French by doubling the internal diameter of the tracheal tube and selecting the next smallest catheter size: 6.0 × 2 = 12, so select the next smallest, 10 Fr. Table 10-3 confirms 10 Fr for a 6.0-mm tube.

questions.stem: A postoperative patient cannot generate an inspiratory capacity greater than 33% of predicted. You should recommend:
opts: IPPB or intermittent CPAP therapy as alternatives
A larger incentive spirometer
Doubling the frequency of incentive spirometry
Discontinuing all lung expansion therapy
questions.why: To perform IS the patient must be able to cooperate and ideally generate an inspiratory capacity at least one-third of predicted. If the patient cannot cooperate or cannot generate an IC greater than 33% of predicted, recommend either IPPB or intermittent CPAP therapy as alternatives.

questions.stem: During IPPB, the pressure and flow should be adjusted until the delivered tidal volume is:
opts: 1½ to 2 times the patient's baseline VT, as tolerated
Equal to the patient's baseline VT
3 to 4 times the baseline VT
Exactly 500 mL regardless of patient size
questions.why: Have the patient maintain a tight seal, instruct them to inhale slightly until the breath triggers, adjust sensitivity to facilitate triggering, and adjust the pressure and flow until the VT is 1½ to 2 times the baseline as tolerated. Initial settings are sensitivity about −2 cm H₂O and cycle pressure 10–15 cm H₂O with moderate flow.

questions.stem: Why is incentive spirometry no longer recommended for routine prophylactic use after thoracic or upper abdominal surgery?
opts: Current evidence shows little to no benefit; early mobilization and ambulation are the primary means of reducing postoperative complications
It causes an unacceptable rate of barotrauma
Patients cannot be taught the technique postoperatively
It has been replaced by routine IPPB in all surgical patients
questions.why: Because current evidence indicates that IS provides little to no benefit for patients undergoing thoracic or upper abdominal surgery, it is no longer recommended for routine prophylactic use postoperatively. Early mobilization and ambulation are considered the primary means of reducing postoperative complications and promoting airway clearance.

questions.stem: A hypoxemic postoperative patient (P/F ratio < 300) has atelectasis but no retained secretions. The most effective therapy is:
opts: CPAP at 5 to 10 cm H₂O every 4 to 6 hours for up to 30 minutes per session
Incentive spirometry every hour
Postural drainage with percussion and vibration
Tracheal suctioning every 2 hours
questions.why: Among the therapies for postoperative atelectasis, CPAP has proven most effective, especially in patients who are hypoxemic with a P/F ratio below 300 but without retained secretions, where it can decrease the incidence of intubation and pneumonia. Typically 5 to 10 cm H₂O is applied every 4 to 6 hours for up to 30 minutes per session.

questions.stem: To deliver a PRECISE FiO₂ with a pneumatically powered IPPB unit, you must:
opts: Attach it to an O₂ blender and turn the air mix OFF so it delivers pure source gas
Turn the air mix ON to entrain a fixed amount of room air
Bleed 100% O₂ into the delivery circuit of the pneumatic unit
Use the nebulizer flow to dilute the source gas
questions.why: To provide a precise FiO₂ with a pneumatically powered IPPB unit, attach it to an O₂ blender and set the device to deliver pure source gas by turning off air mix. Without a blender, pneumatic units deliver either 100% O₂ or an air mixture varying between 0.40 and 0.60. Bleeding 100% O₂ into the circuit gives only moderate, inexact concentrations and applies to ELECTRICALLY powered units.

questions.stem: High-frequency ventilation operates at what frequency range and tidal volume?
opts: 150–900 breaths/min with tidal volumes of 1–2 mL/kg
60–150 breaths/min with 4–6 mL/kg
900–1500 breaths/min with 3–5 mL/kg
30–60 breaths/min with 6–8 mL/kg
questions.why: High-frequency ventilation is mechanical ventilation at frequencies between 150 and 900 breaths per minute, with tidal volumes as small as 1–2 mL/kg — significantly less than the anatomic deadspace.

questions.stem: Documented hypoxemia in an INFANT is generally defined as a PaO₂ less than:
opts: 50 torr
60 torr
70 torr
40 torr
questions.why: Documented hypoxemia exists in adults when the PaO₂ is less than 60 torr or the arterial saturation is less than 90%. Due to the potential hazards of oxygen therapy, the threshold for infants is lower and generally defined as a PaO₂ less than 50 torr.

questions.stem: Optimal control of sleep apnea on CPAP is indicated by an apnea-hypopnea index of:
opts: Less than 5/hour
Less than 15/hour
Less than 30/hour
Less than 1/hour
questions.why: Assess CPAP effectiveness by the apnea-hypopnea index, with optimum control indicated by an AHI below 5 per hour. CPAP level is set by prescription or auto-CPAP to a maximum of 15 cm H₂O.

questions.stem: In an otherwise healthy patient, oxygen should be titrated to the lowest level maintaining:
opts: PaO₂ of 80–100 torr with saturation ≥ 92%
PaO₂ of 55–60 torr with saturation ≥ 88%
PaO₂ above 150 torr
Saturation of 100% at all times
questions.why: In otherwise healthy patients, adjust flow and FiO₂ to the lowest level needed to maintain normal oxygenation — a PaO₂ of 80–100 torr with saturation of 92% or more. If you cannot maintain normal oxygenation on less than 50% oxygen, accept a PaO₂ of 55–60 torr with SaO₂/SpO₂ of 88% or more.

questions.stem: For a patient with chronic hypercapnia, the PaO₂ target is:
opts: 55–60 torr, to prevent O₂-induced hypoventilation
80–100 torr, as for any adult
Above 100 torr to maximize content
40–50 torr to preserve hypoxic drive
questions.why: For patients with chronic hypercapnia, aim to keep the PaO₂ in the range of 55–60 torr to prevent depression of ventilation — O₂-induced hypoventilation.

questions.stem: In a low birth weight or preterm neonate at risk for retinopathy of prematurity, the PaO₂ goal is:
opts: 50–80 torr
80–100 torr
30–50 torr
Above 100 torr
questions.why: In low birth weight or preterm neonates at risk for retinopathy of prematurity, the goal should be a PaO₂ in the range of 50–80 torr.

questions.stem: A prone positioning trial is recommended for ARDS when oxygenation remains inadequate on:
opts: FiO₂ ≥ 0.6 and PEEP ≥ 10 cm H₂O
FiO₂ ≥ 0.4 and PEEP ≥ 5 cm H₂O
FiO₂ ≥ 1.0 and PEEP ≥ 20 cm H₂O
Any FiO₂ if the P/F ratio is below 300
questions.why: A prone positioning trial is recommended for patients with ARDS if oxygenation is inadequate on FiO₂ of 0.6 or more and PEEP of 10 cm H₂O or more. It should be maintained for a minimum of 12 hours at a time as tolerated.

questions.stem: Prone positioning is NOT recommended for which patient?
opts: One who is morbidly obese or at high risk for needing CPR
One with ARDS and refractory hypoxemia
One whose oxygenation is inadequate on high PEEP
One whose abdomen can be freely suspended
questions.why: Proning is not recommended for patients whose heads cannot be in a face-down position, those with circulatory problems, those with a fractured pelvis, those who are morbidly obese, or those at high risk for needing cardiopulmonary resuscitation. Major risks include extubation and dislodgement of intravascular catheters.

questions.stem: During suctioning the patient's SpO₂ falls from 96% to 86%. You should:
opts: Immediately terminate the procedure and administer 100% O₂
Increase the FiO₂ by 10% and continue
Continue but shorten the pass to 5 seconds
Reduce the vacuum pressure and continue
questions.why: For mild hypoxemia — an SpO₂ drop of more than 4–5% that remains at or above 88–90% — increase the FiO₂. For moderate to severe hypoxemia, where the SpO₂ drops below 88–90%, immediately terminate the procedure and administer 100% O₂.

questions.stem: CPAP for cardiogenic pulmonary edema should be avoided if:
opts: Systolic BP < 90 mm Hg, acute MI, Glasgow ≤ 8, or a need for intubation
The patient is hypoxemic on room air
The SpO₂ is below 95%
The patient has a history of COPD
questions.why: Avoid CPAP for cardiogenic pulmonary edema if the systolic blood pressure is below 90 mm Hg, there is an acute MI, the Glasgow Coma Scale is 8 or less, or intubation is needed. Otherwise start therapy at 10 cm H₂O and 100% O₂, titrating pressure and FiO₂ to maintain SpO₂ above 90%.

questions.stem: Initial settings for neonatal CPAP are:
opts: 4–6 cm H₂O at 40–50% O₂, flow 5–10 L/min
10 cm H₂O at 100% O₂, flow 15 L/min
8–10 cm H₂O at 60% O₂, flow 2 L/min
2 cm H₂O at 21% O₂, flow 20 L/min
questions.why: For neonates, set the flow to 5–10 L/min on continuous-flow systems such as bubble CPAP and start therapy at 4–6 cm H₂O with 40–50% O₂. Adjust to maintain SpO₂ of 87–93%, minimize chest retractions and grunting, and improve aeration on chest x-ray.

questions.stem: Neonatal CPAP should be avoided in an infant with:
opts: Congenital diaphragmatic hernia, T-E fistula, choanal atresia, severe cardiovascular instability, or hypercapnic respiratory failure
Infant respiratory distress syndrome
Apnea of prematurity
Mild chest retractions and grunting
questions.why: Avoid CPAP in infants with a congenital diaphragmatic hernia, tracheoesophageal fistula, choanal atresia, severe cardiovascular instability, or hypercapnic respiratory failure with a PaCO₂ above 60 torr and pH below 7.25. IRDS and apnea of prematurity are indications.

questions.stem: The NBRC generally expects an initial tidal volume setting of:
opts: 6–8 mL/kg of predicted body weight
10–12 mL/kg of actual body weight
4–5 mL/kg of predicted body weight
8–10 mL/kg of actual body weight
questions.why: The NBRC generally expects an initial setting of 6–8 mL/kg of predicted body weight for most patients, except those with acute hypoxemic respiratory failure who follow the NHLBI ARDS protocol. Either volume or pressure control is satisfactory as long as the setting delivers 6–8 mL/kg of PBW to minimize barotrauma.

questions.stem: BiPAP generally should NOT be used in a patient with:
opts: A pH below 7.20
Hypercapnic respiratory failure from COPD
Acute cardiogenic pulmonary edema
Chronic hypoventilation syndrome
questions.why: BiPAP should generally not be used with respiratory or cardiac arrest, a pH below 7.20, an uncooperative patient, excessive airway secretions, the need for airway protection or high aspiration risk, upper airway obstruction, hemodynamic instability, uncontrolled arrhythmias, active upper GI bleeding, facial burns or trauma, or nausea and vomiting. COPD hypercapnic failure and cardiogenic pulmonary edema are indications.

questions.stem: IPAP levels during BiPAP should be kept below what pressure, and why?
opts: 20–25 cm H₂O, the esophageal opening pressure, to avoid gastric insufflation
30 cm H₂O, to prevent barotrauma
15 cm H₂O, to preserve patient comfort
40 cm H₂O, the limit of the blower
questions.why: Keep IPAP levels less than 20–25 cm H₂O — the esophageal opening pressure — to avoid gastric insufflation.

questions.stem: Typical initial BiPAP settings include an IPAP of what, and a backup rate of at least what?
opts: IPAP 10–15 cm H₂O with a backup rate of at least 8/min
IPAP 20 cm H₂O with no backup rate
IPAP 5 cm H₂O with a backup rate of 20/min
IPAP 25–30 cm H₂O with a backup rate of 4/min
questions.why: Initial IPAP is 10–15 cm H₂O, adjusted to normalize pH and PaCO₂, with initial EPAP of 5 cm H₂O. The rate is patient determined but set a backup rate of at least 8/min.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly contrasts HFOV and HFJV?
opts: In HFOV both inspiration and exhalation are active; in HFJV inspiration is active but exhalation is passive
In HFOV both phases are passive; in HFJV both are active
In HFOV exhalation is passive; in HFJV both phases are active
Both modes have entirely passive exhalation
questions.why: HFOV gas delivery is driven by an oscillating rubber diaphragm that pushes gas forward and draws it back, so both inspiration and exhalation are active — unlike conventional ventilation. HFJV uses an interrupter valve creating intermittent jets, so inspiration is active but exhalation is passive.

questions.stem: How does the Bunnell LifePulse HFJV device differ in setup from the CareFusion 3100A HFOV?
opts: The LifePulse is always used with a conventional ventilator that provides background PEEP, FiO₂, and IMV breaths
The LifePulse is free-standing and needs no other ventilator
The LifePulse is used only in adults
The LifePulse provides active exhalation
questions.why: Unlike the free-standing CareFusion HFOV device, the Bunnell LifePulse is always used in conjunction with a conventional ventilator, which provides the background PEEP, FiO₂, and IMV breaths as needed. Its application is limited to infants and small children.

questions.stem: A patient's PaO₂ is 48 torr on an FiO₂ of 0.60. This indicates that:
opts: Hypoxemia is due to significant shunting, and O₂ therapy alone will be insufficient
The FiO₂ simply needs to be raised to 0.80
This is an expected response to oxygen therapy
The patient has simple V/Q mismatch
questions.why: Hypoxemia is due to significant shunting when the P/F ratio drops below 200 or you cannot maintain adequate arterial oxygenation on 50% or more oxygen — that is, PaO₂ of 50 torr or less on an FiO₂ of 0.50 or more. When hypoxemia is caused by shunting, O₂ therapy alone is insufficient; the recommended treatment is CPAP or PEEP.

questions.stem: Thirty minutes after proning, a patient's PaO₂ has risen by 14 torr. This indicates:
opts: A good indicator of success; proning should be maintained at least 12 hours as tolerated
Failure, because a rise of at least 30 torr is required
An equivocal result requiring repeat ABG in 4 hours
That the patient should be returned to supine immediately
questions.why: Not all patients benefit from proning. An increase in PaO₂ of more than 10 torr in the first 30 minutes is a good indicator of success. Proning should be maintained for a minimum of 12 hours at a time, as tolerated.

questions.stem: A patient on volume control requires plateau pressures above 30 cm H₂O. You should recommend:
opts: Switching to pressure control at a safe pressure limit of 30 cm H₂O or less
Increasing the inspiratory flow to lower Pplat
Adding PEEP to reduce the plateau pressure
Accepting the pressure because volume is guaranteed
questions.why: To help avoid or worsen lung injury, patients requiring plateau pressures higher than 30 cm H₂O during VC ventilation should probably be switched to pressure control at a safe pressure limit — 30 cm H₂O or less.

questions.stem: A key DISADVANTAGE of pressure control compared with volume control is that:
opts: Tidal volume varies with changes in compliance and resistance, and those changes are difficult to detect
Airway pressures rise as compliance falls, risking barotrauma
The fixed square flow pattern causes asynchrony
It cannot deliver a decelerating flow pattern
questions.why: With pressure control, VT varies with changes in CRS and Raw, and those changes are difficult to detect, so tidal volume and minute ventilation must be monitored closely. Rising airway pressures with falling compliance and a fixed square flow pattern causing asynchrony are disadvantages of VOLUME control.

questions.stem: In a PEEP study during volume control ventilation, which measurement identifies optimal PEEP?
opts: The PEEP level yielding the smallest Pplat − PEEP difference, and thus the highest static compliance
The PEEP level producing the highest peak inspiratory pressure
The PEEP level producing the lowest plateau pressure regardless of PEEP
The PEEP level at which PIP and Pplat converge
questions.why: Disregard the peak pressure — it is there to confuse you. What matters is the difference between plateau pressure and PEEP. Because tidal volume is constant, the smaller this difference, the greater the compliance, since CRS = VT ÷ (Pplat − PEEP).

questions.stem: During a PEEP study, static compliance peaks at 35 mL/cm H₂O when PEEP is set at 10 cm H₂O. Optimal PEEP for this patient is:
opts: 10 cm H₂O
35 cm H₂O
5 cm H₂O
20 cm H₂O
questions.why: Based on the static compliance method, the optimal PEEP for this patient is 10 cm H₂O — the level yielding the highest static compliance of 35 mL/cm H₂O.

questions.stem: Using the equal pressure method during PC ventilation, a patient's exhaled VT is 390 mL at PEEP 5, 410 mL at PEEP 10, 430 mL at PEEP 15, and 380 mL at PEEP 20. Optimal PEEP is:
opts: 15 cm H₂O
10 cm H₂O
20 cm H₂O
5 cm H₂O
questions.why: With the equal pressure method you maintain a constant ΔP (PIP − PEEP), typically 15–25 cm H₂O, and assess the exhaled VT; the largest volume represents optimal PEEP. Here the optimal PEEP is 15 cm H₂O, corresponding to the maximum volume change for a given ΔP at 430 mL.

questions.stem: Once the lower inflection point (LIP) is identified on a static pressure-volume curve, PEEP is typically set:
opts: 2–3 cm H₂O above the LIP
At the LIP exactly
5–10 cm H₂O below the LIP
At the upper inflection point
questions.why: The minimum pressure needed to prevent alveolar collapse corresponds to the lowest pressure needed to exceed the pressure required to open collapsed alveoli — the lower inflection point. Once measured, PEEP is typically set 2–3 cm H₂O above the LIP.

questions.stem: On a static pressure-volume curve, a low slope at HIGH pressures and volumes (the "beak sign") indicates:
opts: The limits of elastic expansion have been reached — overdistention is occurring
High pressures are needed to open collapsed alveoli
The safe and efficient zone for volume exchange
An air leak in the circuit
questions.why: The slope of any line on the P-V graph equals compliance. A low slope at low pressures and volumes indicates that high pressures are needed to open collapsed alveoli; a steep slope at moderate volumes is the sweet spot for safe and efficient volume exchange; and a low slope at high pressures and volumes indicates the limits of elastic expansion have been reached, with overdistention occurring — the beak sign.

questions.stem: Using volumetric capnography to set PEEP, optimum PEEP is reached:
opts: Just before the %VTCO₂ begins to fall
When the %VTCO₂ reaches zero
At the highest PEEP the patient tolerates
When the %VTCO₂ first begins to rise
questions.why: As PEEP rises and additional perfused alveoli are recruited, the %VTCO₂ increases. If PEEP becomes high enough to overdistend alveoli, deadspace increases, lung perfusion is impeded, and %VTCO₂ begins to fall. Optimum PEEP is reached just before the %VTCO₂ begins to fall.

questions.stem: Using the oxygen-delivery approach with noninvasive surrogates, optimum PEEP is the level that:
opts: Maintains SpO₂ ≥ 88–90% without lowering the patient's blood pressure
Produces the highest possible SpO₂ regardless of blood pressure
Produces the lowest plateau pressure
Maximizes the peak inspiratory pressure
questions.why: The NBRC may substitute arterial blood pressure as an indicator of cardiac output and SpO₂ for ABGs. Using these data, optimum PEEP is the level needed to maintain SpO₂ at 88–90% or above without lowering blood pressure — and you would back off any PEEP increase that significantly lowers blood pressure. PEEP is optimized when the desired increase in CaO₂ is not offset by decreases in cardiac output.

questions.stem: Bedside estimates of respiratory mechanics for PEEP titration require:
opts: Complete relaxation of the respiratory muscles and at least 2–3 seconds of zero flow for pressures to equilibrate
Spontaneous breathing effort to be preserved
A pulmonary artery catheter in place
An FiO₂ of 1.0 throughout the study
questions.why: Common to the mechanics-based methods is that bedside estimates require complete relaxation of the patient's respiratory muscles and adequate time under static conditions of zero flow for airway and alveolar pressures to equilibrate — at least 2–3 seconds. Getting accurate data can be challenging and may require sedation or paralysis.

questions.stem: An order reads "CPAP + PS of 5+10 cm H₂O." The resulting PIP and driving pressure are:
opts: PIP 15 cm H₂O, ΔP 10 cm H₂O
PIP 10 cm H₂O, ΔP 5 cm H₂O
PIP 5 cm H₂O, ΔP 10 cm H₂O
PIP 15 cm H₂O, ΔP 15 cm H₂O
questions.why: With CPAP+PS, the PS level is the pressure ABOVE CPAP. A CPAP+PS order of 5+10 cm H₂O means a CPAP of 5 cm H₂O plus 10 cm H₂O of pressure support, giving a PIP of 15 cm H₂O and a driving pressure of 15 − 5, or 10 cm H₂O.

questions.stem: An order reads "BiPAP 5/10 cm H₂O" (EPAP/IPAP). The resulting PIP and driving pressure are:
opts: PIP 10 cm H₂O, ΔP 5 cm H₂O
PIP 15 cm H₂O, ΔP 10 cm H₂O
PIP 10 cm H₂O, ΔP 10 cm H₂O
PIP 5 cm H₂O, ΔP 5 cm H₂O
questions.why: With BiPAP you independently set IPAP and EPAP. An order for BiPAP 5/10 cm H₂O looks similar to a CPAP+PS order but results in a PIP equal to the IPAP of 10 cm H₂O, and a ΔP only half as large: 10 − 5 = 5 cm H₂O.

questions.stem: A patient is on BiPAP 10/5 cm H₂O IPAP/EPAP. You need to improve OXYGENATION ONLY. You should:
opts: Increase both IPAP and EPAP equally, for example to 12/7 cm H₂O
Increase only the IPAP to 15 cm H₂O
Decrease the EPAP to 3 cm H₂O
Decrease both IPAP and EPAP equally
questions.why: Increase both IPAP and EPAP equally — to 12/7 cm H₂O, an increase of 2 cm H₂O each. This keeps ΔP constant so ventilation is unchanged, while the increase in baseline pressure may help improve oxygenation.

questions.stem: A patient is on BiPAP 10/5 cm H₂O IPAP/EPAP. You need to increase VENTILATION ONLY. You should:
opts: Increase only the IPAP, to 15 cm H₂O
Increase both IPAP and EPAP equally to 12/7 cm H₂O
Increase only the EPAP to 8 cm H₂O
Decrease the IPAP to 8 cm H₂O
questions.why: Increase only the IPAP, to 15 cm H₂O. This increases ΔP and therefore ventilation, but because the baseline pressure is unchanged it will not have a major effect on oxygenation. Alternatively, if oxygenation is stable and comfort is an issue, you could decrease the EPAP by 2 cm H₂O to 3 cm H₂O, which also increases ΔP.

questions.stem: A patient on BiPAP 10/5 cm H₂O needs BOTH improved oxygenation and increased ventilation. You should:
opts: Increase both, raising IPAP more than EPAP — for example IPAP to 15 and EPAP to 7 cm H₂O
Increase both equally to 15/10 cm H₂O
Raise EPAP more than IPAP, to 12/9 cm H₂O
Increase IPAP only, to 20 cm H₂O
questions.why: Increase both IPAP and EPAP, but increase IPAP more than EPAP — IPAP to 15 cm H₂O and EPAP to 7 cm H₂O. This increases ΔP, increasing ventilation, while also raising the baseline pressure, which may help improve oxygenation.

questions.stem: On BiPAP, a patient's PaCO₂ is rising and pH is falling. The correct adjustment is:
opts: Increase IPAP or increase ΔP, and increase the mandatory rate if the patient's rate is low
Decrease IPAP or decrease ΔP
Increase EPAP while keeping ΔP constant
Increase the FiO₂
questions.why: To decrease PaCO₂ or raise pH, increase IPAP or increase ΔP, and also increase the mandatory rate if the patient rate is low. To increase PaCO₂ or lower pH, decrease IPAP or ΔP. Oxygenation is instead adjusted via FiO₂ and EPAP.

questions.stem: A patient on BiPAP has a PaO₂ of 48 torr on an FiO₂ of 0.55. The correct adjustment is:
opts: Increase EPAP while keeping ΔP constant, because shunting is present
Raise the FiO₂ to 0.70
Increase IPAP only
Decrease EPAP to reduce deadspace
questions.why: If simple V/Q imbalance is present and FiO₂ is below 0.50, raise the FiO₂. If shunting is present — PaO₂ of 50 torr or less with FiO₂ of 0.50 or more — increase EPAP, keeping ΔP constant to avoid altering the PaCO₂.

questions.stem: As a patient's oxygenation improves on BiPAP, the correct order of weaning is:
opts: Decrease FiO₂ first until ≤ 0.50, then lower EPAP while keeping ΔP constant
Lower EPAP first, then reduce FiO₂
Lower IPAP and EPAP together, then reduce FiO₂
Reduce the backup rate first, then the FiO₂
questions.why: When oxygenation improves, first decrease FiO₂ until it is 0.50 or less, and then lower EPAP — keeping ΔP constant to avoid altering the PaCO₂.

questions.stem: Why might HFV reduce ventilator-associated lung injury?
opts: Less pressure is transmitted to the distal airways and alveoli
It eliminates the need for PEEP
It completely prevents any gas exchange abnormality
It uses tidal volumes larger than anatomic deadspace
questions.why: Because less pressure is transmitted to the distal airways and alveoli, HFV may decrease the risk of ventilator-associated lung injuries such as barotrauma and bronchopulmonary dysplasia in neonates. HFV may also improve gas exchange in the presence of air leaks such as persistent pneumothoraces or PIE.

questions.stem: Based on current evidence, when should HFV NOT be applied?
opts: When conventional ventilation can provide adequate support, and it should not be used as rescue therapy
In any neonate with meconium aspiration syndrome
Whenever an air leak is present
In patients with severe IRDS
questions.why: Based on current evidence, HFV should not be applied if conventional ventilation can provide adequate patient support, and it should not be used as rescue therapy. Recent studies have shown a transient improvement in oxygenation but an increase in mortality among ARDS patients. Meconium aspiration, air leaks, and severe IRDS are among the indications.

questions.stem: Which is a relative CONTRAINDICATION to high-frequency ventilation?
opts: Hypotension or unstable cardiovascular status, air trapping/dynamic hyperinflation, or intracranial hemorrhage in neonates
Severe ARDS with an air-leak syndrome
Bronchopulmonary dysplasia
Congenital diaphragmatic hernia
questions.why: Relative contraindications to HFV include hypotension or unstable cardiovascular status, the presence of air trapping or dynamic hyperinflation, and, among neonates, intracranial hemorrhage. Severe ARDS with air leak, BPD, and congenital diaphragmatic hernia are indications.

questions.stem: For a patient on invasive ventilatory support for hypoxemic respiratory failure, which suctioning approach best prevents derecruitment?
opts: An in-line/closed catheter system, ideally, with a lung recruitment maneuver afterward if volume was lost
Open suctioning with sterile technique and a 20-second pass
Disconnecting from the ventilator and bagging with room air
Instilling saline before each pass to loosen secretions
questions.why: If the patient is receiving invasive ventilatory support for hypoxemic respiratory failure, use an in-line/closed catheter system (ideal) or a bronchoscope ventilator adapter. Use the ventilator's 100% O₂ button if available, and recommend or implement a lung recruitment maneuver after any suctioning episode likely to have reduced lung volume, such as a loss of PEEP.

questions.stem: Which modes constitute FULL ventilatory support for an intubated patient in respiratory failure?
opts: A/C (VC or PC) and normal-rate SIMV (VC or PC), usually with PS or a dual mode such as PRVC
CPAP with pressure support alone
Low-rate SIMV without pressure support
Pressure support alone at 20 cm H₂O
questions.why: In NBRC scenarios you generally start an intubated patient in respiratory failure on full ventilatory support, with the ventilator initially responsible for the full minute volume and workload. Full ventilatory support modes include A/C (VC or PC) and normal-rate SIMV (VC or PC), usually with PS, or dual-mode ventilation such as PRVC.

questions.stem: A patient with sleep apnea cannot tolerate CPAP. Appropriate recommendations include:
opts: Alternative masks, humidification, ramp feature, auto-titration, or pressure relief such as C-flex or BiPAP
Discontinuing therapy permanently
Increasing the CPAP above 15 cm H₂O to overcome obstruction
Switching to supplemental oxygen alone
questions.why: If the patient cannot tolerate CPAP, assess and recommend equipment or interface alternatives to improve tolerance — various mask options, humidification, the ramp feature, auto-titration, and pressure relief such as C-flex, expiratory pressure relief, or bilevel positive airway pressure. CPAP is set by prescription or auto-CPAP to a maximum of 15 cm H₂O.

questions.stem: An infant on CPAP of 8 cm H₂O and FiO₂ 0.65 has a PaO₂ of 45 torr. You should:
opts: Switch to ventilatory support
Increase the CPAP to 12 cm H₂O
Increase the FiO₂ to 1.0 and continue CPAP
Decrease the CPAP to reduce overdistention
questions.why: Switch to ventilatory support if the PaO₂ is below 50 torr on CPAP above 7 cm H₂O and FiO₂ above 0.60, or if hypercapnic respiratory failure develops.

questions.stem: Aerosolized antibiotics such as Colistin, Cayston, and TOBI are generally indicated only in patients with:
opts: Cystic fibrosis and suspected or confirmed Pseudomonas aeruginosa infection
Community-acquired pneumonia
Ventilator-associated pneumonia
Chronic bronchitis with any gram-positive organism
questions.why: Aerosolized antibiotics (Colistin, Cayston, TOBI) are generally indicated only in patients with cystic fibrosis and suspected or confirmed Pseudomonas aeruginosa (gram-negative) pulmonary infections.

questions.stem: Which inhaled steroid preparation is NOT intended for MDI or DPI delivery?
opts: Budesonide (Pulmicort)
Fluticasone
Beclomethasone
Mometasone
questions.why: Except for budesonide (Pulmicort), common inhaled steroid preparations are all intended for use in an MDI or DPI, so proper patient technique is critical.

questions.stem: Optimal MDI technique includes actuating during a deep inhalation of what duration, followed by what breath-hold?
opts: 3- to 5-second inhalation, followed by a 10-second breath-hold
1-second inhalation, followed by a 3-second breath-hold
10-second inhalation, followed by a 3-second breath-hold
A rapid forceful inhalation with no breath-hold
questions.why: The patient should open the mouth wide, keep the tongue down, and actuate during a 3- to 5-second deep inhalation, followed by a 10-second breath-hold. Holding the MDI 2 inches away from the open mouth may enhance lung deposition.

questions.stem: A cystic fibrosis patient is prescribed a bronchodilator, a mucolytic, an inhaled steroid, an aerosolized antibiotic, and airway clearance therapy. The correct order is:
opts: Bronchodilator, mucolytic, airway clearance, steroid, antibiotic
Antibiotic, steroid, mucolytic, bronchodilator, airway clearance
Steroid, bronchodilator, antibiotic, mucolytic, airway clearance
Airway clearance, bronchodilator, steroid, mucolytic, antibiotic
questions.why: If the patient is receiving several inhaled medications, the recommended order is bronchodilator first, followed by mucolytic, then airway clearance therapy, then steroids, and finally the aerosolized antibiotic.

questions.stem: Which beta agonist property should you generally seek when recommending a bronchodilator?
opts: The least β1 (cardiac) and most β2 (bronchodilation) effects, such as albuterol or levalbuterol
The most β1 effects to support cardiac output
Equal β1 and β2 activity
Pure alpha-adrenergic activity
questions.why: All β-agonists have some cardiovascular and CNS effects. In general, recommend those with the least β1 (cardiac) and most β2 (bronchodilation) effects, such as albuterol or its isomer levalbuterol.

questions.stem: During an acute asthma exacerbation, the standard bronchodilator dose should be:
opts: Repeated every 20 minutes up to three times, or given as continuous nebulization until symptoms are relieved
Given once and reassessed in 4 hours
Repeated every 5 minutes up to ten times
Replaced by a long-acting β-agonist
questions.why: In acute exacerbations of asthma, repeat the standard dose every 20 minutes up to three times, or provide continuous nebulization until symptoms are relieved.

questions.stem: Which statement about long-acting β-agonists (LABAs) in asthma is correct?
opts: They may increase the risk of severe exacerbations or death and should be used only in combination with inhaled steroids, never for acute exacerbations
They are the drug of choice for acute exacerbations
