They should be used as monotherapy in persistent asthma
They have no cardiovascular effects
questions.why: LABAs may increase the risk of severe exacerbations or death in some patients with asthma, should only be used in combination with inhaled steroids in these patients, and should not be recommended or used to treat acute exacerbations of asthma.

questions.stem: For maintenance therapy of bronchospasm in COPD, appropriate choices include:
opts: A LABA such as salmeterol, a long-acting anticholinergic such as tiotropium, or a combination such as umeclidinium + vilanterol
Short-acting albuterol scheduled four times daily as the sole therapy
An aerosolized antibiotic
A mucolytic alone
questions.why: For maintenance therapy of bronchospasm in patients with COPD, consider a LABA such as salmeterol, a long-acting anticholinergic such as tiotropium, or a LABA plus long-acting anticholinergic combination such as umeclidinium plus vilanterol.

questions.stem: Why must a bronchodilator always precede mucolytic therapy?
opts: All mucolytics are irritating to the airway and can cause bronchospasm
Mucolytics inactivate bronchodilators if given first
Bronchodilators thin secretions more effectively
Mucolytics require a higher inspiratory flow
questions.why: All mucolytics are irritating to the airway, so to prevent bronchospasm always precede treatment with a bronchodilator. Mucolytics should also be administered in combination with airway clearance therapy to facilitate removal of secretions.

questions.stem: Why must patients rinse the mouth after inhaled steroid therapy?
opts: To prevent pharyngitis and oral candidiasis
To improve drug absorption
To clear residual propellant taste
To reduce systemic β1 effects
questions.why: Rinsing the mouth after therapy is essential to prevent pharyngitis and oral candidiasis. Using spacers or valved holding chambers with MDI-delivered steroids minimizes pharyngeal deposition and the incidence of pharyngitis and candidiasis.

questions.stem: Which aerosol device should most infants and small children receive?
opts: An MDI with a holding chamber and mask, with an SVN as an alternative if tolerated
A dry-powder inhaler
A breath-actuated MDI
A slow-mist Respimat
questions.why: Most infants and small children should receive aerosolized drugs via an MDI with a holding chamber and mask, with an SVN as an alternative if tolerated. SVN administration should be reserved for acutely ill adults who cannot use either a DPI or MDI, and DPIs are ideal for maintenance therapy in outpatient adults, larger children, and adolescents who can generate enough inspiratory flow.

questions.stem: Which aerosol device CANNOT be used for drug delivery during mechanical ventilation?
opts: A dry-powder inhaler
A small-volume jet nebulizer
A vibrating mesh nebulizer
An MDI with an in-line adapter
questions.why: A DPI requires high inspiratory flow, can result in pharyngeal deposition, is difficult for high doses, and cannot be used for drug delivery during mechanical ventilation. Electronic nebulizers are in fact favored during mechanical ventilation because they add no flow or volume to the circuit.

questions.stem: Normal fluid intake and output for adults is:
opts: 2–3 liters/day
1 liter/day
4–5 liters/day
500 mL/day
questions.why: The normal fluid intake and output for adults is 2–3 liters per day. Maintaining the balance between intake and output is essential to maintain proper metabolic functions.

questions.stem: During permissive hypercapnia, respiratory acidosis is generally accepted until the pH falls below:
opts: 7.20 exactly
questions.why: Permissive hypercapnia accepts a higher-than-normal PaCO₂ in exchange for a lower risk of lung injury from smaller tidal volumes or PIPs. In general, hypercapnia and respiratory acidosis can be accepted until the pH falls below 7.25–7.30, at which point recommend either an increase in rate or administration of sodium bicarbonate.

questions.stem: Lung-protective volume-control ventilation uses tidal volumes of:
opts: 4–6 mL/kg of predicted body weight
8–10 mL/kg of predicted body weight
10–12 mL/kg of actual body weight
2–3 mL/kg of predicted body weight
questions.why: Lung-protective strategies include volume-control ventilation with low tidal volumes of 4–6 mL/kg of PBW, low plateau pressures of 30 cm H₂O or less, pressure-control ventilation with PIP of 30 cm H₂O or less, dual-mode ventilation such as PRVC, APRV, and high-frequency percussive ventilation.

questions.stem: Signs of an allergic reaction such as hives, swelling, or redness appear after a new medication. The RT should:
opts: Immediately recommend the medication be stopped, alert the medical emergency team, and closely monitor the patient
Halve the dose and continue
Document and reassess at the next scheduled treatment
Administer a bronchodilator and continue the medication
questions.why: Anytime an adverse patient response is noted, the RT should immediately ensure therapy is stopped, notify the nurse and doctor, and carefully monitor and help stabilize the patient. With signs of allergic reaction after a new medication, immediately recommend it be stopped, alert the medical emergency team, and monitor closely.

questions.stem: Which finding constitutes a marked change in vital signs warranting concern during therapy?
opts: A change 20% above or below initial baseline, or outside critical limits
Any change of 5% from baseline
A change only if the patient reports symptoms
A change of 50% or more from baseline
questions.why: Adverse effects to monitor include marked changes in vital signs — 20% above or below initial baseline or outside of critical limits — along with a greater than 4% drop in SpO₂ or any fall below 90%, new or worsening arrhythmia, cyanosis, severe paroxysmal coughing, changes in level of consciousness, and hemoptysis.

questions.stem: If a serious adverse effect is observed during therapy, the RT should always:
opts: Stop therapy, stay with and monitor the patient, and stabilize by providing oxygen
Complete the treatment then notify the nurse
Leave to summon the physician immediately
Reduce the dose and observe
questions.why: If a serious adverse effect is observed during therapy, always stop therapy, stay with and monitor the patient, and stabilize the patient by providing oxygen therapy — calling for assistance if necessary. In a hospital, notify the nurse and physician immediately; if life-threatening, call a MET/rapid-response team or code blue. At an alternate care site, dial 911.

questions.stem: The RT identifies a major contraindication to an ordered therapy. The correct action is:
opts: Do not initiate the therapy; contact the prescribing physician for guidance or an alternative
Initiate the therapy but monitor more closely
Modify the therapy independently and document
Withhold the therapy without notifying anyone
questions.why: The RT must prescreen all patients for potential contraindications and hazards before therapy. If any major contraindications exist, the RT should not initiate the therapy; instead contact the prescribing physician for guidance on whether to proceed or provide an alternative.

questions.stem: A patient has rhonchi and tactile fremitus. The most likely problem and recommendation are:
opts: Secretions in the large airways — airway clearance therapy
Bronchospasm — bronchodilator therapy
Laryngeal edema — cool mist and racemic epinephrine
Pulmonary edema — CPAP and diuretics
questions.why: Rhonchi and tactile fremitus indicate secretions in the large airways, and the recommendation is airway clearance therapy. Wheezing indicates bronchospasm, CHF, or airway inflammation; inspiratory stridor indicates laryngeal edema.

questions.stem: A patient develops inspiratory stridor after extubation. Appropriate recommendations include:
opts: Cool mist and racemic epinephrine, with diagnostic bronchoscopy if needed
Airway clearance therapy and suctioning
Diuretics and positive inotropes
Lung expansion therapy and oxygen
questions.why: Inspiratory stridor suggests laryngeal edema — for example post-extubation or from infection — as well as tumor/mass, inhalation injury, or foreign-body aspiration. Recommend cool mist or racemic epinephrine, and diagnostic bronchoscopy.

questions.stem: Frothy, pink secretions indicate what problem, and what should be recommended?
opts: Pulmonary edema — treat the underlying cause such as CHF, apply CPAP/BiPAP, give oxygen, and consider inotropes and diuretics
Acute airway infection — antibiotic therapy
Excessive secretions — airway clearance and suctioning
Atelectasis — lung expansion therapy
questions.why: Frothy pink secretions indicate pulmonary edema. Recommendations are to treat the underlying cause such as CHF, apply positive airway pressure (CPAP/BiPAP), give oxygen therapy, and use medications including positive inotropes and diuretics. Yellow/opaque sputum instead indicates acute airway infection.

questions.stem: Which finding during mechanical ventilation suggests a pneumothorax?
opts: A sudden increase in airway pressure in volume control, or a decrease in VT in pressure control
A gradual decrease in peak pressure over several hours
A rise in exhaled tidal volume
An increase in static compliance
questions.why: Clinical signs of pneumothorax include sudden respiratory distress, decreased chest expansion and breath sounds on the affected side, tracheal deviation away from the affected side, a hyperresonant percussion note, absent lung markings on x-ray, and — during mechanical ventilation — a sudden increase in airway pressure in volume control or a decrease in VT in pressure control.

questions.stem: A pneumothorax is suspected in a ventilated patient. Initial recommendations include:
opts: A stat chest x-ray, 100% O₂ to help reabsorb the gas, and settings changed to minimize peak pressures
Increasing PEEP to re-expand the lung
Increasing tidal volume to improve ventilation
Immediate extubation
questions.why: If a pneumothorax is suspected, recommend obtaining a stat chest x-ray and placing the patient on 100% O₂, which helps reabsorb the gas. If the patient is on positive-pressure ventilation, recommend changing settings to minimize peak inspiratory pressures — decrease PIP, lower PEEP, lower VT.

questions.stem: A patient has dry mucous membranes, hypotension, decreased urine output and skin turgor, an increased hematocrit, and thick tenacious secretions. You should recommend:
opts: Increasing IV fluid intake, heated humidification, mucolytics, and avoiding diuretics
Diuretic therapy and fluid restriction
Dialysis and inotropic agents
Restricting oral intake and monitoring closely
questions.why: These are the signs of dehydration (negative fluid balance). Management is to increase IV fluid intake, minimize sensible and insensible water loss, use heated humidification during mechanical ventilation, administer mucolytics for thick secretions, insert a CVP or PA catheter in critically ill patients to monitor fluid status, and AVOID the use of diuretics.

questions.stem: A patient has pedal edema, pulmonary edema, hepatomegaly, jugular venous distention, a decreased hematocrit, and increased CVP and PAWP. You should recommend:
opts: Fluid restriction, diuretic therapy, inotropic agents if heart failure is suspected, and dialysis if renal failure is present
Increasing IV fluid intake and heated humidification
Administering mucolytics and avoiding diuretics
Withholding all monitoring until the x-ray is reviewed
questions.why: These are the signs of overhydration (positive I/O). Management is to restrict and closely monitor fluid intake, initiate diuretic therapy, administer inotropic agents if heart failure is suspected, implement dialysis if renal failure is present, and insert a CVP or PA catheter to monitor fluid status if indicated.

questions.stem: Which artificial airway permits phonation and allows testing of upper airway patency and control?
opts: A cuffed, fenestrated tracheostomy tube
A cuffed, unfenestrated tracheostomy tube
An oral endotracheal tube
A laryngeal mask airway
questions.why: A cuffed, fenestrated tracheostomy tube has the same indications as a standard tracheostomy tube with the added benefit of permitting phonation (speaking) and testing upper airway patency and control.

questions.stem: An ETT has an excessive cuff leak despite adding air to the pilot balloon. Recommendations include:
opts: Reintubation with a proper-size tube, using an ETT exchanger, deflating and repositioning the tube, or a pilot balloon repair kit
Adding progressively more air until the leak stops
Increasing the ventilator tidal volume to compensate
Switching to pressure control and accepting the leak
questions.why: Excessive ETT cuff leak despite adding air may be caused by a blown cuff, a broken or defective pilot balloon or tube, too small an ETT, or the tube sitting too high with the cuff at vocal cord level. Recommendations are reintubation with a proper-size tube, using an ETT exchanger, deflating the cuff and repositioning the ETT, or a pilot balloon repair kit.

questions.stem: For a thoracentesis, the patient should be positioned:
opts: Sitting on the edge of the bed, leaning forward over a pillow-draped bedside table, arms crossed, with an assistant in front
Supine with the involved side elevated and the arm flexed over the head
In Trendelenburg with the affected side down
Prone with the abdomen freely suspended
questions.why: For thoracentesis, the patient sits on the edge of the bed leaning forward over a pillow-draped bedside table, arms crossed, with an assistant in front for stability. For chest tube insertion, the involved side is slightly elevated with the arm flexed over the head.

questions.stem: An immobile patient at risk for decubitus ulcers should have position changed:
opts: Side to side every 2 hours, with a decubitus mattress
Every 8 hours
Only when the patient requests it
Every 30 minutes
questions.why: For an immobile patient at risk for bedsores, change position side to side every 2 hours and use a decubitus mattress.

questions.stem: A patient on a 4-L/min nasal cannula complains of nasal and mouth dryness. You should:
opts: Add a humidifier, particularly because the input flow is ≥ 4 L/min
Reduce the flow to 2 L/min
Switch to a nonrebreathing mask
Add a heat and moisture exchanger
questions.why: Insufficient humidity causes drying of the mucosa. Add a humidifier, particularly if the input flow of the nasal cannula is 4 L/min or more.

questions.stem: A patient receiving noninvasive positive pressure support complains of dryness. You should:
opts: Add a blow-by humidifier and never use an HME during noninvasive positive pressure therapy
Add an HME to conserve moisture
Reduce the IPAP to lower flow
Switch to a nasal cannula
questions.why: Cold dry gas delivered at very high flows causes this complaint. Add a blow-by humidifier — and never use heat and moisture exchangers during noninvasive positive pressure therapy.

questions.stem: A ventilated patient using an HME has developed very thick secretions. You should:
opts: Add heated humidity, because HMEs are contraindicated in patients with thick secretions
Replace the HME with a new one of the same type
Increase the tidal volume
Instill saline before each suction pass
questions.why: The use of an HME may be contraindicated for this patient. Add heated humidity — HMEs are contraindicated in patients with thick secretions.

questions.stem: A stroke patient at risk for increased intracranial pressure should be instructed to:
opts: Use a "huff" cough, or sit up until the cough subsides, rather than cough strenuously
Cough as forcefully as possible to clear secretions
Avoid all coughing indefinitely
Use only mechanical insufflation-exsufflation
questions.why: Discourage strenuous coughing for stroke patients or those otherwise predisposed to increased intracranial pressure. Instead, instruct these patients to use a huff cough, or sit them up until the cough subsides.

questions.stem: A patient using a flow-oriented incentive spirometer cannot generate enough flow to activate the indicator. You should recommend:
opts: A volume-oriented device or one designed for patients with obstructive disorders; consider IPPB or Metaneb
A larger mouthpiece
More frequent attempts at the same device
Discontinuing lung expansion therapy
questions.why: An obstructive disorder or muscle weakness may prevent the patient from generating the flow needed to use a flow-oriented device. Recommend a volume-oriented device or one designed for patients with obstructive disorders, and consider another modality such as IPPB or Metaneb.

questions.stem: During IPPB, the pressure does not rise after triggering. The likely cause and fix are:
opts: A major leak or poor airway seal — fix circuit leaks, coach a tight mouth seal, use nose clips, or consider a flanged lip seal or mask
Excessive pressure setting — lower the pressure
Hyperventilation — coach slower breathing
Inadequate FiO₂ — turn off air mix
questions.why: If pressure does not rise after triggering, the cause is a major leak or poor airway seal. Fix any circuit leaks, coach the patient to achieve a tight mouth seal, use nose clips, and consider a flanged lip seal or mask. The same modifications apply if the machine does not cycle off at end-inspiration.

questions.stem: A ventilated patient on PEEP 10 cm H₂O and FiO₂ 0.75 has a PaO₂ of 175 torr. You should:
opts: Lower the FiO₂, because the high FiO₂ poses the greater risk (O₂ toxicity)
Lower the PEEP, because barotrauma is the greater risk
Leave both settings unchanged
Increase PEEP and lower FiO₂ simultaneously
questions.why: If hyperoxia is present (PaO₂ above 100 torr), lower the parameter — FiO₂ or PEEP — that is potentially most dangerous at that moment. With PEEP 10 and FiO₂ 0.75, the high FiO₂ is of most concern for O₂ toxicity and should be lowered.

questions.stem: A ventilated patient on PEEP 18 cm H₂O and FiO₂ 0.45 has a PaO₂ of 150 torr. You should:
opts: Lower the PEEP, because the high PEEP poses the greater risk (barotrauma)
Lower the FiO₂, because O₂ toxicity is the greater risk
Increase the FiO₂ to allow a PEEP reduction
Make no change until the next ABG
questions.why: With hyperoxia present, lower whichever parameter is most dangerous at that moment. For a patient on 18 cm H₂O PEEP and FiO₂ 0.45 with a PaO₂ of 150 torr, the high PEEP level is of most concern for barotrauma and should be lowered.

questions.stem: A ventilated patient has a PaO₂ of 52 torr on an FiO₂ of 0.70. Using the 60-60 rule, you should:
opts: Add or increase PEEP/CPAP, because the problem is shunting
Simply increase the FiO₂, because the problem is V/Q imbalance
Decrease PEEP to improve cardiac output
Increase the tidal volume
questions.why: By the 60-60 rule: if PaO₂ is above 60 torr on an FiO₂ below 0.6, the problem is mainly V/Q imbalance and will respond to a simple FiO₂ increase. If PaO₂ is below 60 torr on an FiO₂ above 0.6, the problem is shunting and PEEP/CPAP must be added or increased.

questions.stem: A ventilated patient has a PaO₂ of 55 torr on an FiO₂ of 0.40. The correct adjustment is:
opts: Increase the FiO₂, because it is less than 0.60
Increase PEEP, because hypoxemia is present
Lower the FiO₂ and add PEEP
Make no change; this is acceptable
questions.why: If the PaO₂ or SaO₂ is low — below 60 torr or 90% — hypoxemia is present. Increase the FiO₂ if it is less than 0.60; increase PEEP if the FiO₂ is 0.60 or greater.

questions.stem: When setting a desired PaCO₂ target in a COPD patient with acute-on-chronic ventilatory failure, the goal should be:
opts: The PaCO₂ that normalizes the pH, which may be substantially higher than 40 torr
Always exactly 40 torr
Always below 35 torr
The lowest PaCO₂ the ventilator can achieve
questions.why: Be careful specifying the desired PaCO₂ — the goal should be the PaCO₂ that normalizes the pH. Although in most situations this means a normal PaCO₂ of 40 torr, in a COPD patient who develops ventilatory failure on top of a compensated respiratory acidosis (acute-on-chronic), the desired PaCO₂ could be substantially higher than normal.

questions.stem: If a ventilated patient's tidal volume is already properly set, the preferred method to alter minute ventilation is:
opts: Rate changes
Tidal volume changes
Changing the inspiratory flow
Changing the FiO₂
questions.why: Minute ventilation can be changed by changing either the respiratory rate or the delivered VT. If the patient's VT is properly set — 6–8 mL/kg PBW with a plateau pressure below 30 cm H₂O — rate changes are the preferred method to alter minute ventilation.

questions.stem: During volume-control A/C ventilation, inspiratory time is determined by:
opts: The set flow and volume: I-time = volume (L) ÷ flow (L/sec)
The clinician setting it directly
The respiratory rate alone
The patient's inspiratory effort
questions.why: During volume-control A/C, I-time is a function of the set flow and volume — I-time = volume in liters divided by flow in L/sec. During pressure-control A/C, the I-time is usually set by the clinician. In both modes E-time is the time remaining between breath cycles, determined by the I-time and frequency.

questions.stem: A patient with severe expiratory airflow obstruction has auto-PEEP and an I:E ratio of 1:2. The first step is to:
opts: Adjust settings to allow enough time for complete exhalation, decreasing the I:E ratio toward 1:4 or 1:5
Increase the I:E ratio toward 1:1
Add extrinsic PEEP equal to the auto-PEEP
Increase the tidal volume
questions.why: Patients with severe expiratory airflow obstruction typically exhibit prolonged E-times and low I:E ratios such as 1:4 or 1:5 during spontaneous breathing. If similar ratios are not provided during mechanical ventilation, air trapping or auto-PEEP occurs. If auto-PEEP is present and the I:E ratio is high (1:1 or 1:2), the first step is to adjust settings to allow enough time for complete exhalation, decreasing the I:E ratio to 1:4 or 1:5. The ratio is decreased by increasing E-time and decreasing I-time.

questions.stem: A patient on volume-control A/C develops respiratory alkalosis because the total respiratory rate is too high. You should recommend:
opts: Switching to normal-rate SIMV, adding deadspace, or sedation if the patient is agitated
Increasing the tidal volume
Increasing the set rate on A/C
Switching to pressure support alone
questions.why: When full ventilatory support is needed but the total respiratory rate results in hyperventilation (respiratory alkalosis) on A/C mode, switch to volume- or pressure-control normal-rate SIMV, add deadspace, or recommend sedation if the patient is agitated.

questions.stem: To reduce plateau pressure in an ARDS patient with low lung compliance on volume-control A/C, recommend:
opts: Switching to pressure control A/C with a maximum PIP of less than 30 cm H₂O
Increasing the inspiratory flow rate
Adding pressure support
Switching to CPAP with pressure support
questions.why: To reduce airway pressures (plateau pressure) in patients with low lung compliance such as ARDS on volume-control A/C, switch to pressure control A/C with a maximum peak inspiratory pressure of less than 30 cm H₂O.

questions.stem: An ARDS patient is failing the NHLBI protocol. You should consider:
opts: High-frequency ventilation or airway pressure release ventilation (APRV)
Returning to conventional volume control at 10 mL/kg
Discontinuing PEEP
Switching to CPAP alone
questions.why: To support ventilation and oxygenation in patients with ARDS when the NHLBI protocol fails, consider a high-frequency ventilation modality or airway pressure release ventilation (APRV).

questions.stem: To overcome the imposed work of breathing caused by artificial airways or the ventilator circuit, recommend:
opts: Adding or increasing pressure support, or implementing automatic tube compensation if available
Increasing PEEP
Increasing the set tidal volume
Switching to pure control mode
questions.why: To overcome the imposed work of breathing caused by artificial airways or the ventilator circuit, add or increment the pressure-support level, or implement automatic tube compensation if available.

questions.stem: A patient develops mild to moderate HYPERCAPNIA after extubation. To avoid reintubation, recommend:
opts: Noninvasive positive-pressure ventilation
A high-flow nasal cannula at 20–40 L/min
A nonrebreathing mask
Immediate reintubation
questions.why: To avoid reintubation of patients who develop mild to moderate hypercapnia after extubation, provide NPPV. For those who develop mild to moderate HYPOXEMIA after extubation, recommend a high-flow nasal cannula at 20–40 L/min, titrating FiO₂ as needed.

questions.stem: "Open-lung" recruitment maneuvers for patients at risk of atelectasis may involve periodic PEEP levels as high as:
opts: 20–30 cm H₂O for a short period
10–15 cm H₂O sustained indefinitely
40–50 cm H₂O for 10 minutes
5–10 cm H₂O continuously
questions.why: Patients on a ventilator who are particularly at risk for developing atelectasis may be candidates for open-lung techniques such as recruitment maneuvers involving the periodic use of PEEP levels as high as 20–30 cm H₂O for a short period of time.

questions.stem: A patient with a clinically significant bronchopulmonary fistula is not ventilating or oxygenating well on conventional settings. Consider:
opts: High-frequency ventilation such as HFOV, jet, or percussive ventilation
Increasing tidal volume to 10 mL/kg
Removing all PEEP
Switching to pressure support alone
questions.why: Patients with a clinically significant bronchopulmonary fistula who do not ventilate or oxygenate well on other settings may respond well to high-frequency ventilation — HFOV, jet ventilation, or percussive ventilation.

questions.stem: A COPD patient becomes lethargic and disoriented soon after being placed on a nasal cannula at 5 L/min. You should recommend:
opts: Reducing input flow to 2 L/min or switching to an air-entrainment system at 24–28% O₂, monitoring closely and notifying the nurse
Increasing the flow to 6 L/min to correct hypoxemia
Switching to a nonrebreathing mask
Discontinuing oxygen entirely
questions.why: This is oxygen-induced hypoventilation. Recommend that the input flow be reduced to 2 L/min or switch to an air-entrainment system at 24–28% O₂, continue to monitor the patient closely, and notify the nurse.

questions.stem: A physician orders oxygen via a simple mask at an input flow of 2 L/min for an adult. You should:
opts: Recommend increasing the flow to a minimum of 5 L/min to ensure CO₂ washout, or change to a nasal cannula
Set it as ordered, since low flows reduce drying
Recommend a nonrebreathing mask instead
Add a bubble humidifier and proceed
questions.why: The physician may be unaware of the risk of CO₂ rebreathing at low flows with O₂ masks and enclosure devices. Recommend that the input flow be increased to a minimum of 5 L/min to ensure washout of exhaled CO₂, or change to a nasal cannula device.

questions.stem: A patient on a simple mask at 10 L/min has a PaO₂ of 212 torr. You should recommend:
opts: Reducing the FiO₂ — for example, switching to a nasal cannula at about 5 L/min (FiO₂ about 0.40)
Maintaining the current settings
Switching to a nonrebreathing mask
Adding PEEP via mask CPAP
questions.why: A PaO₂ of 212 torr means too much FiO₂ is being delivered. Recommend a reduction in FiO₂ — for example, switching to a nasal cannula at about 5 L/min, which gives an FiO₂ of about 0.40.

questions.stem: After switching an adult from a simple mask to a nonrebreathing mask, the SpO₂ only rises from 83% to 87%. You should consider:
opts: A high-flow nasal cannula at 20–40 L/min with titrated FiO₂, or mask CPAP with high FiO₂ if alveolar shunting is present
Returning to the simple mask at a higher flow
Reducing the FiO₂ to avoid absorption atelectasis
A nasal cannula at 6 L/min
questions.why: A minimal rise reflects an inability to meet high inspiratory flow demands at high FiO₂, or alveolar shunting. Recommend a high-flow nasal cannula at 20–40 L/min, titrating FiO₂ to the desired SpO₂, and consider mask CPAP with high FiO₂ for shunting.

questions.stem: A house-fire victim has an SpO₂ of 98% on a nasal cannula at 5 L/min. You should:
opts: Place the patient on the highest possible FiO₂, usually a nonrebreather, and perform CO-oximetry; consider hyperbaric oxygen
Leave the cannula in place, since the SpO₂ is normal
Reduce the flow to avoid oxygen toxicity
Obtain a chest x-ray before changing therapy
questions.why: SpO₂ cannot detect carboxyhemoglobin saturations in suspected smoke inhalation victims. Place the patient in the highest possible FiO₂ — usually a nonrebreather mask — and perform a CO-oximetry test. Consider hyperbaric oxygen therapy if available.

questions.stem: A chest x-ray shows atelectasis in a patient receiving a high FiO₂. The likely cause and correction are:
opts: Nitrogen-washout atelectasis — use the lowest possible FiO₂ and implement alveolar recruitment techniques
Secretion plugging — increase suctioning frequency
Overhydration — begin diuretics
Air trapping — decrease the I:E ratio
questions.why: Signs of atelectasis on chest x-ray in a patient receiving a high FiO₂ suggest nitrogen-washout atelectasis. Use the lowest possible FiO₂ and implement alveolar recruitment techniques.

questions.stem: An air-entrainment aerosol mask is delivering a HIGHER FiO₂ than set. Likely causes include:
opts: Obstruction of the entrainment ports by bedding or clothing, or condensate rainout in the tubing
Insufficient input flow from the flowmeter
A leak in the aerosol tubing
A patient with a high minute ventilation
questions.why: An air-entrainment aerosol mask delivering a higher FiO₂ than set is caused by obstruction of the entrainment ports with bedding, clothing, or other items — remove obstructions and monitor the patient — or obstruction from condensate rainout in the tubing, for which a water trap is recommended.

questions.stem: A physician orders a nonrebreathing mask for a code blue patient in respiratory arrest. You should:
opts: Immediately recommend a bag-valve-mask, because nonrebreathing masks do not provide ventilation
Apply the nonrebreathing mask at 15 L/min as ordered
Apply a high-flow nasal cannula at 40 L/min
Apply CPAP at 10 cm H₂O
questions.why: Nonrebreathing masks do not provide additional ventilation. Immediately recommend a bag-valve-mask that can provide 100% O₂ and can be used to ventilate the patient effectively.

questions.stem: A patient with a high or unstable minute ventilation on a nasal cannula at 2 L/min requires an FiO₂ of 0.28. You should recommend:
opts: A high-flow device such as a 28% air-entrainment mask, which meets inspiratory flow needs and maintains a stable FiO₂
Increasing the cannula to 4 L/min
Adding a bubble humidifier to the cannula
A partial rebreathing mask at 8 L/min
questions.why: A standard nasal cannula is not suitable for patients with high or variable minute volume. Recommend a high-flow device such as a 28% air-entrainment mask, which can meet the patient's inspiratory flow needs and maintain a stable FiO₂.

questions.stem: A patient on a 40% air-entrainment system has an SpO₂ of 89%. Possible causes and fixes include:
opts: Insufficient FiO₂ — raise it; or insufficient device flow — add a second nebulizer in tandem or bleed in supplemental O₂
Excessive flow — reduce the flowmeter setting
Too much humidity — remove the nebulizer
Obstructed entrainment ports — the FiO₂ is too high
questions.why: An SpO₂ of 89% on a 40% air-entrainment system reflects either insufficient FiO₂ to correct the hypoxemia — increase it and monitor closely — or insufficient device flow to meet inspiratory demand and maintain a stable FiO₂, for which you add a second aerosol nebulizer in tandem or bleed in supplemental O₂ to increase total output flow.

questions.stem: A patient develops mild stridor after extubation. The cause and recommendation are:
opts: Subglottic tissue edema from the ETT cuff — provide cool aerosol therapy via an aerosol mask
Retained secretions — increase suctioning
Bronchospasm — give a bronchodilator
Pulmonary edema — apply CPAP
questions.why: Mild stridor after extubation is caused by subglottic tissue edema from the endotracheal tube cuff. Provide cool aerosol therapy via an aerosol mask.

questions.stem: An infant's SpO₂ on nasal-prong CPAP drops during episodes of crying. You should:
opts: Collaborate with the nurse to address reasons for crying; if it continues, consider an enclosure such as an oxyhood at the same FiO₂
Immediately increase the CPAP pressure
Sedate the infant
Switch to a nasal cannula at the same flow
questions.why: The SpO₂ drop reflects a decrease in FiO₂ due to mouth breathing associated with crying. Collaborate with the nurse to address reasons for crying such as hunger. If crying and the SpO₂ decrease continue, consider an enclosure such as an oxyhood with the same FiO₂.

questions.stem: For acute airway obstruction associated with asthma, the recommended drug therapy is:
opts: A short-acting β-agonist such as albuterol, considering continuous nebulization and systemic steroids such as prednisone
A long-acting β-agonist alone
A leukotriene inhibitor such as montelukast
A mast-cell stabilizer such as cromolyn sodium
questions.why: For acute airway obstruction associated with asthma or a similar condition — the reliever scenario — recommend a short-acting β-agonist such as albuterol, and consider continuous nebulization and systemic steroids such as prednisone. LABAs, leukotriene inhibitors, and mast-cell stabilizers are controllers for long-term management.

questions.stem: A patient with cystic fibrosis has retained, thick, tenacious secretions. Appropriate recommendations include:
opts: Acetylcysteine, dornase alpha, or hypertonic saline 3–7%
A long-acting anticholinergic
A leukotriene inhibitor
An inhaled corticosteroid alone
questions.why: For retained, thick or tenacious secretions, recommend acetylcysteine (Mucomyst), dornase alpha (Pulmozyme), or hypertonic saline 3–7% (Hypersal) if cystic fibrosis or bronchiectasis is present. An aerosolized treatment with 3–10% hypertonic saline is used to increase the volume of a sputum specimen.

questions.stem: A postoperative patient on incentive spirometry can now achieve an inspiratory capacity at or near predicted and has a clear chest x-ray. You should:
opts: Discontinue the therapy, because the goals of therapy have been achieved
Continue for another 48 hours as a precaution
Switch to IPPB to maintain the gains
Increase the frequency to consolidate the improvement
questions.why: The RT should terminate or recommend discontinuing therapy when the goals or objectives of the therapy have been achieved. If a post-op patient receiving incentive spirometry can achieve an inspiratory capacity at or near predicted and the chest x-ray is clear, the therapy is no longer needed and should be discontinued.

questions.stem: Which research design provides the STRONGEST evidence?
opts: A meta-analysis
A randomized controlled trial
A cohort study
An expert panel report
questions.why: The research hierarchy places the strongest evidence at the top. A meta-analysis thoroughly examines several valid studies on a topic and mathematically combines the results using accepted statistical methodology, reporting them as if one large study. Below it come systematic reviews, RCTs, cohort studies, case-control studies, and expert panels.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes a cohort study?
opts: It identifies patients already undergoing a treatment or exposure, follows them forward, and compares outcomes with a similar unaffected group
It compares patients who already have a condition with people who do not, looking back for associated factors
It introduces a treatment to study its effect on real patients
It mathematically combines several valid studies into one large result
questions.why: Cohort studies identify a group of patients already undergoing a particular treatment or exposure, follow them forward over time, and compare their outcomes with a similar group not affected. They are observational and not as reliable as RCTs because the two groups may differ in ways other than the variable under study.

questions.stem: Why are case-control studies generally less reliable than RCTs and cohort studies?
opts: They rely on medical records and patient recall, and showing a statistical relationship does not mean one factor caused the other
They cannot include a control group
They are always too small to reach significance
They are conducted only by expert panels
questions.why: Case-control studies compare patients who already have a specific condition with people who do not, looking back to identify associated factors or exposures. They often rely on medical records and patient recall for data collection, and are less reliable than RCTs and cohort studies because showing a statistical relationship does not mean that one factor necessarily caused the other.

questions.stem: What limits the value of expert panel reports as evidence?
opts: Subjectivity in defining who the actual experts are, and potential biases
They cannot address clinical topics
They are never published in peer-reviewed form
They require randomization that is rarely feasible
questions.why: Expert panels report the professional opinion of a group of recognized experts in a particular clinical area. Although potentially useful, the subjectivity associated with defining who the actual experts are, and potential biases, limit their value.

questions.stem: Which set of findings indicates that the ARDSNet protocol should be considered?
opts: P/F ratio < 300, bilateral diffuse infiltrates consistent with pulmonary edema, and no clinical evidence of left atrial hypertension or LV failure
P/F ratio < 200 with unilateral infiltrates and elevated PAWP
Any patient requiring an FiO₂ above 0.50
Bilateral infiltrates with clinical evidence of left ventricular failure
questions.why: Consider implementing the ARDSNet protocol for any patient with an acute onset of respiratory failure who has a P/F ratio below 300, bilateral diffuse infiltrates on x-ray consistent with pulmonary edema, and no clinical evidence of left atrial hypertension or left ventricular failure.

questions.stem: Under NAEPP EPR-3 guidelines, how often should lung function be measured by spirometry in a patient with asthma?
opts: At least every 1–2 years, and more frequently if asthma is not well controlled
Only at the initial diagnostic visit
Every 5 years
At every visit without exception
questions.why: Obtain lung function measured by spirometry at least every 1–2 years, and more frequently for asthma that is not well controlled. At each visit assess asthma control, medication technique, the written asthma action plan, adherence, and patient concerns.

questions.stem: Under the ARDSNet protocol, the initial tidal volume is set at what value, and how is it reduced?
opts: 8 mL/kg PBW initially, reduced by 1 mL/kg at intervals ≤ 2 hours until 6 mL/kg PBW
6 mL/kg PBW initially, increased to 8 mL/kg if tolerated
10 mL/kg PBW initially, reduced by 2 mL/kg every 4 hours
4 mL/kg PBW initially, held constant
questions.why: Calculate PBW, select any mode while trying to ensure an I:E of 1:1 or less, set the initial VT to 8 mL/kg PBW, then reduce VT by 1 mL/kg at intervals of 2 hours or less until VT equals 6 mL/kg PBW.

questions.stem: The ARDSNet oxygenation goal is to maintain:
opts: PaO₂ between 55 and 80 torr or SpO₂ between 88% and 95%, using PEEP of at least 5–8 cm H₂O
PaO₂ between 80 and 100 torr or SpO₂ above 95%
PaO₂ above 100 torr with PEEP of at least 10 cm H₂O
SpO₂ above 98% on the lowest possible FiO₂
questions.why: To ensure adequate oxygenation the goal is to maintain a PaO₂ between 55 and 80 torr or an SpO₂ between 88% and 95%. To achieve these targets, PEEP levels of at least 5–8 cm H₂O should be used, with incremental FiO₂/PEEP combinations applied from the protocol table.

questions.stem: Under ARDSNet, a patient's plateau pressure is 34 cm H₂O on a VT of 6 mL/kg PBW. You should:
opts: Decrease VT in 1-mL/kg steps to a minimum of 4 mL/kg
Increase VT by 1 mL/kg
Leave VT unchanged and increase PEEP
Increase the rate to 35/min
questions.why: Keep the plateau pressure at 30 cm H₂O or less, measuring it every 4 hours and after each change in PEEP or VT. If Pplat exceeds 30 cm H₂O, decrease VT in 1-mL/kg steps to a minimum of 4 mL/kg.

questions.stem: Under ARDSNet, a patient's plateau pressure is 22 cm H₂O on a VT of 5 mL/kg PBW. You should:
opts: Increase VT by 1 mL/kg until Pplat exceeds 25 cm H₂O or VT reaches 6 mL/kg
Decrease VT by 1 mL/kg
Leave the settings unchanged
Decrease PEEP by 2 cm H₂O
questions.why: If Pplat is below 25 cm H₂O and VT is below 6 mL/kg, increase VT by 1 mL/kg until Pplat exceeds 25 cm H₂O or VT reaches 6 mL/kg.

questions.stem: Under ARDSNet, breath stacking and dyssynchrony occur while Pplat is 27 cm H₂O. You may:
opts: Consider increasing VT in 1-mL/kg steps to 7–8 mL/kg, provided Pplat remains below 30 cm H₂O
Decrease VT to 4 mL/kg immediately
Paralyze the patient and leave VT unchanged
Increase PEEP to 15 cm H₂O
questions.why: If Pplat is below 30 cm H₂O and breath stacking or dyssynchrony occurs, consider increasing VT in 1-mL/kg steps to 7–8 mL/kg as long as Pplat remains below 30 cm H₂O.

questions.stem: Under ARDSNet, the acid-base goal is to keep the pH between:
questions.why: In terms of acid-base balance, the ARDSNet goal is to keep the pH between 7.30 and 7.45. If the pH rises above 7.45, which is rare, decrease the ventilator rate.

questions.stem: Under ARDSNet, a patient's pH is 7.22. You should:
opts: Increase the rate until pH exceeds 7.30 or PaCO₂ falls below 25, to a maximum rate of 35/min
Increase the rate directly to 35/min
Increase VT in 1-mL/kg steps immediately
Administer sodium bicarbonate before any rate change
questions.why: If the pH is above 7.15 but below 7.30, increase the rate until the pH exceeds 7.30 or the PaCO₂ falls below 25, with a maximum rate of 35/min. If the pH is below 7.15, increase the rate to 35/min; and if the rate is already 35/min with a pH below 7.15, increase VT in 1-mL/kg steps until pH exceeds 7.15 — the Pplat target may be exceeded — and consider sodium bicarbonate.

questions.stem: Which set of criteria indicates readiness for a spontaneous breathing trial under the NHLBI ARDS protocol?
opts: FiO₂ ≤ 0.40 and PEEP ≤ 8, or FiO₂ ≤ 0.50 and PEEP ≤ 5; settings no higher than the previous day; acceptable spontaneous efforts; systolic BP ≥ 90 without vasopressors; no neuromuscular blockade
FiO₂ ≤ 0.60 and PEEP ≤ 10, with any blood pressure
Any patient breathing spontaneously for 24 hours
FiO₂ ≤ 0.21 with no PEEP and a normal chest x-ray
questions.why: Readiness criteria are FiO₂ of 0.40 or less with PEEP of 8 cm H₂O or less, or FiO₂ of 0.50 or less with PEEP of 5 cm H₂O or less; PEEP and FiO₂ no higher than the previous day's settings; acceptable spontaneous breathing efforts, detected by reducing the vent rate by 50% for 5 minutes; systolic BP of 90 mm Hg or more without vasopressors; and no neuromuscular blocking agents or blockade.

questions.stem: During an ARDS-protocol spontaneous breathing trial, which finding indicates the trial should be STOPPED?
opts: Two or more of: HR > 120% of baseline, marked accessory muscle use, abdominal paradox, diaphoresis, marked dyspnea
A spontaneous VT of 5 mL/kg PBW
A respiratory rate of 30/min
A pH of 7.34
questions.why: The trial is tolerated when SpO₂ is 90% or more with PaO₂ of 60 mm Hg or more, spontaneous VT is at least 4 mL/kg PBW, respiratory rate is 35/min or less, pH is 7.30 or more, and there is no respiratory distress. Distress is defined as two or more of: HR above 120% of baseline, marked accessory muscle use, abdominal paradox, diaphoresis, and marked dyspnea.

questions.stem: A patient tolerates the ARDS-protocol spontaneous breathing trial for 35 minutes. You should:
opts: Consider extubation
Continue the trial for a full 4 hours
Resume pre-weaning settings and retry tomorrow
Reduce PEEP to 3 cm H₂O and continue
questions.why: The trial is conducted on a T-piece, trach collar, or CPAP of 5 cm H₂O or less with PS below 5 cm H₂O. If tolerated for at least 30 minutes, consider extubation. If not tolerated, resume pre-weaning settings.

questions.stem: Under NAEPP guidelines, a patient using a short-acting β-agonist more than 2 days per week (other than for exercise-induced asthma) indicates:
opts: The patient may need to start or increase long-term control medications
The SABA dose should be doubled
The patient is well controlled
Long-term control medication should be discontinued
questions.why: Quick-relief medications (SABAs) relax airway muscles for fast symptom relief but do not provide long-term control. If used more than 2 days per week — except as needed for exercise-induced asthma — the patient may need to start or increase long-term control medications. Inhaled corticosteroids are the most effective long-term control therapy.

questions.stem: Why is frequent or chronic use of a LABA to prevent exercise-induced bronchospasm discouraged?
opts: It may disguise poorly controlled persistent asthma
It causes tolerance to short-acting agents within days
It has no protective effect against EIB
It is contraindicated during physical activity
questions.why: Teach patients to take treatment before exercise; SABAs prevent EIB in most patients, and leukotriene receptor antagonists, cromolyn, or LABAs are also protective. However, frequent or chronic use of LABAs to prevent EIB is discouraged because it may disguise poorly controlled persistent asthma. EIB is often a marker of inadequate asthma control and responds well to regular anti-inflammatory therapy.

questions.stem: The key steps in basic life support now follow which sequence?
opts: CABD — circulation, airway, breathing, defibrillation
ABCD — airway, breathing, circulation, defibrillation
DABC — defibrillation, airway, breathing, circulation
BACD — breathing, airway, circulation, defibrillation
questions.why: The key steps in BLS now follow a CABD sequence, standing for circulation–airway–breathing–defibrillation. The NBRC exam counts on your current BLS certification to apply this knowledge to any patient scenario requiring basic life support.

questions.stem: The four cardiac dysrhythmias producing pulselessness in adults are:
opts: Ventricular fibrillation, ventricular tachycardia, pulseless electrical activity, and asystole
Atrial fibrillation, atrial flutter, heart block, and asystole
Sinus bradycardia, sinus tachycardia, PVCs, and PACs
Ventricular fibrillation, atrial fibrillation, asystole, and first-degree block
questions.why: The most common adult cardiopulmonary emergencies stem from one of four cardiac dysrhythmias that produce pulselessness: ventricular fibrillation, ventricular tachycardia, pulseless electrical activity, and asystole.

questions.stem: The initial adult IV dose of epinephrine during cardiac arrest is:
opts: 1 mg every 3–5 minutes with flush
0.5 mg every 3–5 minutes up to 3 mg/kg
300 mg rapid infusion
questions.why: Epinephrine is given as 1 mg every 3–5 minutes with flush; it is a vasoconstrictor that may improve cerebral perfusion. Atropine is 0.5 mg every 3–5 minutes up to a maximum of 3 mg/kg, amiodarone is 300 mg rapid infusion, and lidocaine is 1.0–1.5 mg/kg initially.

questions.stem: When an ACLS medication must be instilled via endotracheal tube because IV/IO access is unavailable, you should:
opts: Double the dose and follow with 10 mL of normal saline
Halve the dose and follow with 5 mL of sterile water
Use the same dose with no flush
Dilute the dose in 50 mL of saline
questions.why: Certain medications — epinephrine, atropine, and lidocaine — may be instilled via ETT if IV or IO access is not established. In such cases it is recommended that the dose be doubled and followed with the instillation of 10 mL of normal saline.

questions.stem: The initial biphasic defibrillation dose for an ADULT is:
opts: 120–200 J, or as recommended by the manufacturer
2 J/kg
4 J/kg
questions.why: For biphasic defibrillators, the initial adult dose is 120–200 J or as recommended by the manufacturer, with subsequent doses the same (higher energy levels may be considered). For children the initial dose is 2 J/kg with subsequent doses of at least 4 J/kg. For older monophasic devices, apply 360 J to adults and 2 J/kg to children.

questions.stem: For preterm newborns less than 35 weeks' gestation, resuscitation should begin with:
opts: Low O₂ of 21–30%, titrated to targeted preductal SpO₂ ranges
100% O₂ until the heart rate normalizes
60% O₂ regardless of gestational age
Room air with no titration
questions.why: Babies who are flaccid, cyanotic, or apneic in the delivery room usually require stimulation and supplemental O₂. For preterm newborns under 35 weeks of gestation, low O₂ of 21–30% should be used and titrated to achieve preductal SpO₂ ranges from the protocol table.

questions.stem: During CPR the PetCO₂ is 8 mm Hg and the intra-arterial diastolic pressure is 16 mm Hg. This indicates:
opts: The quality of CPR should be improved
Return of spontaneous circulation has occurred
Resuscitation should be terminated immediately
Ventilation is excessive and should be reduced
questions.why: Capnography is recommended as a standard of care during resuscitation because it assesses both the adequacy of ventilation and the effectiveness of cardiac compressions. If the PetCO₂ is less than 10 mm Hg and the intra-arterial diastolic pressure is less than 20 mm Hg, the quality of CPR should be improved.

questions.stem: Which capnography finding can be used as an indicator to terminate resuscitative efforts?
opts: Failure to achieve a PetCO₂ greater than 10 mm Hg after 20 minutes of CPR
A PetCO₂ above 40 mm Hg at any point
Any PetCO₂ reading below 35 mm Hg
A PetCO₂ that rises suddenly during compressions
questions.why: Failure to achieve a PetCO₂ greater than 10 mm Hg after 20 minutes of CPR can be used as an indicator to terminate resuscitative efforts. A sudden rise in PetCO₂ instead suggests return of spontaneous circulation.

questions.stem: Which set represents the "5 Hs" of reversible causes of cardiac arrest?
opts: Hypovolemia, hypoxia, hydrogen ion (acidosis), hypo-/hyperkalemia, hypothermia
Hypertension, hypoxia, hyperglycemia, hypothermia, hemorrhage
Hypovolemia, hypercapnia, hyperthermia, hypoglycemia, hemothorax
Hypoxia, hypotension, hyperkalemia, hepatic failure, hypothermia
questions.why: The 5 Hs are hypovolemia, hypoxia, hydrogen ion (acidosis), hypo- or hyperkalemia, and hypothermia. The 5 Ts are tension pneumothorax, cardiac tamponade, toxins, pulmonary thrombosis, and cardiac thrombosis.

questions.stem: Which set represents the "5 Ts" of reversible causes of cardiac arrest?
opts: Tension pneumothorax, cardiac tamponade, toxins, pulmonary thrombosis, cardiac thrombosis
Tachycardia, tamponade, trauma, toxins, thrombosis
Tension pneumothorax, tracheal obstruction, trauma, toxins, thyrotoxicosis
Tamponade, thrombosis, tachyarrhythmia, tension pneumothorax, transfusion reaction
questions.why: The 5 Ts are tension pneumothorax, cardiac tamponade, toxins such as drug overdose and anaphylactic reactions, pulmonary thrombosis (pulmonary emboli), and cardiac thrombosis (myocardial infarction or ischemia).

questions.stem: If color, heart rate, and breathing are not restored within 30 seconds after birth, you should:
opts: Provide manual positive-pressure ventilation via face mask, with PEEP of 5 cm H₂O or less
Begin chest compressions immediately
Administer epinephrine and intubate
Continue stimulation for another 60 seconds
questions.why: If color, heart rate, and breathing are not restored within 30 seconds after birth, provide manual positive-pressure ventilation via face mask. PPV is the most effective intervention in the delivery room for improving outcomes, and can be delivered with a flow-inflating bag, self-inflating bag, or T-piece resuscitator. A PEEP of 5 cm H₂O or less is always recommended.

questions.stem: A neonate's heart rate is 52/min despite effective positive-pressure ventilation. You should:
opts: Begin chest compressions, because a heart rate below 60 always requires them in a neonate
Continue PPV alone and reassess in 60 seconds
Administer epinephrine before compressions
Intubate before starting compressions
questions.why: A heart rate of less than 60 always requires chest compressions in a neonate. If the infant does not respond to these measures, epinephrine should be administered and intubation with mechanical ventilation considered.

questions.stem: At 5 minutes after birth, the targeted preductal SpO₂ is:
questions.why: Targeted preductal SpO₂ after birth rises over time: 60–65% at 1 minute, 65–70% at 2 minutes, 70–75% at 3 minutes, 75–80% at 4 minutes, 80–85% at 5 minutes, and 85–95% at 10 minutes.

questions.stem: Which findings distinguish COMPLETE from partial airway obstruction?
opts: Absence of air movement and breath sounds, the universal choking sign, and inability to talk or cough while conscious
Sonorous breathing, stridor, or wheezing with some air movement
Choking, drooling, or gagging with accessory muscle use
Anxiety and agitation with retractions
questions.why: Complete airway obstruction shows absence of air movement and breath sounds, severe anxiety and agitation while conscious, the universal choking sign, inability to talk or cough, accessory muscle use, retractions or paradoxical breathing, and eventual lethargy, cyanosis, and unconsciousness. Partial obstruction still has some air movement with sonorous breathing, stridor, or wheezing, plus choking, drooling, or gagging.

questions.stem: How does the PALS pulseless arrest algorithm differ from the adult algorithm?
opts: The defibrillation shock and medication dosages vary by patient weight
Defibrillation is not used in children
Epinephrine is omitted entirely
Compressions are not performed until an airway is secured
questions.why: The PALS algorithm for pulseless arrest is similar to the adult algorithm, with the exception that the defibrillation shock and medication dosages vary by patient weight. One of the most common pediatric emergencies is airway obstruction by a foreign body.

questions.stem: What is the ONLY absolute contraindication to endotracheal intubation?
opts: A documented DNR/DNI order
Severe airway trauma or obstruction
Head/neck injury requiring cervical spine immobilization
A Mallampati Class 4 airway
questions.why: Primary indications for ET intubation include respiratory or cardiac arrest, airway compromise and protection, and invasive ventilatory support. The only absolute contraindication against intubation is a documented do-not-resuscitate/do-not-intubate order. Severe airway trauma, cervical immobilization needs, and a Mallampati Class 4 airway are relative concerns.

questions.stem: A difficult airway protocol is meant to guide action whenever a trained professional cannot insert an ETT using conventional laryngoscopy in how many attempts?
opts: Three or fewer
One
Five
Ten
questions.why: Difficult airway protocols vary by institution but are all meant to guide action whenever a trained professional experiences difficulty with mask ventilation or cannot quickly insert an ETT using conventional laryngoscopy in three or fewer attempts.

questions.stem: Which device is generally the FIRST option for establishing an airway if endotracheal intubation fails?
opts: A supraglottic airway such as an LMA, Combitube, or cuffed oropharyngeal airway
A percutaneous cricothyrotomy kit
A retrograde intubation kit
A lighted stylet
questions.why: A supraglottic airway — LMA, Combitube, or cuffed oropharyngeal airway — is generally the first option in establishing an airway if ET intubation fails. It can be inserted with the head and neck in a neutral position, but is contraindicated if there is a high risk of aspiration.

questions.stem: Before assisting with any procedure, the RT should:
opts: Verify and evaluate the order or protocol, review the record for contraindications and consent, wash hands and apply precautions, gather equipment, identify the patient, and take a time-out if appropriate
Gather equipment and begin immediately to avoid delay
Wait for the physician to review the chart
Document the procedure in advance
questions.why: Before each procedure: verify, interpret, and evaluate the physician's order or protocol; review the medical record for contraindications, hazards, and informed consent if appropriate; wash hands and apply standard transmission-based precautions; gather all equipment; identify the patient; and take a pre-procedure time-out if appropriate, as for bronchoscopy.

questions.stem: Before intubation, the RT should prepare the ETT cuff by:
opts: Inflating it, checking for leaks, then fully deflating it
Inflating it to 25 cm H₂O and leaving it inflated
Leaving it untouched until after insertion
Filling it with sterile water
questions.why: Among the RT's pre-procedure duties is to inflate the ETT cuff, check it for leaks, then fully deflate it — confirming cuff integrity and preparing the tube for insertion.

questions.stem: During intubation, why should dentures or dental appliances be removed beforehand?
opts: To facilitate laryngoscopy and avoid aspiration of the appliances
To improve mask seal during BVM ventilation
To allow accurate capnography readings
To prevent damage to the laryngoscope blade
questions.why: Remove dentures or dental appliances such as bridges if present, in order to facilitate laryngoscopy and avoid aspiration of the appliances.

questions.stem: After three unsuccessful intubation attempts, the RT should:
opts: Recommend proceeding with the institution's difficult airway protocol
Attempt intubation personally
Place the patient on a nonrebreathing mask and wait
Increase the sedation and reattempt
questions.why: If three unsuccessful intubation attempts occur, recommend proceeding with the difficult airway protocol, which varies by institution — this ensures patient safety.

questions.stem: After intubation, the RT's responsibilities include:
opts: Noting and marking the ETT insertion depth, securing the tube, ensuring a chest x-ray is obtained, reassessing the patient, and verifying documentation
Leaving the tube unsecured until x-ray confirmation
Waiting 4 hours before reassessing the patient
Documenting only the ventilator settings
questions.why: After the procedure: note and mark the ETT insertion depth and secure it; ensure a chest x-ray is obtained and the tube repositioned as needed; reassess the patient's clinical status; suction if necessary; ensure appropriate humidification, ventilation, and oxygenation; and verify that intubation and follow-up orders have been documented in the chart.

questions.stem: To block the gag reflex in a conscious patient during intubation, you may:
opts: Spray the pharynx with a local anesthetic such as 2% tetracaine, or nebulize 4% lidocaine via SVN for elective intubation
Administer a neuromuscular blocking agent without sedation
Apply cricoid pressure alone
Hyperventilate the patient with 100% O₂ only
questions.why: Once the patient is positioned, clear secretions or vomitus from the pharynx with a Yankauer suction catheter. Spraying the pharynx with a local anesthetic such as 2% tetracaine (Cetacaine) aids intubation in conscious patients by blocking the gag reflex, and for elective intubation you can nebulize a 4% lidocaine solution via a small-volume nebulizer.

questions.stem: How is the position of a gum elastic bougie confirmed?
opts: Visually, or by a "clicking" feel as the tip moves over the tracheal rings
By a midline glow below the thyroid cartilage
By aspirating air with a syringe
By auscultating the epigastrium
questions.why: A gum elastic bougie or ventilating tracheal tube introducer is a long, narrow, flexible plastic rod with an angled tip inserted via laryngoscopy into the trachea. Its position is confirmed visually or via a clicking feel as the tip moves over the tracheal rings. The ETT is then inserted over the introducer, which is withdrawn. A midline glow below the thyroid cartilage instead confirms a lighted stylet.

questions.stem: Percutaneous cricothyrotomy generally requires that the patient be at least what age?
opts: 5 years old
12 years old
1 year old
18 years old
questions.why: A percutaneous cricothyrotomy kit punctures the cricothyroid membrane and dilates the opening until it is large enough to place an ETT or trach tube. Patients generally must be at least 5 years old.

questions.stem: Why is jet ventilation the surgical airway of choice for children younger than 12 years?
opts: Their small tracheal diameter makes cricothyrotomy hazardous
It requires no oxygen source
It provides better humidification
It does not require a 50-psi gas source
questions.why: A jet ventilation setup provides manually triggered ventilation with 100% O₂ via a ventilating stylet inserted orally or a 13- to 14-gauge angiocath inserted percutaneously into the trachea. It is the surgical airway of choice for children younger than 12 years due to their small tracheal diameter and the resulting hazard of cricothyrotomy.

questions.stem: Educational sessions should be limited to approximately what duration to avoid information overload?
opts: About 1 hour or less
About 3 hours
About 15 minutes
There is no recommended limit
questions.why: Limit educational sessions to about 1 hour or less to avoid information overload. Thoroughly demonstrate all procedures and equipment and request a return demonstration.

questions.stem: Which water should be used in nebulizers versus humidifiers in the home?
opts: Sterile water in nebulizers; distilled water is acceptable for humidifiers
Tap water is acceptable for both
Distilled water in nebulizers; tap water for humidifiers
Sterile water for both, with no exceptions
questions.why: Sterile water should be used in nebulizers; distilled water is acceptable for humidifiers. Noncritical reusable items such as blood pressure cuffs can be cleaned with a detergent.

questions.stem: Before disinfection, reusable semicritical items such as nebulizers and breathing circuits should be:
opts: Scrubbed with detergent to remove organic material, thoroughly washed, rinsed, and allowed to air-dry
Soaked directly in a high-level disinfectant without cleaning
Wiped with alcohol and reused immediately
Autoclaved after every use
questions.why: Before disinfection, all reusable semicritical objects — such as nebulizers, breathing circuits, and tracheal airway components — should be scrubbed with detergent to remove organic material, then thoroughly washed, rinsed, and allowed to air-dry.

questions.stem: When teaching a patient who may have limited literacy, you should:
opts: Leave printed "EZ read" information with pictures if possible
Provide a detailed written manual only
Rely entirely on verbal instruction with no materials
Ask a family member to read the materials aloud later
questions.why: Remember that not all patients have the same cognitive abilities or literacy — some may read only at an elementary level or be unable to read at all. Leave printed EZ read information, with pictures if possible, about the procedures and equipment.

questions.stem: When educating a patient with a hearing impairment, you should:
opts: Speak clearly at an appropriate volume, allow for lip reading, and ensure hearing aids are in place
Speak as loudly as possible and avoid written materials
Rely solely on printed instructions
Use an interpreter for all hearing-impaired patients
questions.why: For hearing-impaired patients, speak clearly and at an appropriate volume so they can hear you. Keep in mind that some patients might be reading your lips to some degree, and those with hearing aids should have them in during instruction. For visual difficulties, use larger print, easy-to-distinguish fonts, and contrasting colors.

questions.stem: Why does teaching alone often fail to change patient behavior?
opts: Knowledge does not always change behavior; motivation, perceived benefit, and removal of barriers are key to compliance
Patients rarely retain any information from teaching
Written materials are always more effective than demonstration
Compliance depends only on the physician's instructions
questions.why: Remember that knowledge does not always change behavior. Motivation, perceived level of benefit, and removal of barriers — physical, financial, past experiences, misconceptions — are key factors in getting patients to comply with medications, therapies, or smoking cessation.

questions.stem: A homecare patient on oxygen continues to smoke. You should educate them to:
opts: Not smoke while wearing oxygen and not cook over an open flame while wearing oxygen
Smoke only in a well-ventilated room while wearing oxygen
Reduce the oxygen flow by half before smoking
Remove the cannula for 30 seconds before smoking
questions.why: Use no-smoking zones and signage and remove potential ignition sources such as cigarette lighters. While cessation is preferable, for those who continue to smoke, educate them not to smoke while wearing oxygen, and not to cook over an open flame while wearing oxygen.

questions.stem: In the hospital, life-support equipment should be connected to:
opts: Only "red" or emergency outlets with a backup power supply
Any available grounded outlet
A portable power strip
An outlet shared with monitoring equipment
questions.why: For electrical failure risk, in the hospital use only red or emergency outlets with a backup power supply. In home care, ensure the outlet is functioning and grounded and that the circuit amperage is adequate for the equipment being used.

questions.stem: When instructing a patient on safe ambulation and lifting technique, you should teach them to:
opts: Exhale on exertion, plan the course around obstacles, choose a ramp instead of stairs, rest as needed, and bend at the knees rather than the waist
Hold the breath during exertion to stabilize the trunk
Take the shortest route regardless of obstacles
Bend at the waist to conserve leg strength
questions.why: Teach the patient to exhale on exertion — for example when going up a step — plan the course such as going around obstacles rather than over them, choose a ramp instead of stairs, stop and rest if needed, and bend at the knees instead of the waist when picking something up. Caregivers should maintain a straight spine, lift with the legs, and use a lift assist device.
